entities/henry-clay.title: Henry Clay (1777–1852)
entities/henry-clay.content:
Henry Clay
Henry Clay (1777–1852) — Speaker, Kentucky senator, Secretary of State, and perennial presidential aspirant — was the Western architect of war, compromise, and the protective “American System.” Contemporaries credited him (with Monroe in the Cabinet) with making the declaration of 1812 obtainable in Congress; at Ghent he fought for Mississippi equivalents against British fisheries claims; later Adams took Clay’s House support in 1825 and made him Secretary of State — the act that Jackson’s friends named a corrupt bargain. That charge became a people’s slogan; Clay’s tariff years run in a sequence from 1816 through the compromise of 1833. The last great act was the Omnibus of 1850, its Senate defeat, and the separate-bills sequel Clay did not live to dominate.
War Speaker and Ghent
Except for the exertions of two men — Monroe in the Cabinet and Clay in Congress — contemporaries held that the declaration of 1812 could not have been obtained. The war was fought under broken finances after the First Bank’s expiration, closed honorably, and made a proud era: Clay’s early identity is already that of the War Hawk Speaker who later appears in 1814 laying Edwards’s A.B. charges before the House.
At Ghent he sat among the American commissioners with Adams, Gallatin, Bayard, and Russell. August 1814 brought the British commissioners, the American refusal to meet on British terms of lodging as a pretension of superiority, and the exchange of powers at the Hôtel des Pays-Bas. Negotiation turned on Indian trade, Mississippi navigation, and fisheries: Clay pressed Western and Mississippi interests against any sacrifice for Atlantic fisheries stipulations; Gallatin sided with Adams on navigation as equivalent. The treaty was signed on Christmas Eve 1814; Christmas Day sealed copies under agreed secrecy; Adams left Ghent in January 1815 after more than seven months he called the most memorable period of his life. The Clay of Ghent is already the Western bargain-maker — not yet the presidential candidate, but already the man who would sell compromise as statesmanship.
American System and the tariff of 1824
The successive tariffs of 1816, 1824, 1828, and the compromise of 1833 form one commercial-policy arc: protection places “loom and anvil beside plough and harrow,” tested by consumption over long periods. The act of 1816 appears as a planters’ and farmers’ measure; 1828 as the first really protective tariff after the low-duty years. For the session of 1823–24 the revision’s object was the protection of home industry — the “American System” — with protection the object and revenue the incident, reversing earlier practice. Webster led New England opposition; Van Buren warned manufacturers not to tie themselves to one party; Monroe approved the bill without denying its revenue character. Clay’s name thereafter attached to the programme. By 1828 the high tariff stood as the origin of nullification doctrine — woolens expanded by log-rolling into lead, hemp, and the rest — and Democratic members who voted it intended to repudiate the system after Jackson’s victory. In 1832 Clay still told the Senate that the protective system was an “overruling necessity” for other sections and that the danger was abandonment, not continuation.
1824–25 and the Secretaryship
The electoral college of 1824 gave Jackson 99, Adams 84, Crawford 41, Clay 37 — no majority of 131. Clay, fourth and out of the House ballot, led Kentucky and other Western friends to Adams; on 9 February 1825 the House chose Adams on a single ballot, thirteen States to Jackson’s seven and Crawford’s four. Clay’s friends (Letcher among them) sounded Adams; Adams himself walked “Incedo super ignes”; the offer of the Department of State came on the 10th for “talents and services” and Western confidence; Webster’s committee notified the President-elect. Senate confirmation of Clay as Secretary drew twenty-seven yeas to eighteen nays — Randolph, Hayne, and Macon among the nays; about half the yeas Clay’s political opponents. Jacksonians treated the sequence as a violation of the democratic principle that the plurality man should have prevailed; Clay “took the lead in the House for Mr. Adams,” then tried by public speeches to reconcile the country, and was himself “crippled,” losing his place in the Democratic party and joining the National Republicans who became Whigs. Popular politics named the same story: House elects Adams; charge of a corrupt bargain. The charge followed Clay through the Adams years and into the defeat of 1828, when Jackson and Rush buried Adams and Clay together in the public mind, 178 electoral votes to 83.
Randolph duel, Panama, and the C&O
Panama mission politics — Adams’s effort to reverse the tide of the House election and inaugural doctrines of internal improvement — inflamed Senate and House and led to the duel between Clay and John Randolph of Roanoke. On Saturday 1 April 1826 Randolph came to Benton’s room at Brown’s Hotel, asked whether Benton was blood-kin to Mrs. Clay (Lucretia Hart), and declined Benton as second for that reason; he accepted Clay’s challenge with Col. Tatnall as second and Gen. Jesup for Clay, and told Benton secretly that he did not intend to fire at Clay — wanting a witness, not a second who knew. The provocation Benton traced to Randolph’s Panama speech daring the President and “the bravest of his compeers,” not necessarily a personal “scoundrel” charge. Cards were exchanged after the meeting; Benton ranked it among the last high-toned duels.
Under Adams, Clay as Secretary pressed the Panama mission (eventually sanctioned though it never took effect), urged force to protect Creek rights against Georgia surveyors when Adams preferred civil process, and watched the tariff fights culminating in 1828. The House’s million-dollar Chesapeake and Ohio Canal subscription — five annual installments, majority of forty-four — stood as a practical blessing of internal improvement. May 1828 Cabinet talk already feared an all-northern administration except Clay’s West. The American System, Panama, and canal together defined Clay’s State Department years as much as the bargain charge defined his enemies’ memory of them.
Compromise of 1833 — public settlement and secret history
In the nullification winter Clay’s compromise tariff swept the House — engrossment 105–71, final passage 119–85 — beside the Force Bill’s concurrent struggle. In the Senate Clay introduced the compromise on 12 February 1833 with a speech that the tariff was in imminent danger without change and that its fall would ruin manufacturing capital; the home-valuation amendment passed 26–16 with Clay, Calhoun, and Tyler among the yeas and Benton and Webster among the nays. Webster supported Jackson against nullification despite party opposition.
Secret history of the winter strips the pacificator legend. The Clay–Calhoun coalition of 1833 was a “hollow truce”: Calhoun humiliated by protective features yet kept alive to oppose Jackson and Van Buren. Floor quarrel later had Calhoun claiming he had Clay “on his back,” Clay answering he would not own him for the meanest of his slaves. Inside, via Letcher and Clayton: Josiah S. Johnson of Louisiana’s night visit to Letcher with word that Jackson would brook no delay and that decisive action against Calhoun (arrest for treason understood) was near; Letcher warned Calhoun in bed — “evidently disturbed.” Clayton of Delaware, Benton insisted, was the real architect; Letcher the conduit. Outside, Clay and Calhoun posed as peacemakers; inside, Clay saved protection and manufacturer support, Calhoun escaped Jackson’s coercion, and both freed their hands to reunite against Jackson and Van Buren. He refused to call the act “sacred and inviolable”; unlike the Missouri Compromise of 1820 (mutual consent, geographic line), the 1833 settlement was rivals laying the tariff aside for two presidential elections under patriotic alarm — received as deliverance, soon gone to neglect and oblivion.
Bank War, Whig leadership, and the Tyler rupture
Clay opened the Bank opposition of 1830–31 and stood for recharter against Jackson’s veto of 10 July 1832. The election of that year put Clay and Sergeant against Jackson and Van Buren with Bank and American System on the ballot; Clay took 49 of 288 electoral votes — “complete and overwhelming” defeat. In the panic session after deposit removal he joined Webster and Calhoun in the “great combination” against Jackson. Clay’s speech cast deposit removal as revolution hitherto bloodless, Caesar seizing the treasury, “premonitory symptoms of despotism,” Congress obliged to remedy or leave the nation “base, mean, and abject slaves.” Benton answered that Clay’s resolution was impeachment in substance and a Senate usurpation of the House’s power. Calhoun’s support renewed the mastery quarrel of 1833.
Harrison’s death and Tyler’s accession made the extra session of 1841 dominated by Clay. His programme: repeal of the Independent Treasury first; a national fiscal agent (bank) next — Tyler’s message also asking a bank. Clay personally carried sub-treasury repeal with instant effect and no substitute. The bankrupt act passed by logroll outside his original list. A first bank bill passed the Senate 26–25; Tyler’s qualified veto (1 August) and a second “fiscal corporation” followed by a second veto brought gallery hisses Benton defended as assaults on presidential dignity. Secret history of the rupture has Tyler and Whig dissidents plotting a third party, Tyler leading the second bill knowing he would veto — a “Jonas” to save the new combination. On 11 September the Cabinet resigned (Webster staying briefly); the Whig manifesto of that day declared twelve years’ fruits destroyed by Tyler. Clay remained Whig head; Tyler was later rejected by Democrats too. The quarrel, bank vetoes, and cabinet resignations opened the Tyler revenue and tariff struggles that preceded Texas.
Texas stance
Clay’s Texas weather was more surrounding politics than a single manifesto. The Florida treaty of 1819 had “given away Texas”; southern presidential candidates had accepted the cession to avoid slavery extension — context for later annexation fights. In the 1838 session the Texas republic applied for admission while still at war with Mexico; annexation meant annexing war. Preston of South Carolina’s resolution for a legislative expression toward a tripartite treaty was laid on the table 24–14 — the period not ripe. Clay–Calhoun debates of 1840–41 show the old allies concurred in nothing: Clay mocked Calhoun’s Edgefield letter; Calhoun answered that Clay had not led the tariff of 1816 (Lowndes had Ways and Means) and that Clay’s 1813 speech had opposed non-importation as too much protection. Tyler–Calhoun negotiations, the treaty’s Senate rejection, the election of 1844 as Polk’s platform and the defeat of Clay, and annexation by joint resolution as the mandate for expansion followed. Clay’s public identity in that canvass was the Whig alternative to immediate annexation’s war risk — defeated when the expansion mandate carried Polk and, under Tyler’s final push, Texas itself.
Compromise of 1850 — the Omnibus
Taylor’s only annual message recommended California’s admission if her constitution conformed, and territorial governments for New Mexico and Utah without mixing slavery — let them ripen to statehood and decide themselves. Clay answered with eight resolutions “to settle and close up once and for ever” all slavery contestation in one general compromise, and was placed at the head of a Committee of Thirteen to combine them into a single bill — the Omnibus. Benton opposed the whole plan: incongruous measures tacked together; California degraded by confounding her admission with general slavery agitation; futile; a concession to disunion threats; a repetition of the error of 1833. Settle each measure separately, beginning with California; leave consequences to God and the country; make no compromise with the threat of disunion. The Omnibus was not even a new draft: five old bills from different places on the calendar, tied together and required to be voted as one. Clay made ample report and elaborate speech; Benton answered in a counter-speech.
One Clay resolution declared slavery did not exist by law in the Mexican cession and that it was “inexpedient” for Congress to legislate for or against its introduction, territorial governments for Utah and New Mexico to be established without slavery restriction (California’s boundaries excepted). Jefferson Davis of Mississippi saw no compromise in a measure that gave the South nothing: never less than the Missouri line extended to the Pacific with specific recognition of the right to hold slaves south of that line, and slaves importable from any state before statehood. Clay met it with a declaration Benton called manly and lifelong: he utterly refused to plant slavery where it did not previously exist. Seward’s renewal of the Wilmot proviso failed, 23–33, Clay among the nays.
On 4 March Calhoun’s last speech — too weak to deliver, read by Mason — proclaimed Union or disunion, held Clay’s and Taylor’s plans inadequate, and demanded a constitutional amendment with a dual executive, one slave and one free — equivalent, Benton judged, to dissolution. Calhoun died 31 March; Butler’s eulogy compared him to Chatham. Benton’s own speech against the Omnibus ridiculed the “bill of thirty-nine sections — forty, save one — an ominous number,” denied the country’s “five gaping wounds” Clay counted on his fingers, and denounced giving Texas a veto over California’s admission as a “monstrosity.” He moved indefinite postponement so the bills might be taken one by one.
Taylor’s death on 9 July, after Fourth of July sun exposure, Benton called a public calamity: a Southern slaveholder of Union devotion and military reputation uniquely placed to settle the questions. Fillmore was sworn in the House chamber on the 10th — solemnity without joy — and soon made Webster Secretary of State and Crittenden Attorney General. The Omnibus was rejected: the Committee of Thirteen had reported for Clay’s plan; a committee nearly a quarter of the Senate should have insured concurrence; it did not. Incongruities too glaring for one yea or nay; injustice to California (a free-state applicant) too apparent; no spirit of concession in which giving and taking could make a compromise. Whatever was done would be ordinary majoritarian legislation. The Wilmot proviso was rejected again as unnecessary and irritating — not on non-intervention principle but because there had already been intervention. California’s separate admission followed, with Southern senators’ protest; Gwinn and Frémont took their seats. Clay’s last great design thus failed as Omnibus and succeeded only as the politics of separate bills under Fillmore — the pacificator’s method Benton had opposed since 1833, still naming the struggle.
For this wiki Clay is the attested man of Ghent, bargain, American System, 1833’s double history, Bank War and Tyler rupture, Texas defeat, and the 1850 Omnibus.

entities/james-k-polk.title: James K. Polk (1795–1849)
entities/james-k-polk.content:
James K. Polk
James K. Polk (1795–1849) of Tennessee was the Democratic eleventh President and the expansion executive of the mid-1840s. In one term he closed texas-annexation, settled the Oregon boundary with Britain at the forty-ninth parallel, and waged the mexican-american-war that brought the Mexican cession. Personality sketches are thin in the sources used here; war and territory are dense. No private Polk diary sits in this library. What follows is the administration the deposits attest.
1844 and the rainy inaugural
The Democratic campaign of 1844 made continental expansion the mandate. Polk ran on Texas and a hard line on Oregon; Henry Clay’s caution on annexation helped defeat him. On 4 March 1845, after a dying Congress’s midnight scramble, Polk took the oath in hard rain before a large assemblage of umbrellas. He rode to the Capitol with outgoing President john-tyler; George M. Dallas was sworn as Vice President; Chief Justice Taney administered the presidential oath; inaugural balls followed. Contemporaries likened the calm after that Congress to the sudden quiet after a storm.
Texas annexation, unfinished under Tyler, was completed by joint resolution and admission. Oregon talk of “Fifty-four Forty or Fight” settled, in practice, into the Oregon Treaty of 1846 along the forty-ninth parallel with Britain — a compromise short of the extreme slogan but enough to clear the northwest flank before the Mexican conflict deepened. In later compact-theory lists Polk appears among presidents who held the Union to be a compact of States — a one-sentence doctrinal placement, not a biography.
War with Mexico
Boundary dispute over the Rio Grande, Taylor’s Army of Occupation, and the battles of Palo Alto, Resaca de la Palma, and Monterey opened the war in the north. Congress declared war; Santa Fe and California were occupied; Winfield Scott’s amphibious campaign ran from Vera Cruz through Cerro Gordo, Contreras, Churubusco, and Chapultepec to the City of Mexico. Junior officers such as Ulysses S. Grant learned their trade in those columns. The Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo and the Mexican cession closed the formal map-making; Nicholas Trist’s friction with the administration and the Senate ratification fight showed how messy peace could be after a victorious war.
Critics charged that the war’s cause owed much to the Texas course associated with Calhoun, and that war was declared while peace intrigue was already in motion. From the field, the conflict looked like a political war: a Democratic administration treating victories as party capital and hesitating to give Scott — a Whig with presidential aspirations — unchecked glory as head of the “army of conquest.” House opposition recorded Oregon notice debates, European interference complaints, and the slide into war measures; John Quincy Adams remained among the war’s conspicuous critics until his collapse in the House in 1848.
Slavery extension and the term’s close
Victory abroad reopened slavery’s future at home. The Wilmot Proviso — a proposal to bar slavery from territory taken from Mexico — split parties along sectional lines more than partisan ones. Free Soil organized for 1848; Zachary Taylor won the presidency as a Whig war hero. Polk’s last messages and the handing over of power close the administrative story; he died soon after Taylor’s inauguration. The sibling war page holds campaigns and generals; this page is the President who willed the war and the continental map that the compromise-of-1850 then had to manage.
Abraham Lincoln’s later House service in the Thirtieth Congress sat against that Polk-war backdrop — a reminder that the expansion presidency shaped the generation that would fight over the cession’s meaning in the 1850s. For a beginner, Polk is the one-term Democrat who finished Texas, split Oregon with Britain, beat Mexico, and left the Union a vastly larger slavery quarrel than he inherited.

entities/jefferson-davis.title: Jefferson Davis (1808–1889)
entities/jefferson-davis.content:
Jefferson Davis
Jefferson Davis (1808–1889) — Mississippi senator, Secretary of War under Pierce, and President of the Confederate States — is the executive face of secession and the Southern war government. The story follows him from Montgomery through Sumter diplomacy to flight and capture. Alexander H. Stephens, his Vice President, insisted there was no personal feud while recording deep differences over conscription, habeas, impressment, and peace. A British officer’s June 1863 Richmond interview — part of the longer journey on fremantle-tour-confederacy-1863 — supplies a foreign visitor’s snapshot. This page is the wartime President, not a cradle-to-grave life before 1860.
Montgomery and Sumter
After the cotton republics left the Union, the Montgomery Congress made Davis provisional President and Stephens Vice President. Commissioners went to Washington while Beauregard waited at Charleston; the Sumter crisis opened the war (fort-sumter-1861, secession-winter-1860-61). Formation of the Confederate government closed the people’s crisis decade of the late 1850s. Davis’s inaugural and the claim that South Carolina, once seceded, held Sumter by right belong to the compact reading prepared on compact-theory-and-state-sovereignty.
Richmond interview and policy fights
On 17 June 1863 the visiting Coldstream officer, presented through Judah P. Benjamin, found Davis marked by quiet heaviness rather than noisy grief, speaking of British neutrality, wishing he might have joined the army, and recalling West Point and the War Department as schools of Confederate generals. The full Texas-to-Richmond road that brought that interview is on fremantle-tour-confederacy-1863. Policy differences with Stephens — conscription, suspension of habeas corpus, impressment, and peace initiatives — ran deep without personal hatred. After emancipation and the arming of Black troops, Davis held a hard line on Negro soldiers and retaliation.
Hampton Roads, flight, capture
After the hampton-roads-conference-1865 Davis’s public temper was wrathful where Lincoln’s was conciliatory. When Richmond fell on the night of 2 April 1865 Davis fled toward Danville, hoping still for a junction of Lee and Johnston that Grant’s pursuit prevented. Capture and the collapse of remaining Confederate arms close his wartime story here.

entities/john-c-calhoun.title: John C. Calhoun (1782–1850)
entities/john-c-calhoun.content:
John C. Calhoun
John C. Calhoun (1782–1850) — South Carolinian, Secretary of War under Monroe, Vice President under Adams and Jackson, and the leading theorist of nullification — was a Cabinet colleague who became the Carolina champion of State interposition. He appears in the Seminole Cabinet, the Missouri opinions, and the Holy Alliance panic of 1823; later in the Jackson–Calhoun rupture, the 1831 pamphlet, and the Senate nullification fight; and beside the Exposition and Protest and the Tariff of Abominations. Postwar compact writers still named him the unanswered master of the 1833 arena against Webster.
Monroe’s War Department
Under Monroe, Calhoun sat as Secretary of War beside Adams at State and Crawford at the Treasury. In the Seminole and Pensacola Cabinet he carried surrender orders while Adams defended Jackson’s Florida stroke. The later rupture between Jackson and Calhoun turned on whether Calhoun had early moved to punish Jackson — a quarrel Van Buren was blamed for fomenting. In written Cabinet opinions on Missouri he conversed with Adams on slavery’s moral taint even as the compromise settled the immediate bill.
Vice President and rupture
In 1824 Calhoun withdrew from the presidential canvass in Pennsylvania and took the Vice Presidency with 182 electoral votes; he was sworn at Adams’s inaugural on 4 March 1825. The Jackson–Calhoun ticket of 1828 followed (Georgia’s shortfall remembered against old Crawford plots), then the 1831 pamphlet war that broke the Cabinet. Van Buren resigned the State Department amid the strife; Calhoun’s Carolina politics hardened toward Exposition and Protest.
Nullification
The Tariff of Abominations and South Carolina’s ordinance made Calhoun the public face of nullification — the claim that a State convention might void a federal law within her limits. His resolutions and the Senate contest filled the session; Adams watched Force Bill and Clay’s compromise from the House; proclamation, enforcement preparation, and the ordinance’s withdrawal closed the crisis. Compact vocabulary kept alive after the war still returned to Calhoun versus Webster in 1833: State sovereignty as the Union’s foundation, nullification as remedy short of immediate secession. This page is the arc from Monroe Cabinet to Carolina doctrine; later Senate years may thicken when denser material is added.

entities/john-jacob-astor.title: John Jacob Astor (1763–1848)
entities/john-jacob-astor.content:
John Jacob Astor
John Jacob Astor (1763–1848) was a German immigrant who rose to become New York’s great fur capitalist and the projector of an American trading empire on the Columbia River. In the sources used for this wiki he appears chiefly as the mind behind the pacific-fur-company and the fort named Astoria — not as a full ledger of his later American Fur Company power or his Manhattan real-estate fortune. The story that matters here is how a private merchant tried to seize the Pacific fur circuit for the United States, how war and rival companies took the post away, and how that loss became an Oregon argument for a generation. The wider trade system sits on pacific-fur-trade-and-astoria-enterprise.
From immigrant stake to continental bid
Astor left his native village with a small sum invested in merchandise suited to the American market. He sailed for Baltimore in November 1783 and reached Hampton Roads in January. Ice held the Chesapeake for nearly three months. Ashore among delayed passengers he met a countryman who was a furrier. That acquaintance explained qualities and prices of furs and the methods of the trade. Astor went on to New York, sold his goods, and put the proceeds into peltries. From that modest beginning he built a fur business that reached into the interior and linked New York capital to Indian country.
British and Canadian companies already dominated much of the northern traffic. Hudson’s Bay and the Northwest Company pushed deep into the lakes and forests. The Mackinaw Company traded from Michilimackinac toward the Mississippi and the western tribes. United States factory houses tried to pull Indian trade into national channels. Astor bought into the Mackinaw Company’s Indian establishments inside United States territory — first one half, then, by agreement, the whole within five years — on terms that kept the American company out of British dominions. The war-of-1812 suspended that bargain. After the war Congress barred British traders from operating inside United States territories, and the old arrangement dissolved. By then Astor’s ambition had already moved beyond the lakes. He meant to plant an American emporium at the mouth of the Columbia, collect sea-otter and interior peltries, ship them toward China, and rival Hudson’s Bay and the Northwest Company on a continental scale. Russian posts on the northwest coast were to be met by agreement rather than by endless friction. The Pacific Fur Company was the association through which he tried to do it.
Astoria: sea arm, land arm, and catastrophe
Astor devised twin expeditions. The ship Tonquin, under Lieutenant Jonathan Thorn of the navy on leave, carried partners, goods, guns, and the frame of a coasting schooner. Thorn’s naval standing was later remembered as a mark of national countenance on what was still a private enterprise. The Tonquin sailed in September 1810. Wilson Price Hunt led the overland party up the Missouri and across the Rocky Mountains toward the same point. In April 1811 the sea party raised a picketed trading post at Point George on the Columbia estuary and named it Astoria. Chinook neighbors under Comcomly became local allies and suppliers. Interior partners built houses upriver and began to gather beaver.
Disaster followed on several fronts. Coastal Indians destroyed the Tonquin and killed most of her people after Thorn neglected the caution Astor had urged about trusting the shore trade. The loss crippled the coastal arm and frightened the thin garrison at the fort. Astor learned of the calamity months later. He felt it as a blow that might defeat the whole scheme, yet he refused theatrical grief. The same evening he appeared at the theatre with his usual calm; when a friend wondered at it, he asked whether he was expected to stay home and weep for what he could not help. He kept fitting out relief. The Beaver and later the Lark were sent; a provisional agreement with the Russian company aimed to secure a supply and commission business on the northern coast. Hunt’s overland party eventually reached the Columbia after extreme hardship. For a time the infant colony collected packs and looked as if the country could pay.
War between the United States and Great Britain ended the experiment. Northwest Company agents reached the Columbia with news of British ships coming to crush American establishments. Duncan M’Dougal and other partners on the spot chose to sell goods and furs to the Northwest Company rather than await capture. The British flag rose over Astoria; the sloop Raccoon completed the wartime transfer. Astor preferred a fair enemy capture of place and property to what he treated as a virtual gift. M’Dougal’s later appearance as a Northwest partner confirmed, for Astor and for several who had been on the ground, the suspicion of a hollow bargain. After peace the post was restored in diplomatic form, but Astor’s plea for the American flag and a small military force to reinstate him in real possession was met with what later western writers called national supineness. Northwest Company traders kept the Columbia; after 1821 the Hudson’s Bay Company held that trade. American mountain men built a different fur system eastward among the Rockies — free trappers, yearly rendezvous, Ashley and Sublette’s world — while the Pacific emporium Astor had projected remained a lost chance.
National stake and later memory
In Congress and in western argument Astoria was not only a merchant’s failure. It was private enterprise begun with government countenance, then left exposed when joint occupation and British traders ripened a claim to harbor and river that American discovery, settlement in 1811, and continuity of title were said to have already secured. Advocates of occupying the Columbia listed objects that went beyond peltries: keeping a foreign power out, gaining a Pacific seaport and naval station, saving the fur trade and the loyalty of western tribes, opening communication between the Mississippi and the Pacific, and carrying American influence toward eastern Asia. Floyd’s early occupation proposals and later fights over ending joint tenancy drew on Astoria’s story as evidence. Astor the projector thus stands in this period as the New York capitalist who tried to americanize the Pacific fur circuit, lost his fort in the War of 1812, and left Oregon politics a concrete American beginning to remember — and to regret.

entities/john-quincy-adams.title: John Quincy Adams (1767–1848)
entities/john-quincy-adams.content:
John Quincy Adams
John Quincy Adams (1767–1848) — son of John Adams, diplomat, Secretary of State, sixth President of the United States, and afterward Representative from Massachusetts — was the continuous diarist of American statecraft from the 1790s through the Mexican War. Day-by-day entries preserve missions, State, presidency, and House years; the same career sits inside the social and senatorial politics of the Union. The figure who emerges is not a party chieftain of the Jacksonian mold, but a servant of the Constitution who measured every deposit removal, petition gag, boundary note, and war bill against law, duty, and the rights of his constituents.
Early missions
Born 11 July 1767 and named for his great-grandfather John Quincy — colonial councillor and Indian negotiator then near death — he grew up in wartime education and European travel with his father before the formal diary begins. Few men left more abundant materials from cradle to grave. Washington sent him to Holland; small paper books precede the continuous journal, which opens 1 March 1795 at The Hague under a Greek motto and Bacon on Truth — neutrality problems, Batavian politics, self-training in languages and the law of nations, reading and self-examination when public pressure allowed. After Jay’s treaty, a London assignment to exchange ratifications consumed twenty-eight days of vexatious travel and arrived too late for that labor (Deas had already acted), but other pending questions kept him in negotiation; appointment to Portugal shifted to Prussia after Washington, days before leaving office, urged John Adams not to withhold promotion because the minister was the President’s son — “the most valuable public character we have abroad,” sure to prove “the ablest of our diplomatic corps.” Marriage to Louisa Catherine Johnson (1797) and the Berlin mission occupied the turn of the century. Recalled after the political revolution at home, he resumed the law under the disadvantage of long absence, lost a bankruptcy commissionership when Jefferson’s statute transferred appointments (Abigail reading ill will; Jefferson later disavowing knowledge), then served in the Massachusetts Senate and the United States Senate. The Senate chapter is the densest early political narrative: Jeffersonian measures, embargo and non-importation, party pressure, an independent course that alienated Federalist friends, committee minutes on commercial retaliation. In 1809 a major mission abroad — totally unsolicited — was confirmed by every Senate vote except personal enemies and two who opposed the mission rather than the man. He prayed for clearness of intellectual vision, courage, fortitude, and temperance; Harvard seniors and juniors asked publication of his lectures; on the twelfth wedding anniversary instructions arrived. Russian service, the Ghent negotiation, and the London mission fill the middle years before the homecoming of August 1817 — Neversink highlands at daylight, Tammany Hall dinner with De Witt Clinton, mixed gratitude and anxious forecast of the new scene.
Ghent, State, Florida, Monroe Doctrine
Adams later marked the anniversary of his arrival at Ghent as bringing placid recollections: the transactions there were the most fortunate occurrences of his life. Landing at New York 6 August 1817 after eight years abroad, he found Monroe returned from a long tour and the President’s House again habitable after the British burning. As Secretary of State he became the steady hand of Florida and the Adams–Onís settlement. Early cabinets take up Amelia Island and Galveston marauders, Buenos Ayres recognition postponed, Bagot, Hyde de Neuville, and Onís on the diplomatic calendar. Cabinet fights over Jackson’s seizure of Spanish posts found Crawford urging immediate disavowal and restoration lest the Administration own an unconstitutional war; Adams answered that to disavow and publish now would look like putting Jackson down, that Pensacola might be restored and its capture still justified, that he did not believe war would follow. He marked on the map the Trinity–Red River–mountain boundary authorized at the President’s, told Onís that Jackson had taken Pensacola without orders yet that no blame could be admitted against the General, and on 22 February 1819 signed and sealed the treaty copies with Onís — English and Spanish collated, Senate receiving the message with universal satisfaction. The same years bring South American recognition debates, fisheries consultations with Massachusetts members, and Missouri slavery agitation in which Adams rejected House restriction on the new State as incompatible with the Constitution and the Louisiana treaty, even while scorning slave-state bluster about oceans of blood and recording Rufus King as the great Northern champion against charges of personal ambition.
The climax of the second State term is the non-colonization / non-interposition policy of 1823. Adams drafts Rush instructions on neutral and belligerent rights; Cabinet debate on Canning’s proposal for a joint Anglo-American declaration runs for weeks. Adams opposes a pledge that would bind the United States against annexation of Texas or Cuba while yielding little; Southard inclines the same way; Monroe is averse to appearing subordinate to Britain. Calhoun stimulates panic after Cadiz falls to the French; Adams presses a dual rule — no American meddling in European politics, European abstention from subjugating any part of the American hemisphere. The final Monroe message, though varied from Adams’s draft, was conformable to his views. The same years saw growth of the Monroe Doctrine and the breaking of the Republican party that would send the succession to the House.
Presidency: Georgia, Panama, 1828
Succession politics fill 1824: rumor of a Crawford–Adams caucus coalition rejected; R. M. Johnson relating Calhoun’s proposed arrangement (Adams President, Jackson Vice-President, Clay at State) “not as a bargain”; Clay’s friends sounding Kentucky if the election went to the House — “Incedo super ignes.” Of the electoral votes Jackson led with ninety-nine, Adams eighty-four, Crawford forty-one, Clay thirty-seven. On 9 February 1825 the House, voting by States, gave Adams thirteen, Jackson seven, Crawford four — completed unexpectedly on a single ballot. Benton and the Jackson men forever branded a “corrupt bargain” when Clay took State. The presidency was beset by Georgia–Creek conflict, the Panama mission and Congress’s fight over mission funds, tariff and canal politics, Scott–Macomb command claims, Northeastern boundary agents, and the long campaign that ended in Jackson’s victory of 1828. In August 1828 he recorded a Jackson-party meeting haranguing three hours on the Administration’s unpardonable sins while he dined nearby. He left office without bitterness toward the forms of the Constitution, began 1829 in gloom — shaded lamp self-extinguished, first Psalm after prayer — crowded last New Year’s drawing-room, and on 11 February heard Jackson and Calhoun declared elected.
Two years of leisure at Quincy followed — Cicero completed over ten months, horticulture, Anti-Masonic conversation with Stone of the Commercial Advertiser on Letters upon Masonry, Eaton–Campbell–Ely intelligence treated as incomplete and not fully authentic. Richardson and Lincoln brought the Plymouth nomination; Turner of Scituate was put up to divide the vote. November 1830 returns: 1817 for Adams of 2565, with Thompson and Baylies trailing; he noted that no prior ex-President had sat in either House, that refusal would have been arrogance and ridicule, and that the call ended hope of quiet old age — “launched again upon the faithless wave of politics.” The Adams years and the Jackson triumph remade the social-political map of the Union.
House years: Bank, gag, petitions
From the Twenty-Second Congress his floor record becomes denser. Adams is repeatedly chairman of Manufactures; tariff paragraphs, Bank questions, nullification and the Force Bill, and Clay’s compromise fill the first sessions. In autumn 1833 he notes Jackson’s order removing the deposits, Duane’s dismissal, and Taney at the Treasury, telling intimates he will wait on the evidence before declaring for or against the Bank. Through 1834 he watches Senate censure, the presidential protest, and House struggle over custody of the public moneys. French spoliation under the treaty of 1831 and the Northeastern boundary recur; at the midnight close of the short session his resolution on the French dispute carries unanimously — two hundred votes and gallery applause, the first of his great House triumphs.
From 1835 the right of petition absorbs him. Pinckney’s select-committee report on abolition petitions drew extreme violence on the floor; Waddy Thompson would commit it to the flames or the hangman. Successive gag resolutions culminate, in the Twenty-Fifth Congress, in Patton’s rule that slavery petitions shall not be read or acted upon — which Adams answered, when his name was called, as a violation of the Constitution, of his constituents’ right of petition, and of his own freedom of speech. The special session of 1837 brings Sub-Treasury, specie suspensions, and renewed assaults on the call of the States for petitions. Atherton’s anti-petition resolutions continue the fight through the late 1830s. Benton, from the Senate, fights Bank and Independent Treasury in parallel winters; Adams holds the House petition memory of the same Union.
Amistad and Smithsonian
The Amistad densifies the record: Spanish ship into New London with African captives and Cuban claimants; murder and piracy charges; knotty questions for Judge Thompson and the Supreme Court — Adams follows as law and conscience. The Smithsonian bequest arrives when Rush recovers about half a million dollars; college interests lobby against a national university destructive of existing colleges; he recorded the Act of Congress and his own views of the trust, later briefing a new Secretary who receives the history with courteous indifference and helping defeat what he calls a “swindling Smithsonian bill” at a midnight close. Petition warfare never drops while these trusts and cases run.
Ashburton, Creole, Texas
Under Tyler, Adams on Foreign Affairs noted Lord Ashburton’s arrival and the Webster negotiation on the Northeastern boundary and related questions. The Creole — brig from Norfolk to New Orleans with tobacco and some 135 slaves; mutiny 7 November; course forced to a British port — filled the record with official narratives and the diplomatic storm. Texas annexation agitation rose through the early 1840s; Adams already saw the impulse of national aggrandizement “doomed beyond the reach of all but Almighty power.” Clay’s and Van Buren’s letters against annexation at this time appear; Jackson’s letter to Aaron V. Brown alleging treacherous surrender of Texas to Spain in 1819 becomes the text of Adams’s two-hour-plus Tremont Temple address of 7 October 1844. Oregon jurisdiction bills and China mission talk interleave with gag fights and censure attempts from Southern members.
Mexican War and death in the House
The Twenty-Eighth Congress closes in convulsive midnight business: Adams helps defeat a “swindling Smithsonian bill”; Tyler vetoes a steamer-payment prohibition and is overridden in both Houses — the first law passed over the veto “precisely as midnight came.” Polk’s rainy inaugural of 4 March 1845 opens the Twenty-Ninth Congress; Adams declines the Senate committee’s invitation to the ex-Presidents’ place, watches Polk and Tyler ride from Coleman’s, Dallas sworn, Polk’s half-hour address delivered in hard rain “to a large assemblage of umbrellas,” Taney administering the oath. He likens the day after a dying Congress to sudden calm after typhoon or hurricane. Texas annexed, Oregon contested, Mexican War debates fill the floor; he is renominated for the Thirtieth Congress even as war measures multiply. After a break in the continuous diary, a posthumous memoir in Adams’s hand dates his “decease” for useful purposes from the Boston seizure of 20 November 1846. The final return to Washington, last letter threads into early 1848, and death in the Capitol, 21–23 February 1848 — the old man stricken at his House post — close the life. Across three decades the same character holds: a New England constitutionalist who treated the House as a court of the people, measured executive power by the compact of the States, and made the right of petition the test of whether the Union still heard the governed.

entities/john-tyler.title: John Tyler (1790–1862)
entities/john-tyler.content:
John Tyler
John Tyler (1790–1862) of Virginia was elected Vice President on the Whig Log-Cabin ticket of 1840 and became the tenth President when William Henry Harrison died in April 1841. He is remembered as the accidental President who broke with the whig-party over a new national bank, and who then drove texas-annexation so hard that the work spilled into the morning of James K. Polk’s inauguration. Pre-1841 biography is thin here; this page is the 1841–45 executive.
Succession and the quarrel with the Whigs
The campaign of election-of-1840 used log-cabin and hard-cider symbols to elect Harrison of Ohio with Tyler of Virginia. Whig leaders in Congress expected a return to Henry Clay’s American System — above all a new Bank of the United States after Jackson’s Bank War. Harrison’s death left Tyler President before that programme could be signed into law.
Tyler vetoed the bank bills his party sent him, including a “fiscal corporation” substitute meant to meet his constitutional objections halfway. Most of the cabinet resigned. Whigs in Congress repudiated their own President; only a few allies such as Caleb Cushing stood by him for a time. Daniel Webster remained longer at State, long enough to finish the Webster–Ashburton negotiation with Britain over the northeastern boundary and related issues. The party that had just taken power found itself fighting the man in the White House. Patronage fights filled those years: Wise rejected for France, Cushing blocked and reshuffled, Spencer confirmed for Treasury by a narrow vote. The American System never recovered a clean presidential majority after that rupture.
Foreign and slavery-tinged crises ran beside the bank fight. The Creole case — a slave brig whose mutineers forced a course to a British port — stirred Anglo-American anger over asylum and property claims. Tariff and revenue bills, an exchequer plan, and the Tariff of 1842 filled the domestic calendar once the bank was dead. Tyler was still a President without a party in the ordinary Whig sense.
Texas
Texas annexation became Tyler’s great unfinished ambition. With John C. Calhoun at the State Department he pressed a treaty of annexation; the Senate rejected it amid cries of “Texas or Disunion” and hard opposition from Benton, Adams, and others who saw slavery extension and war with Mexico in the project. The election of 1844 then gave Democrats under james-k-polk a campaign mandate for expansion, while Clay’s caution on annexation cost him Northern and Southern friends in different ways.
Even after Polk’s election, in the months that remained of his term, Tyler pursued annexation with renewed vigor. He treated Texas as the measure that would specially illustrate his administration and preserve it from oblivion. Anson Jones held the Texas presidency; the republic was in a more thriving condition than before. Joint resolution in Congress and legislative admission closed the path Tyler could not finish by treaty alone. On 4 March 1845 he rode with Polk from Coleman’s hotel to the Capitol through a hard rain for the inaugural ceremonies — a visible handoff from the President who would not leave Texas unfinished to the President who would inherit Oregon, Mexico, and the map that followed.
The sibling event texas-annexation holds the full diplomatic and legislative path. This page is the Virginian Whig-turned-outsider who used the presidency’s last months to force the Union’s southwestern border into a new shape.
After the White House
Tyler’s later Confederate-era role lies mostly outside this page’s focus. For the wiki’s 1800–65 political spine he matters as the veto that shattered Whig unity and the executive will behind Texas. Without the bank quarrel, the second party system might have looked different in the 1840s; without the Texas push, Polk’s war and the Compromise of 1850 would have had a different map to argue over.

entities/martin-van-buren.title: Martin Van Buren (1782–1862)
entities/martin-van-buren.content:
Martin Van Buren
Martin Van Buren (1782–1862) — New York senator, Jackson’s Secretary of State and Vice President, eighth President — was the organizer of Jacksonian succession and the executive of the Panic of 1837 and the Independent Treasury. Early Albany Regency biography is thin here; this page follows him from opposition to Adams through Jackson’s Cabinet to the defeat of 1840.
Senate and opposition to Adams
In the Senate Van Buren sat as a younger New York colleague of Rufus King, and warned in the tariff debates of 1824 that manufacturers should not fuse with a single party. He voted against Clay’s confirmation as Secretary of State and sat in the Senate opposition to the Adams administration. New York’s anti-caucus struggles belonged to the same decade that broke the old Republican party — the political weather in which Van Buren’s organizational reputation was made, even when Albany detail remains sparse.
Jackson’s Cabinet and the London mission
Under Jackson, Van Buren took the Department of State (James A. Hamilton briefly interim). The Calhoun strife, Van Buren’s resignation, the London mission, and the Senate’s rejection of that nomination followed — Clay, Webster, and Calhoun interests converging to clear a presidential path by wounding Jackson’s favorite. Van Buren returned as Vice President; on 4 March 1837 Jackson stood at Van Buren’s left as the new President took the oath.
Panic, Sub-Treasury, and 1840
The Panic of 1837 opened the presidency with specie suspension and a special session. Sub-Treasury debates filled the House — Bell against, Cambreleng for, challenges to propose a new Bank — beside the renewed war over petitions. The Independent Treasury was the hard-money sequel to the Bank War: divorce of public moneys from banks of discount. Hard times then fed the Log-Cabin campaign that turned Van Buren out for Harrison and Tyler. This page is the man who carried Jackson’s succession into that fiscal and electoral sequel.

entities/pacific-fur-company.title: Pacific Fur Company
entities/pacific-fur-company.content:
Pacific Fur Company
The Pacific Fur Company was john-jacob-astor’s association to plant an American fur emporium on the Columbia River. It was not a lasting chartered monopoly like the great British companies. It was a partnership of capital and experienced traders, formed to send one expedition by sea and another by land, raise a fortified post at the river mouth, push interior houses into the beaver country, and tie that coast trade to China. The fort they built took Astor’s name — Astoria — and for a short season it stood as the American bid for the Pacific slope. Rivalry with the Northwest Company, the loss of the ship Tonquin, and the war-of-1812 broke the venture. Goods and furs were sold under wartime pressure; the British flag rose; and after peace the Columbia trade remained in British company hands. The company’s story therefore ends as a failed American corporate attempt, not as a permanent Pacific charter. Its national meaning is treated more fully under pacific-fur-trade-and-astoria-enterprise.
Association, design, and twin expeditions
Astor furnished the funds and bore the main risk. The articles of association joined him with partners who included Duncan M’Dougal, Alexander M’Kay, David Stuart and his nephew Robert Stuart, Wilson Price Hunt, and Donald M’Kenzie. Hunt was named the agent who was to reside at the principal establishment on the northwest coast for the first five-year term. The commercial design was a triangle. Ships and coastal trade would collect sea-otter and other peltries; interior posts would feed beaver and other skins down the Columbia; China markets would close the circuit, while a temporary understanding with Russian posts on the far northern coast was meant to reduce hostile rivalry and open a supply business.
Two expeditions carried the plan into action. For the sea arm, Astor fitted out the Tonquin, a ship of about two hundred and ninety tons, mounting ten guns, with merchandise for trade, the frame of a schooner for coasting work, seeds for cultivation, and stores for a fortified post. Jonathan Thorn, a lieutenant in the United States navy on leave — a veteran of the Tripolitan war — took command. Four partners sailed with him: M’Kay, M’Dougal, David Stuart, and Robert Stuart. The Tonquin put to sea in September 1810, touched at the Sandwich Islands, and after a hard passage over the Columbia bar reached Baker’s Bay. In April 1811 the party chose Point George as the site of the trading house. They landed, cut timber, and raised log buildings for residence, stores, and a powder magazine. Neighboring Chinooks under the one-eyed chief Comcomly visited and traded. A picketed fort, later strengthened with bastions and small cannon, became the factory known as Astoria.
The land arm was entrusted chiefly to Hunt, with M’Kenzie associated for his Northwest Company experience in the interior. Their route ran by the lakes and Mackinaw to St. Louis, then up the Missouri, across the plains, and over the Rocky Mountains to the same Columbia mouth. Delays at Montreal, Mackinaw, and St. Louis, competition with the Missouri Fur Company for hunters and interpreters, winter ice, and Indian dangers on the upper Missouri threw the march far behind schedule. Hunt’s party struggled through Sioux and Arickara country, crossed the mountains by a hard and hungry route, and reached Astoria after the sea party had already planted the fort. The twin-expedition design had worked in outline: sea stores and land explorers met on American ground at the estuary. Interior detachments then went upriver. David Stuart built the first interior post of the company near the Oakinagan. Other brigades pushed toward Spokan country and the upper branches, gathering packs that showed what a settled trade might become.
Loss of the Tonquin, rivalry, and wartime sale
Almost at once the coastal arm was crippled. After leaving men and cargo at Astoria, Captain Thorn took the Tonquin northward to trade. He neglected the caution Astor had urged about admitting natives on board. Coastal Indians destroyed the ship and massacred most of the crew; the catastrophe reached Astoria only later and struck the garrison with fear. Numbers were already small. Rumors of a combined Indian attack led the Astorians to throw up pickets and exercise with arms. M’Dougal, facing tribes who dreaded smallpox, once held up a bottle and claimed he could uncork the pestilence — a stratagem of fear that bought a measure of respect. Relief and trading ships followed in later seasons. The Beaver carried Hunt toward Russian New Archangel and the sealing islands. Interior rivalry sharpened when the Northwest Company planted a house on the Spokan. Astorian posts answered as best they could with thin detachments and limited goods.
War between the United States and Great Britain decided the company’s fate. Northwest partners appeared on the Columbia with news that British warships — among them the frigate Phoebe and the armed ship Isaac Todd — were coming to take or destroy American establishments on the coast. M’Dougal received John George M’Tavish and his party with open hospitality. Trade was suspended except for provisions. Plans to abandon the post and cross the mountains were debated, postponed, and revived. Hunt, long absent on coastal and island business, returned to find his colleagues bent on winding up. In the crisis M’Dougal sold the stock of goods and furs at Astoria and in the interior to the Northwest Company. The British flag replaced the American. When the sloop of war Raccoon arrived, Captain Black completed the wartime seizure of a place already bargained away. Astor later said he would have preferred a fair capture of place and property to seeing them virtually given away. M’Dougal soon appeared as a Northwest partner, which deepened suspicion among clerks and among Astor himself that the sale had been a hollow piece of management rather than a necessity forced only by enemy guns.
Aftermath and meaning
The Pacific Fur Company did not survive as an American Pacific institution. After the war the post was restored in form under treaty arrangements, yet Northwest Company traders — and after their 1821 merger into the Hudson’s Bay Company, Hudson’s Bay men — kept the practical command of the Columbia trade. Astor’s later appeals for a protecting force and a restored American flag at Astoria went unanswered in any strength that could reverse the commercial facts on the ground. The company’s short life still mattered. It had planted the first American commercial town at the river mouth, explored lines of communication across the continent, and shown both the promise and the fragility of private empire on a coast where British capital and naval reach were strong. Western advocates in Congress treated Astoria as private enterprise carried out with the countenance of the United States — Thorn’s naval leave was cited as a seal of nationality — and as a stake lost by wartime disaster and postwar neglect. The mountain fur trade of the 1820s and 1830s, with its free trappers and yearly rendezvous, was the American sequel east of Hudson’s Bay’s Columbia hold. The Pacific Fur Company itself remains the name of the association that tried, and failed, to make that hold American in Astor’s generation.

entities/robert-e-lee.title: Robert E. Lee (1807–1870)
entities/robert-e-lee.content:
Robert E. Lee
Robert E. Lee (1807–1870) commanded the Army of Northern Virginia, the Confederacy’s principal eastern army, through the middle and late years of the war. The sources behind this wiki show him as the wartime opponent of Meade and Grant — the invader of Pennsylvania in 1863, the defender of Richmond’s approaches in 1864–65, and the general who surrendered at Appomattox — not as a full cradle-to-grave biography. Mexican War engineer glory and early West Point chapters are not dense in these digests; what follows stays with the attested wartime person.
Virginia and the eastern command
After Lincoln’s 15 April 1861 call for seventy-five thousand militia, Virginia’s secession cascade carried many of her soldiers out of the old Union. Lee is named among Virginians who went with their State. Thereafter Union and Confederate chronicles treat him as the principal Confederate sword in the East. He led the invasion of Pennsylvania that ended at gettysburg-1863, then the long defense against Grant’s overland-campaign-1864, the siege lines at Petersburg, and the final flight that ended at appomattox-and-end-of-confederate-arms-1865. Campaign pages hold those battles in detail; this entity gathers the commander as the deposits show him.
Person and manners in the Gettysburg summer
A British officer traveling with Longstreet’s headquarters met Lee on 30 June 1863, on the eve of Gettysburg. Lee was then about fifty-six — described as almost the handsomest man of his age the visitor had seen — courteous, wearing a grey jacket with three stars and no arms, and said never to sleep in a house while on campaign. His working relation with James Longstreet struck the visitor as unusually close and touching; both men appeared as simple servants of their country in the same spirit once associated with Stonewall Jackson.
At Chambersburg the army’s discipline was under Lee’s non-retaliation orders: private houses were not to be searched for hidden keys or plunder, and whisky was destroyed rather than looted. Through 1–3 July the same observer watched Lee with A. P. Hill as the first day’s fight drove Union troops to Cemetery Ridge, then the long wait and late assault of the second day, and on the third the failed attack afterward linked to Pickett’s charge. Lee, rallying broken troops, called it a sad day and took the loss on himself — saying it was he who had lost the fight. Those hours are the wiki’s densest personal deposit: a composed commander in defeat, not a paper statue.
Opponent of Grant; Appomattox
In 1864 Grant made Lee and Richmond the main eastern objective of a coordinated Union plan. The Overland battles — Wilderness, Spotsylvania, Cold Harbor — and the shift to Petersburg stretched Lee’s lines westward until they broke after Five Forks in April 1865. Even then the remnant of the Army of Northern Virginia answered orders with discipline; the gain of a day still seemed worth fighting for while Richmond’s government fled. Pursuit ended at the McLean House at Appomattox Court House. Terms provided for stacking arms; officers kept side-arms and horses; conversation followed the surrender papers. Documentary appendices print the Grant–Lee correspondence and Lee’s last order. Johnston, Taylor, and Kirby Smith still had forces in the field, but Lee’s surrender was the stroke that made the rebellion’s collapse feel general.
For this wiki Lee is the attested 1863–65 commander — Gettysburg’s defeated invader and Appomattox’s surrendering general — without invented boyhood or Mexico chapters the present sources do not carry.

entities/thomas-hart-benton.title: Thomas Hart Benton (1782–1858)
entities/thomas-hart-benton.content:
Thomas Hart Benton
Thomas Hart Benton (1782–1858) — United States Senator from Missouri for thirty years — was the great Jacksonian chronicler of the working of the federal government from the Missouri struggle to the Compromise of 1850. Near the end of life he prepared an auto-sketch in mortal pain, a preliminary view of parties about 1820, then chapter after chapter of Senate and executive contest — not a detached history but a participant’s narrative. The same years also unfold from other rooms of the Capitol and in the monetary weather of 1836–7 through which he fought. The Benton of this wiki is the Union Democrat of the Jackson school — hard money, anti-Bank, anti-nullification, anti-Omnibus lumping — who watched parties and sectional questions remake the Senate he had dominated for a generation.
Auto-sketch: North Carolina, Tennessee, Missouri
The outlines Benton prepared near the end of life were not a full biography but salient points of character and chief incidents. Born in Orange County near Hillsborough, North Carolina, 14 March 1782, son of Col. Jesse Benton and Ann Gooch of Hanover County, Virginia, he took his given names from the Hart connection and was cousin to Lucretia Hart Clay — often mistaken for a blood relative of Henry Clay himself. He lost his father before he was eight and fell under a young mother of reading and Revolutionary observation. History and geography were his light reading; national law, civil law, common law, and the law itself his studies — all carried on while he opened a farm. Licensed by Judges White, Overton, and Campbell in Tennessee, he practiced with the countenance of Jackson, Robertson, McNairy, and Hardeman as a young man who might become useful to the State. Legislative service opened; marriage to Elizabeth McDowell of the Preston connection followed; four daughters survived to respectability in church and life. Widowhood after her 1854 death — paralysis from 1844 — left him never again at festivity or amusement. Motives for writing he stated as justice to the men and cause with which he acted, usefulness to republican government by showing its working, gratitude to the founders, and self-defense against an indiscriminate posthumous publication of speeches.
Missouri admission and the early Senate
Benton enters the federal story with Missouri’s admission in 1820–21. The restriction fight had been “compromised” the session before by admitting the State without restriction and forbidding slavery in the remainder of the Louisiana purchase north of 36°30′. He insisted the compromise was the work of the South, sustained by Monroe’s cabinet and by every slave-State Senate vote present. When the State constitution came in, House and Senate still stalled on the slavery clause until conditional admission settled the agitation. He was minute because he wanted history to see the controversy as a political movement for the balance of power, balked by Northern democracy that foresaw geographical parties and eventual separation. The same sessions bring Oregon’s first congressional proposition (Floyd, with Benton and the Astorians Crooks and Farnham at Brown’s hotel), Benton’s St. Louis newspaper war against the Florida treaty’s cession of Texas, Indian factory abolition, tariff and American System debates, and the personal aspect of Monroe’s government — Adams at State, Crawford at Treasury, Calhoun at War — which Benton held up as a comparison any friend of popular institutions might challenge against the world.
Oregon and the West
From 1820–21 onward Benton is a western expansionist in the Jeffersonian grain. Floyd’s select committee on the Columbia — granted more through courtesy than business expectation — drew on essays Benton had published the year before and on evenings with Crooks and Farnham, Astor’s men from Astoria. Jefferson’s “North American road to India,” joint occupation with Britain, and the danger of delay while Britain already held possession recur through his Oregon colonization speeches, notice to terminate joint occupation, Frazer’s River and Utrecht boundary history, and the treaty settled at forty-nine after the administration’s quandary when Britain offered that line. He foreshadowed unauthorized occupation — adventurers entering as Æneas on the Tiber — if government neglected the coast. He denounced the 1819 Spanish treaty for mutilating the Mississippi valley, bringing a non-slaveholding foreign dominion near New Orleans, and sheltering a wilderness barrier between Missouri and New Mexico — all the national reasons later paid for in war and a hundred millions to get Texas back. Land relief for public-land debtors (the credit system’s twenty-three millions owed, forfeiture hanging over new-State purchasers), reduction of the army in the distress of 1820, Indian factory abolition after twenty-five years of costly abuse, and Monroe’s elaborate veto opinion on internal improvement within the States complete the early western dossier. The same Oregon and Texas questions later filled the people’s politics of the Tyler and Polk years.
Jackson’s lieutenant: Bank and nullification
Benton rises as the tireless Senate ally of Andrew Jackson. The Jefferson Birthday toast, the rupture with Calhoun, the Bank fight from non-renewal through veto, investigation, and downfall, the nullification ordinance and proclamation, the Force Bill and the “secret history” of the compromise of 1833 — these are the spine of his Jackson years. He holds hard money and the Union together: hostile to a national bank of the Biddle type, hostile to nullification as a remedy, ready to sustain executive measures that kept the public deposits out of a corporation he thought dangerous to republican government. On removal of the deposits he was in Donelson’s office when the decision came, felt that a great blow had been struck, and came to Washington determined to stand by the President. He drafted the Specie Circular’s rough form when asked. He carried the expunging resolution through rejection and renewal until the journal was purged and Jackson, too weak to dine, placed the head-expunger in the presidential chair. That senatorial war sat inside the social panic of 1834 — suspended specie and broken confidence — while the House watched the same Bank and petition winters from across the Capitol.
Hard money, Independent Treasury, and the monetary weather
Under Van Buren the Bank fight changes form: financial and monetary crisis, general suspension of specie payments, transmigration of the Bank of the United States into a Pennsylvania state institution still using defunct federal notes, Independent Treasury and hard-money payments, divorce of bank and state. Benton argues an estimate of some eighty millions in gold and silver and the determination of sound banks to resume once Biddle’s institution was forced into resumption or open insolvency — suspension then obliged to be brief. The divorce bill passed the Senate in the called session and received the impetus that soon carried it through the House. He speaks for a specie basis — one third of liabilities the lowest safe proportion — on District bank recharters, for a bankrupt act against banks, and against Clay’s tenderness toward resuming banks that had not earned favor. The American agitation of 1836–7 read as the effect of surplus revenue and currency operations — an analysis that frames Benton’s hard-money speeches without making him a disciple of that school. The Panic of 1837 and the Log-Cabin years showed the popular cost; Benton noted New York’s resumption lead, Pennsylvania’s follow, tax on bank notes, Tyler-era repeal of the Independent Treasury, and its later restoration under Polk.
Texas annexation opposition
Benton had opposed giving Texas away in 1819; he also opposed the annexation treaty intrigue of 1844 as a presidential and disunion scheme. His first speech against the treaty mocked Calhoun’s “gunpowder popularity” and the attempt to “play Jackson” — Jackson having staked himself for the country without intrigue when he acted the real hero. “Texas or Disunion” threats from Southern conventions met Benton’s Union answer. Legislative admission of Texas as a State he treated as a separate, later fact; the war with Mexico he charged in significant part on Calhoun’s April 1844 letter renewing a strife that good men would have let sleep. The Tyler quarrel and Texas–Mexican War politics framed those Senate speeches.
Mexican War, Wilmot, and the 1850 Omnibus
Later years carry Oregon notice and treaty, the Wilmot Proviso as a “thing of nothing in itself” magnified to conflagrate the States — abolitionists and nullifiers as two halves of a pair of shears, neither cutting until joined — and Calhoun’s slavery resolutions denying Congress power to prohibit slavery in a territory. Benton applies the Ordinance of 1787’s anti-slavery rule to Oregon and affirms the Missouri line’s renewal in the Texas resolutions of 1845. Against Clay’s Omnibus he speaks for taking measures one by one: California suffering for admission, New Mexico for protection, public business and the character of Congress suffering for want of progress — the wedding of California to ill-suited spouses postponed by indefinite postponement of the unmanageable mass. Calhoun’s last speech demanding a dual executive, Calhoun’s death, Taylor’s death, Fillmore’s accession, California’s admission, and the fugitive-slave act close the arc; he returned at the end to the hope that republican government, shown working through thirty eventful years, may be maintained in purity.
Union Democrat close
Benton’s self-portrait is consistent: a Democrat of the Jackson school who would not dissolve the Union to save a party dogma, would not recharter Biddle’s Bank to calm a panic, and would not swallow an Omnibus to quiet a session. For this wiki he is the principal Senate witness to Missouri’s admission, the Bank’s destruction, the Independent Treasury idea, nullification’s settlement as Jackson’s friends understood it, Texas intrigue resisted, and the Compromise of 1850 dissented.
