entities/ulysses-s-grant.title: Ulysses S. Grant (1822–1885)
entities/ulysses-s-grant.content:
Ulysses S. Grant
Ulysses S. Grant (1822–1885) — West Pointer, Mexican War lieutenant, Galena clerk, and finally general-in-chief of the Union armies — was the operational commander who carried the western river war from Belmont and Donelson through Vicksburg and Chattanooga, then the Overland pressure that ended at Appomattox. His rise runs from Donelson’s shock to the Confederate line, through the bayou patience before Vicksburg, the elevation to lieutenant-general, and the Wilderness–Cold Harbor sequence. This page is that wartime sword, not a postwar President.
West Point, Mexico, and Galena
In the winter of 1838–39 Grant’s father secured an appointment to West Point; the son objected that he lacked the acquirements to get through, then went when his father insisted. He reported at the Academy at the end of May, passed the examination to his own surprise, and later confessed that a military life had no charms for him and that he rarely read a lesson twice — preferring the library’s novels to the course. Graduating in 1843, he joined the 4th Infantry at Jefferson Barracks under Kearny’s discipline, then followed the regiment to Camp Salubrity, Corpus Christi, and Taylor’s advance to the Rio Grande.
The Mexican War put him under fire at Palo Alto and Resaca de la Palma as a young second lieutenant who had never heard a hostile gun and who “felt sorry that he had enlisted.” Monterey, Vera Cruz, Cerro Gordo, Contreras, Churubusco, Molino del Rey, Chapultepec, and the entry into the city followed. He entered Mexico City still a second lieutenant after sixteen months and every engagement possible for one man in a regiment that lost more officers than it ever had present at a single fight; Sidney Smith’s mortal wound raised him to first lieutenant. The war’s lasting gift, he later wrote, was personal acquaintance with nearly the whole regular officer corps — Lee, both Johnstons, Holmes, and many who would face or serve him in the rebellion — and contact with volunteers who reappeared after Sumter. Pacific Coast service and the Isthmus crossing followed; unable to support a wife and children on army pay in California, he resigned in 1854, farmed near St. Louis, sold out after fever and ague, and by the coming crisis was a clerk in the family leather store at Galena.
Belmont, Donelson, and Halleck
After Sumter he mustered Illinois troops, failed to catch McClellan’s eye at Cincinnati, and received from Governor Yates the colonelcy of the 21st Illinois — a regiment that had refused its elected colonel. Marching into Missouri, he learned that Hardee’s tactics were common sense applied to Scott’s system and that he could put a regiment where he wanted it without the officers discovering he had never studied the book. Illinois Congressmen put him first on a list of brigadiers; confirmation followed, then commands at Ironton, Jefferson City, Cape Girardeau, and Cairo, with the seizure of Paducah.
Belmont in November 1861 was his first pitched fight in independent command: a demonstration ordered to detain Polk at Columbus, a camp overrun, then a scramble back to the transports when the alarm of being surrounded rose — answered by the order that they had cut their way in and could cut their way out. Northern criticism called the battle barren; Grant answered that without it Oglesby’s column might have been destroyed. Early 1862 brought Halleck’s department and the Tennessee River opening. Fort Henry fell to the navy; Donelson, invested by land while Foote’s gunboats suffered, held until Pillow and Floyd gave way and Buckner asked terms. Grant’s reply — no terms except unconditional and immediate surrender — fixed a Northern slogan. Forrest escaped with about a thousand men; the Confederate force on the fifteenth was reckoned near twenty-one thousand against Grant’s twenty-seven thousand covering the supply road. Sherman, then senior, forwarded reinforcements from Smithland with notes of encouragement.
Halleck’s telegrams briefly shifted credit toward C. F. Smith and then relieved and restored Grant under a cloud of explanations Grant later judged unjust. Restored, he found Smith dying at Savannah on the Tennessee — a severe loss to the western army. That same spring shattered Albert Sidney Johnston’s Kentucky–Tennessee line and made a western general the Cabinet could not ignore.
Shiloh
The army concentrated at Pittsburg Landing. On the morning of 6 April 1862 the Confederates struck. Grant’s narrative insists the lasting “surprise” story is false in the form popularly told, yet records a day of hard pressure back toward the river until night and Buell’s arrival reversed the field. On the seventh the Union became the attacking party; the enemy was driven until the last point near the Corinth road gave way. Gathering fragments of regiments, Grant formed a line and marched in front to prevent premature long-range firing across a clearing, knowing the enemy was ready to break. He was struck by a bullet that did no serious harm. Correct reports, he later wrote, appeared only long after public opinion had been “most erroneously formed”; he made no full report to Halleck beyond an immediate letter announcing the result. Halleck then moved headquarters to the landing, assumed field command, and ignored Grant — next in rank and nominally still commanding his old army — as if he had been at the farthest edge of the district, denying him even the subordinate reports of troops he had led at Shiloh.
The advance on Corinth was slow, methodical, and, in Grant’s later judgment, a missed chance: had Buell gone straight to Chattanooga after Corinth fell, Bragg would have lacked time to raise the army that contested middle and east Tennessee; Stone River, Chickamauga, the siege of Knoxville, and Chattanooga itself might never have been fought as they were. Halleck’s promotion east left Grant at the head of the western armies, still stripped for Buell’s needs and holding the Memphis–Corinth line against Van Dorn and Price — Iuka and Corinth battles that kept the railroad and prepared the Mississippi campaign.
Vicksburg persistence
The Vicksburg campaign of 1862–63 was a long lesson in persistence. Holly Springs’s capture destroyed supplies and drew smiles from Oxford citizens asking what an army would eat; Grant answered by stripping fifteen miles on each side of the road and advising them to emigrate the same distance. Failed bayous and canals west of the Mississippi consumed a winter; McClernand’s rivalry pushed Grant to take personal charge rather than relieve a senior in Sherman’s favor — the origin of one of the war’s most brilliant chapters. On the night of 22 April transports and barges ran the Vicksburg batteries, five steamers getting through more or less disabled and one sunk, manned largely by army volunteers from Logan’s Illinois and Missouri men when civilian crews refused.
Grand Gulf was assaulted and turned; Bruinsburg became the east-bank landing; Port Gibson opened the interior. Cutting loose from a secure base, the army struck Jackson, then swung west through Champion’s Hill and the Big Black bridges to invest Vicksburg. Early assaults failed; the siege settled into trenches in clay hills and ravines two hundred feet above the river. Johnston hovered to the rear; Haines’ Bluff and the Yazoo line sealed the north. On 4 July 1863 Pemberton surrendered — some 31,600 men paroled in Grant’s reckoning — the same day Gettysburg closed in Pennsylvania. Port Hudson followed, and the Mississippi was free. The May battles in Mississippi, the siege, and the fall made the campaign the western hinge of 1863.
Chattanooga and the lieutenant-generalcy
After Chickamauga the Army of the Cumberland clung to Chattanooga half-starved. Grant, ordered east, opened the “cracker line” through Lookout Valley, rebuilt the railroad, and prepared the November battles. Thomas carried the first Confederate line; Missionary Ridge broke in a charge that exceeded orders and collapsed Bragg’s hold. Relief of Knoxville followed. Winter camps about Chattanooga filled the months while Congress revived the grade of lieutenant-general.
Commissioned in March 1864, Grant chose to remain with the eastern armies and sent Sherman against Johnston in Georgia. The two conferred on the rail to Cincinnati: the grand campaign would press Lee continuously while Sherman took Atlanta and the Confederate heartland. Plans for simultaneous movement replaced the old pattern of idle theaters while one army fought.
Overland, Petersburg, Sherman and Franklin
Crossing the Rapidan, the Army of the Potomac met Lee in the Wilderness — tangled woods, confused assaults, Early’s threat on a flank, then, instead of Hooker’s retrograde, a night march toward Spotsylvania that drew cheering when troops saw the road pointed at Richmond rather than Washington. Spotsylvania’s Bloody Angle, the North Anna, and Cold Harbor followed. Grant wrote Stanton that the enemy seemed “very shaky,” kept up only by officers’ exertions and by entrenchments in every position. Cold Harbor’s assault he later ranked among the war’s hardest sacrifices; the justification he offered was the same logic he had used at Vicksburg — the cost of a long summer siege in a Southern climate — though he admitted the gain was slight for the loss. The left-flank transfer across the Chickahominy and James put the armies before Petersburg; investment replaced open battle, with the Weldon Railroad contested and the Army of the James holding Bermuda Hundred and the north bank.
Meanwhile Sherman took Atlanta, turned the city into a military base, expelled the citizens, and limited sutlers — news that, Grant notes, set the North aglow as the first great political campaign of the 1864 canvass. The March to the Sea was Sherman’s plan in conception and execution; Grant favored it from the first submission, even when Lincoln asked a pause to think and when Halleck opposed. Hood’s invasion of Tennessee brought Franklin and Nashville under Thomas — pursuit delayed by pontoons gone astray toward Chattanooga, rain-swollen Duck River, and a Confederate lead Grant could not close from Virginia.
Appomattox
Five Forks and the April 1865 break at Petersburg opened the chase. Grant met Lincoln in the captured city, then rode the pursuit toward Amelia Court House, correcting Meade’s orders so as to get ahead of Lee rather than follow him. Sailor’s Creek and Farmville tightened the net. The night before the McLean House interview Grant suffered a sick headache that vanished when a messenger brought Lee’s readiness to meet. In the parlor the conversation drifted so pleasantly that Grant almost forgot the object until Lee recalled him to terms. Grant wrote that officers’ side-arms and private horses might be retained — horses needed for the spring crop — and that the army should lay down its arms not to take them up again unless duly exchanged. After the stacking of arms, fraternization began. Johnston’s surrender to Sherman closed the remaining major Confederate force in the east; the assassination notice fell across the week of victory. For this wiki Grant remains the Union sword of Donelson, Shiloh, Vicksburg, Chattanooga, Overland, and Appomattox.

entities/whig-party.title: Whig Party
entities/whig-party.content:
Whig Party
The Whig Party was the main national rival to the Democrats from the mid-1830s until the early 1850s. It formed out of people who opposed Andrew Jackson’s war on the second-bank-of-the-united-states, gathered behind Henry Clay’s American System of protective tariff, national bank, and internal-improvements, elected William Henry Harrison in the noisy Log-Cabin campaign of election-of-1840, then broke apart when John Tyler vetoed the bank bills his own party expected him to sign. After a last national effort in 1852 the organization collapsed. Many former Whigs drifted into the secret Know-Nothing (American) party; others joined the new Republican coalition after the kansas-nebraska-and-bleeding-kansas fight. By the late 1850s the Whig name no longer organized a national ticket.
How the party formed
Jackson’s veto of the Bank recharter and his removal of the government deposits created a lasting opposition. National Republicans who had followed Clay, Anti-Masons angry at secret orders, and Democrats who disliked the deposit policy began to act together. They took the English name “Whig” to mark themselves as opponents of what they called executive tyranny. Hard times after the deposit fight and the panic-of-1837 fed the coalition. In Congress and in the States they argued for a new national bank, higher duties to protect manufactures, and federal money for roads, canals, and harbors — the same programme Clay had pushed for years.
Victory in 1840 and the Tyler rupture
In 1840 the Whigs ran Harrison of Ohio with John Tyler of Virginia. The campaign used log-cabin and hard-cider symbols to present Harrison as a plain western soldier against Martin Van Buren. Harrison won; within a month of the inauguration he was dead, and Tyler became President. Whig leaders in Congress expected a new Bank of the United States. Tyler vetoed the bank bills, his cabinet resigned except for Daniel Webster for a time, and the party that had just taken power found itself fighting its own President. The quarrel is told more fully on john-tyler and in the House politics of John Quincy Adams’s later diary years. The American System programme never recovered a clean presidential majority after that break.
Compromise, defeat, and disappearance
Southern and Northern Whigs still mattered in the compromise-of-1850, where Clay and others tried to settle the territories taken in the mexican-american-war. The party then lost the presidency in 1852. Immigration and anti-Catholic feeling pulled many Northern Whig voters into Know-Nothing lodges that elected unknown local tickets by 1854 — the social story sits on immigration-nativism-and-know-nothings. At the same time, Free Soil and anti-Nebraska men, including many old Whigs, built the Republican party. The second party system of Democrat versus Whig did not survive that double drain. What remained was memory of Clay’s system, the Bank War opposition, and a generation of politicians who had to find new labels for the 1860s.

events/anti-rent-and-local-insurrections.title: Anti-Rent and Local Insurrections (1830s–1840s)
events/anti-rent-and-local-insurrections.content:
Anti-Rent and Local Insurrections (1830s–1840s)
Anti-Rent and local insurrections of the late 1830s and 1840s bundle three contests against established authority that were not national party platforms: Pennsylvania’s Buckshot War over a disputed legislature, the Aroostook timber-border crisis with Britain, and New York’s Anti-Rent war against the patroon manor system. Rhode Island’s Dorr Rebellion, treated among the forties betterment fights, belongs to the same mood of local constitutional revolt. None replaces the Bank War or nullification; together they show the people fighting sheriffs, landlords, and rival houses as well as Congress.
Buckshot and Aroostook
In Pennsylvania, rival Democratic and Whig (or Anti-Masonic) claims to organize the House brought troops to Harrisburg and a crisis remembered as the Buckshot War — faction violence and militia called to keep a capital from dual legislatures. In Maine, the undeveloped northeastern boundary produced the Aroostook War: rival land agents, militia musters, and raids in the timber country before diplomacy edged toward the Webster–Ashburton settlement. Both sit beside national politics of Sub-Treasury and gag as proof that State and border quarrels could still arm men without becoming civil war.
Patroons and Anti-Rent
New York’s Anti-Rent war grew from the old Dutch patroonships. Between 1630 and 1637 a patroonship of vast acres on the Hudson became, under English rule, a manor whose lord collected perpetual rents — commonly in wheat — and feudal incidents: quarter-sales, extra year’s rent on transfer, quarry and mill privileges. Tenants on the Helderberg Hills and other manor townships, pressed for unpaid rents after the late patroon’s death, formed committees, resisted process servers, and called out community force until the State militia was summoned. The agitation of 1839–46 wore “Indian” disguises, disrupted sales, and forced political parties to bargain over abolishing distress for rent and converting leaseholds. It was a landlords-and-tenants war inside a free State — a Northern counterpart to Southern talk of labor systems, not a slave revolt.
Dorr’s Rhode Island
In Rhode Island the colonial charter’s freehold suffrage left many citizens voteless. A People’s Convention framed a constitution, declared it paramount law, and elected Thomas Wilson Dorr; the charter government and a Freemen’s Convention denied the act. Dual claims to sovereignty, assembly resolutions branding the People’s work an assumption of power, and eventual armed fiasco made the Dorr Rebellion the New England suffrage twin of Anti-Rent’s land quarrel. It belongs with social and political betterment beside temperance and Millerites — reform ending in a clash over who counted as the people.

events/antietam-and-emancipation-proclam.title: Antietam and the Emancipation Proclamation (1862–1863)
events/antietam-and-emancipation-proclam.content:
Antietam and the Emancipation Proclamation
The Maryland campaign of September 1862 and the Emancipation Proclamation that followed were one political-military hinge. Abraham Lincoln had a draft edict ready in July, waited for a victory, treated Antietam as that hinge, and issued the preliminary proclamation on 22 September and the final edict on 1 January 1863. Earlier months had brought Frémont’s and Hunter’s field orders and compensated abolishment messages; Alexander H. Stephens later denounced the proclamations as usurpations against the compact of States.
Prelude: generals and cabinet
John C. Frémont’s August 1861 military emancipation order surprised Lincoln and was modified; David Hunter’s May 1862 Department of the South order was countermanded — the President reclaiming policy from the field. Compensated abolishment messages to border states continued beside the war. On 22 July 1862 Lincoln read a draft emancipation proclamation to the Cabinet and postponed announcement until the Union arms could show a success.
Antietam as hinge
George B. McClellan, restored to command against Robert E. Lee’s Maryland invasion, fought at Antietam with forces he reported near 87,000. The battle mattered less as a full tactical monograph than as the victory that unlocked the drawer: on 22 September the preliminary proclamation warned that States still in rebellion on 1 January would lose slave property as a war measure. McClellan’s removal followed in the same political season. The final “Edict of Freedom” of 1 January 1863 applied to designated rebellious districts; the December 1862 message still urged compensated abolishment where it might apply.
Soldiers and Southern reading
From the July Cabinet onward the arming of Black soldiers was coupled to emancipation policy; Jefferson Davis’s government answered with retaliation threats. Stephens treated the Emancipation Proclamation and the September 1862 martial-law proclamation as twin usurpations against the compact of States. The sibling concept page emancipation-as-war-measure holds the longer arc from contraband to Thirteenth Amendment; Antietam’s timing and the two edicts are the hinge told here.
Chronology

22 Jul 1862: Cabinet draft; postponement.
17 Sep 1862: Antietam.
22 Sep 1862: Preliminary proclamation.
1 Jan 1863: Final proclamation.

events/appomattox-and-end-of-confederate.title: Appomattox and the End of Confederate Arms (1865)
events/appomattox-and-end-of-confederate.content:
Appomattox and the End of Confederate Arms (1865)
The collapse of Confederate arms in April–May 1865 — Five Forks, the evacuation of Petersburg and Richmond, Robert E. Lee’s surrender at Appomattox Court House on 9 April, Joseph E. Johnston’s surrender to William T. Sherman, and the capture of Jefferson Davis — closed the Civil War’s fighting. Ulysses S. Grant’s pursuit ended in Wilmer McLean’s house; Lincoln visited captured Richmond; Alexander H. Stephens, already gone to Georgia, later recorded the Confederate close and the printed terms.
Five Forks to the McLean House
Philip Sheridan’s Five Forks shattered Lee’s right; fighting on 2 April made Richmond and Petersburg untenable. Grant and George G. Meade entered Petersburg on 3 April; Lincoln met Grant there; the pursuit ran through Sailor’s Creek and Farmville into surrender correspondence. On 9 April, in McLean’s house at Appomattox Court House, Grant — free of the sick headache of the night before — wrote terms: arms stacked; officers’ side-arms and private horses retained; then fraternization after the stacking. The same hours brought Lincoln’s visit to captured Richmond; the Confederate Vice President had already left for Georgia.
Johnston, Davis, and the rest
Johnston’s conventions with Sherman, President Andrew Johnson’s refusal of the first broad convention, and the final military surrender followed. Davis fled Richmond on the night of 2 April toward Danville, still hoping for a Lee–Johnston junction Grant’s operations prevented; he was later captured. Richard Taylor and Edmund Kirby Smith in the Trans-Mississippi were the last embers. The end of rebellion was this cascade of surrenders — not a single ceremonial day.
Assassination week
The tranquil happiness of victory week ended on 14 April with Lincoln’s assassination. The war’s military close and the President’s death thus sit in the same April; Reconstruction’s political sequel belongs elsewhere, not to a results-of-the-war page here.
Chronology

1–2 Apr 1865: Five Forks; Petersburg–Richmond untenable.
9 Apr: Lee surrenders at Appomattox.
Apr–May: Johnston and remaining forces; Davis captured.
14 Apr: Lincoln assassinated.

events/bank-war-and-removal-of-deposits.title: Bank War and Removal of the Deposits (1832–1836)
events/bank-war-and-removal-of-deposits.content:
Bank War and Removal of the Deposits (1832–1836)
The Bank War was the contest between President Andrew Jackson and the Second Bank of the United States — Nicholas Biddle’s corporation at Philadelphia — over recharter, the custody of the public deposits, and the place of a great moneyed institution in a federal republic. It runs from House investigation and the veto of recharter through the election of 1832, the removal of the deposits into state banks, the commercial pressure remembered as the panic of 1834, the Senate’s censure of the President, Jackson’s protest, and the speculative aftermath that prepared the panic-of-1837. Thomas Hart Benton led the Senate Jacksonians; the House fought the same war through investigations and votes; the monetary weather that followed is theorized on credit-and-confidence-carey.
Investigation, recharter, and veto
The Twenty-Second Congress was the session at which the great contest for renewal of the charter was brought on and decided. The bank leaders meant to carry the charter quietly through Senate and then House; the opposition determined to attack incessantly, display the evil of the institution, rouse the people, and prepare them to sustain the veto. Benton conceived a House investigation under the charter’s own provision: if denied, guilt shrinking from detection; if admitted, misconduct would be found. The House was preferred as the grand inquest of the nation, and so that a contest might go on there while the Senate passed the charter. Amendments and inquiries in the Senate forced the bank into defences and side-blows. The recharter bill passed both Houses; Jackson vetoed it.
The veto sat in the campaign of 1832: Anti-Masonic side-show, nullification running in parallel, and the President’s re-election as a popular judgment against the Bank. Jacksonians treated the veto as constitutional and democratic necessity — the Bank a monopoly dangerous to liberty and to the equal rights of the States. In the House, Bank and manufactures debates became the ground on which parties were realigning after Clay’s compromise and the Force Bill winter. Effects of the veto and later fights over the three per cents, illegal currency, and sale of the United States stock in the national bank filled the sequel years.
Removal of the deposits: Duane and Taney
From the moment of the removal it was seen that the Bank’s plan was to force return of the deposits and renewal of the charter by operating on the business of the country and the alarms of the people. Loans and accommodations were to cease at the mother bank and branches and at local banks under its control; discounts stopped while curtailments called business men for payment of all they owed; pressure was made to fall on large establishments employing many operatives so as to throw laboring people out of employment. Politicians engaged in making panic obtained large loans — detection of 100,000 to a single agitator and 1,100,000 to a broker relieving distress at usury of two and a half per cent a month.
In September 1833 Jackson determined to withdraw the deposits of public moneys from the Bank and place them in sundry State banks. A paper was read to the Cabinet on the eighteenth of the month; William J. Duane, refusing to execute the policy, was dismissed; Roger B. Taney became Secretary of the Treasury. Jacksonians defended the removal as reclaiming the people’s money from a hostile corporation; the “pet banks,” the congressional reaction, and the commercial pressure of 1834 followed. Biddle assured allies that the Bank was prepared for the crisis; some House members resolved to wait upon the evidence before declaring for or against the institution. Huntington of Connecticut anticipated a bank committee that would report approving the removal; Richard Rush’s intrusion into the deposit controversy hurt Anti-Masonry in Pennsylvania. Taney’s report to Congress on the removal became the official Treasury narrative.
Panic of 1834, censure, and protest
Commercial distress paired with the rise of the Whig party and the Senate’s censure of Jackson. In April 1834 the Senate resolved to censure the President for his interferences with the public revenues. The President sent a protest and demanded that it be entered on the Senate journals; Poindexter moved that it should not be received; Clay, Webster, and Preston were absent when the excitement peaked. In the House, Wise and Baylie Peyton offered competing resolutions on custody of the public moneys and on whether the Senate’s censure had infringed the prerogatives of the House. Ways and Means under Polk, deposit-bank investigations, and appropriation conferences filled the session. The Senate’s attempt to brand an executive act as a usurpation met Jackson’s refusal to accept the brand. Years on, the censure was struck from the journals — Jackson’s “crowning mercy.”
Speculation toward 1837
The deposit system and surplus distribution fed a boom that broke when confidence failed. One contemporary reading compared the federal surplus of the mid-1830s to a great estate forcing mortgage payments into banks or into court in gold — swelling apparent banking profits until the currency snapped. High credit, on that showing, follows security of person and property and density of population; American disorder of 1836–7 was explained by surplus revenue and currency operations rather than by free banking itself (full argument on credit-and-confidence-carey). The Bank War proper ends with the federal charter’s expiration and Biddle’s turn to a Pennsylvania charter; its political legacy is the Democratic identification with hard money and against a national bank, and the Whig identification with recharter — the ground of Van Buren’s Independent Treasury fight and of the Log-Cabin campaign of 1840.
Chronology

1832: House investigation; recharter passes; Jackson vetoes; re-elected.
Sep 1833: Deposit removal ordered; Duane dismissed; Taney at Treasury.
1834: Panic of 1834; Senate censure; presidential protest.
1836–37: Speculative surplus and credit disorder → Panic of 1837.

events/burr-conspiracy.title: Burr Conspiracy
events/burr-conspiracy.content:
Burr Conspiracy
The Burr conspiracy was Aaron Burr’s attempt, after he left the vice presidency, to build a new power in the Mississippi Valley — whether by filibustering into Spanish lands, separating Western States from the Union, or both. It grew out of the unsettled politics that followed the louisiana-purchase-and-governance, drew in General James Wilkinson and the island host Harman Blennerhassett, collapsed when Wilkinson turned against Burr, and ended in a famous treason trial at Richmond in 1807 before Chief Justice John Marshall. Burr was not convicted of treason. The episode left a lasting scare about Western disunion and about how hard it is to prove treason under the Constitution.
After the duel: looking west
Burr killed Alexander Hamilton in 1804 and saw his eastern political career ruin. Talk of a Northern confederacy with himself at its head faded. He turned instead to the West and to foreign diplomats. Through agents he sounded the British minister about aid for separating the country beyond the mountains from the Atlantic States — a fleet on the Mississippi and money to arm fighting men. French representatives also heard versions of a Louisiana independence scheme. Burr cultivated Western congressmen and Creole delegates, talked of living in Tennessee or Orleans Territory, and prepared a journey down the Ohio and Mississippi that would look like politics and settlement while hiding larger designs.
Blennerhassett’s Island and the flotilla
On an island below Parkersburg lived Harman Blennerhassett, an Irish-born gentleman with a library, scientific toys, and more money than judgment. Burr’s charm and promises of western empire drew him in. Boats and stores were gathered; young men were enlisted with talk of adventure on the Spanish border. Rumors raced ahead of the flotilla: Burr would seize New Orleans, Burr would invade Mexico, Burr would split the Union. President Jefferson issued proclamations; State and territorial officers watched the rivers. Wilkinson, commanding the small United States army in the Southwest and long Burr’s correspondent, chose survival over partnership. He fortified New Orleans, arrested associates, and sent Burr’s compromising letters forward as proof that he had saved the republic from his former friend.
Arrest and the Richmond trial
Burr fled, was seized in the Mississippi Territory, and was taken to Richmond for trial in 1807. Crowds packed the court. Wilkinson appeared as the government’s star witness and looked, to many spectators, like a man saving his own neck. Marshall held the grand jury and the bench to a strict reading of the Constitution: treason against the United States consists in levying war, and needs two witnesses to the same overt act. The overt act charged was a military assemblage on Blennerhassett’s Island. Burr himself had not been on the island when the gathering occurred. Marshall’s rulings on evidence, on the definition of levying war, and on whether the President could be forced by subpoena to produce papers (Jefferson refused to appear in person but sent documents) shaped the case. The jury did not convict Burr of treason. Related indictments and later proceedings left him free but politically finished. Blennerhassett paid in fortune and reputation for hosting the dream.
What it meant
The conspiracy showed how thin federal power still was on the frontier, how easily Louisiana’s new map could feed filibuster talk, and how a republic that had just bought an empire feared its own West might peel away. It also fixed Marshall’s narrow treason doctrine in American law. For the purchase and territorial government that made the West Burr’s stage, see louisiana-purchase-and-governance. For later compact and secession language, see compact-theory-and-state-sovereignty — a different generation’s quarrel, not Burr’s flotilla.
Chronology

1804–05: Burr’s eastern fall; Western and diplomatic sounding.
1805–06: Ohio–Mississippi journey; Blennerhassett’s Island preparations.
Late 1806: Wilkinson’s turn; arrests at New Orleans; Burr’s flight.
1807: Richmond treason trial; no conviction for treason.

events/chattanooga-and-atlanta-1863-64.title: Chattanooga and Atlanta (1863–1864)
events/chattanooga-and-atlanta-1863-64.content:
Chattanooga and Atlanta (1863–1864)
Chattanooga in autumn 1863 and Atlanta in summer 1864 form the western mountain-to-Georgia arc of the war. William S. Rosecrans’s reverse at Chickamauga put the Army of the Cumberland under siege; Ulysses S. Grant relieved the town and broke Braxton Bragg on Missionary Ridge; then William T. Sherman advanced until Atlanta fell — news that answered the Democratic platform at Chicago declaring the war a failure. The march-to-the-sea-and-franklin-nashville-1864 is the dedicated sequel that bridges this arc toward Appomattox season.
Chickamauga
The Army of the Cumberland had remained six months on the Murfreesboro field. Rosecrans and his friends defended the long inactivity by winter severity and want of animals; George H. Thomas’s report to Congress lent authority to that plea. When Rosecrans moved, the strategic march brought him to the western base of Lookout Mountain with an elation greater than the success. He sent a brigade into deserted Chattanooga, called Crittenden toward Ringgold, ordered Thomas over Lookout gaps upon Lafayette, and seemed to think he had only to strike a flying enemy. Chickamauga threw the Union army back into the town under siege. Charles A. Dana’s inference that Rosecrans meditated retreat — later modified, always denied by Rosecrans — coloured Grant’s mind when he took the western command. Rosecrans claimed early October plans to seize Lookout Valley, fortify it, and reopen road and river from Bridgeport.
Cracker line and the battles of Chattanooga
Grant assumed command at Chattanooga and made personal inspection with Thomas and William F. Smith to Brown’s Ferry below Lookout Mountain — Confederate pickets opposite not firing, as if the garrison were prisoners feeding themselves. That night he ordered the route to Bridgeport opened — a “cracker line,” as soldiers termed the supply road after long short rations. Chattanooga sits on the south bank of the Tennessee where the river runs nearly west, at the north end of a valley five or six miles wide. Wauhatchie and the picket line secured the opening. The Army of the Cumberland was made comfortable; Ambrose Burnside at Knoxville remained nearly as desperate, a hundred miles from Big South Fork, animals starved, roads lined with carcasses, East Tennessee still giving beef and bread but not ammunition or coffee. Sherman repaired railroad from Memphis toward Corinth through hostile country — bridges destroyed, guerillas and cavalry about — three hundred and thirty miles that his entire command could not have held if completed.
Bragg’s letter warning noncombatants to withdraw Grant read as a device; a deserter and the detachment of Buckner toward Longstreet at Knoxville clarified the deception. On the night of the 21st and the days following, Thomas carried the first line; Sherman struck Missionary Ridge; Joseph Hooker fought Lookout Mountain. At midnight Grant ordered Sherman to attack at daylight, Hooker to intercept retreat or move on Rossville against the left and rear of the Missionary Ridge force, Thomas not to move until Hooker reached the ridge. The gallant charge and complete rout of the enemy — pursuit of Bragg — secured Chattanooga beyond doubt. Grant turned at once to relieving Knoxville; steamers built from old boats carried rations and ammunition up the Tennessee; the President had been particularly anxious for Burnside. Headquarters moved toward Nashville; Bragg gave way to Joseph E. Johnston. Vicksburg had opened the river; Chattanooga opened the gate to Georgia. Burnside’s East Tennessee relief answered Lincoln’s long anxiety for the loyal mountain population — roads, food, and strategic points the President had urged on every successive western commander since the war began.
Grant general-in-chief and the dual clock
After Chattanooga both western armies lay exhausted in winter camps. On the Confederate side Bragg was deprived of command though Jefferson Davis later brought him to Richmond as military adviser; public opinion compelled Johnston into the principal western command. Grant, commissioned lieutenant-general, briefly visited the West; Sherman assumed the Military Division of the Mississippi on 18 March and rode with the general-in-chief as far as Cincinnati — every hour important, conference on the rail. The coordinated clock of 1864 set Grant against Robert E. Lee in Virginia and Sherman against Johnston (then John Bell Hood) toward Atlanta. Grant’s instructions to Sherman were simple confidence: move against Johnston’s army, break it up, get into the interior as far as possible, inflict all damage against war resources — no detailed plan laid down. Sherman answered at once accepting with “infinite satisfaction” and laid his own proposed plan before Grant. Lee with the Confederate capital was the main end; Johnston with Atlanta an important obstacle almost an independent objective — less only because capturing Johnston would not close the rebellion as immediately as possessing Richmond and Lee’s army.
Sherman’s Georgia campaign to Atlanta
The western campaign opened with clockwork precision the same moment Grant crossed the Rapidan. From Dalton to the Chattahoochee, Sherman worked mountain and river lines with flanking marches while Johnston made skillful withdrawals. Peach Tree Creek and the summer battles followed Johnston’s replacement by Hood, who took the initiative as Davis wished. On 17 July Sherman began the march upon Atlanta: Thomas directly toward the city, John M. Schofield toward Decatur, James B. McPherson further left to strike the railroad between Decatur and Stone Mountain. Johnston took position on Peach Tree Creek to throw the greater part of his force against Thomas before Schofield and McPherson came up. Hood’s assaults failed to destroy Sherman; McPherson fell before Atlanta; the city was besieged and fell in September 1864. During the siege an abortive Confederate attempt linked to Andersonville prisoners failed; the capture closed the Georgia gate opened at Chickamauga.
While Democratic streets blazed with torches over a platform declaring the war a failure, Hood prepared evacuation, and the same newspapers that printed Vallandigham utterances announced Sherman’s entry into Georgia’s manufacturing metropolis — bane and antidote together. Lincoln’s reelection campaign rode that antidote. Sherman’s March to the Sea and Hood’s northward counterstroke — Franklin and Nashville — belong to the dedicated sequel march-to-the-sea-and-franklin-nashville-1864.
Chronology

Sep 1863: Chickamauga; siege of Chattanooga begins.
Oct–Nov 1863: Cracker line; Lookout Mountain; Missionary Ridge; Knoxville relief.
Mar–Apr 1864: Grant lieutenant-general; Sherman assumes western division; dual clock set.
May–Jul 1864: Sherman vs Johnston/Hood — Dalton to Peach Tree Creek.
Sep 1864: Fall of Atlanta; Chicago “war failure” platform answered.

events/compromise-of-1850.title: Compromise of 1850
events/compromise-of-1850.content:
Compromise of 1850
The Compromise of 1850 admitted California as a free State, arranged territories from the Mexican cession without a Missouri-style partition line, and stiffened a new Fugitive Slave Act under Millard Fillmore after Zachary Taylor’s death. The settlement postponed disunion for a decade and demoralized the old parties before the Kansas–Nebraska fight. Henry Clay offered the plan; John C. Calhoun, in his last Senate speech, demanded dual executive protection or looked toward dissolution; Thomas Hart Benton often dissented from Clay’s omnibus even while the measures passed; Alexander H. Stephens later read the package as enacting a Southern principle against Congressional restriction in the territories.
Crisis and Clay’s plan
California statehood and a Union in danger followed the failed sessions of 1848–49. Clay offered resolutions and an omnibus; Calhoun’s last speech demanded dual executive protection or looked toward dissolution; Calhoun died in the crisis. Stephens recalled the Speaker fight and Robert Toombs, and stated the principle he held the compromise to enact: abandon territorial partition and refuse Congressional restriction on slavery in the public domain — a claim that would structure his reading of 1854.
Fillmore and the measures
Taylor’s death brought Fillmore. California was admitted; Southern senators protested; the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 stiffened returns compared with 1793. Northern ferment against enforcement rose at once. Stephens printed the Georgia Platform of 1850 and treated Franklin Pierce’s election in 1852 as popular endorsement of the 1850 principle. Looking back, the 1850 contest demoralized old parties before Douglas’s Nebraska bill.
Two vocabularies
Benton opposed parts of Clay’s omnibus even while the settlement went through; Stephens later denied that 1854 “repealed” Missouri so much as applied 1850. The sibling kansas-nebraska-and-bleeding-kansas page carries that quarrel forward. The Compromise was a bundle of 1850 statutes and a grammar of peace that did not last a decade.
Chronology

1849–50: California crisis; Clay resolutions; Calhoun’s last speech.
Jul 1850: Taylor dies; Fillmore President.
Sep 1850: Compromise measures including Fugitive Slave Act.
1852: Pierce elected — Stephens’s endorsement reading.

events/donelson-and-shiloh-1862.title: Donelson and Shiloh (1862)
events/donelson-and-shiloh-1862.content:
Donelson and Shiloh (1862)
The twin western victories of Fort Donelson (February 1862) and Shiloh (6–7 April 1862) made Ulysses S. Grant a national name and cracked the Confederate defensive line in Kentucky and Tennessee. Washington watched the western theater with hope and then with shock at Shiloh’s cost; Henry W. Halleck sidelined Grant after the bloodiest fight the war had yet seen.
Henry and Donelson
Grant moved against the twin forts on the Tennessee and Cumberland. Fort Henry fell; gunboats were hit (the Essex boiler among the damage); Lloyd Tilghman was captured; the army turned on Donelson. Investment, naval operations, and a Confederate breakout attempt preceded the flight of John B. Floyd and Gideon Pillow and Simon B. Buckner’s surrender. Nathan Bedford Forrest escaped with about a thousand men. “Unconditional surrender” entered Northern speech; Halleck briefly skewed credit toward C. F. Smith, then relieved and restored Grant. Albert Sidney Johnston’s line shattered; panic filled Bowling Green’s council as the forts went down.
Shiloh
Advancing toward Corinth, Grant’s army lay at Pittsburg Landing and outlying camps when Johnston struck at dawn on 6 April. William T. Sherman’s stand, the day’s shock, and Don Carlos Buell’s arrival shaped the second day’s reverse. Johnston was killed; Grant later commented on P. G. T. Beauregard and councils of war. He denied the durable Northern story that the army had been simply “surprised,” even as casualties stunned the country. Halleck then took field command, advanced slowly on Corinth, and left Grant without a useful role — the low point before Vicksburg restored him.
Bridge to emancipation timing
Donelson and Shiloh ranked among the spring victories that raised hopes a military success might justify announcing a war measure against slavery — hopes Lincoln kept until Antietam. The forts, the battle, and Halleck’s eclipse of Grant opened the western war’s decisive command.
Chronology

Feb 1862: Henry and Donelson; unconditional surrender.
6–7 Apr 1862: Shiloh.
Spring 1862: Halleck to Corinth; Grant sidelined.

events/dred-scott-decision.title: Dred Scott Decision (1857)
events/dred-scott-decision.content:
Dred Scott Decision (1857)
The Dred Scott decision was the Supreme Court’s ruling in Dred Scott v. Sandford, announced on 6 March 1857 — two days after James Buchanan took the oath as President. The Court held that Scott could not sue in federal court as a citizen of the United States, and that Congress had no power to forbid slavery in the Territories. Those doctrines struck at the heart of the missouri-compromise-1820’s territorial line and at the new Republican party’s platform. Coming after the repeal of that compromise and the fighting in Kansas, the decision roughly doubled the intensity of the slavery quarrel in national politics. The human beings named in the suit were quickly forgotten; the constitutional principle the Court affirmed was defended in the South and denounced in the North with lasting bitterness.
How the case arose
Years before the Nebraska bill was even proposed, a Black man named Dred Scott began a suit in a local court in St. Louis, Missouri. He sought freedom for himself and his family from slavery. The case climbed through the courts until it reached the Supreme Court of the United States. Chief Justice Roger B. Taney delivered the controlling opinion. On the citizenship question, the Court denied that Scott — and, more broadly, persons of African descent held as slaves or descended from slaves — could claim the rights of a citizen for purposes of a federal lawsuit. On the territorial question, the Court denied that Congress could shut slavery out of the Territories. That second holding undermined the old Missouri Compromise logic that Congress could draw a free-soil line across western land, and it challenged every political programme that rested on congressional power to keep slavery out of new country.
The timing mattered. Slavery agitation had already been fierce because of the Kansas-Nebraska Act and the civil war that followed in Kansas. The public at large did not expect a judicial stroke of this kind. When the decision came down immediately after Buchanan’s inauguration, it arrived as a national shock rather than a quiet lawsuit’s end. Reaction in the country ran hot through the same season that also saw the Panic of 1857 — a financial crash kept light on this page, but part of the year’s atmosphere.
North, South, and the political breach
Judges themselves had differed sharply over the law and history of the case, so ordinary citizens were never going to accept the new doctrines with one mind. Far from healing the Union, the decision widened the breach between sections. Southern politicians treated the opinion as a vindication of slaveholders’ rights in the Territories. Northern opponents treated it as a dangerous claim that slavery could follow the flag wherever federal territory stretched. The persons in the litigation dropped from view; the constitutional principle remained the fight.
Stephen A. Douglas tried to show that his doctrine of popular sovereignty — letting settlers in a Territory decide slavery for themselves — could still live beside the Court’s ruling. Abraham Lincoln answered that the decision’s logic threatened freedom in the Territories and fitted a larger political design against free-soil hopes. That clash of readings did not stay in pamphlets. It became the central tension of the lincoln-douglas-debates-1858, especially at Freeport, where Lincoln asked whether the people of a Territory could still keep slavery out in practice despite what the Court had said. Douglas’s answer — that they could, through local police rules and non-cooperation — pleased many Illinois voters and alienated many Southern Democrats. In that sense the Dred Scott decision sits between kansas-nebraska-and-bleeding-kansas and the 1858 debates as the judicial stroke of the late 1850s.
Why it still mattered after the suit ended
The case did not free Scott by Court decree, and it did not settle the Union’s quarrel. It did something more lasting for politics: it moved the slavery fight from Congress and the Territories into the language of the Constitution itself. If Congress could not prohibit slavery in the Territories, Republican platforms that promised exactly that prohibition looked constitutionally doomed until the Court or the Constitution changed. If Black people could not be citizens for federal suit, the moral and legal status of millions became a matter of high judicial dogma rather than local litigation. Those stakes carried forward into the election of 1860 and the secession winter that followed Lincoln’s victory.
Chronology

Years before Nebraska: Scott’s suit begins in Missouri courts.
6 March 1857: Decision announced (two days after Buchanan’s inauguration).
1858: Freeport question and the Lincoln–Douglas debates — sibling page.

events/election-of-1824-house.title: Election of 1824 (House)
events/election-of-1824-house.content:
Election of 1824 (House)
The presidential election of 1824–25 produced no electoral majority. The House of Representatives then chose John Quincy Adams on a single ballot. The episode was the climax of the broken caucus system and the origin of the “corrupt bargain” charge that shaped the election-of-1828. It was both a constitutional contingency — House choice among the top three — and the founding grievance of the Jackson party.
Electoral college
The electoral vote stood Jackson 99, Adams 84, Crawford 41, Clay 37 (total 261; majority needed 131). Calhoun took the Vice Presidency with 182 votes after withdrawing from the presidential canvass in Pennsylvania. Clay, fourth, was excluded from the House contingent election under the Twelfth Amendment’s top-three rule. The figures were not in dispute; the fight was over what the House ought to do with them.
The House ballot of 9 February 1825
Clay’s friends sounded Adams on Kentucky — “Incedo super ignes” (“I walk over fires”). On 9 February 1825 the House elected Adams on a single ballot: thirteen States for Adams, seven for Jackson, four for Crawford. A committee of Webster, Vance, and Archer notified the President-elect. Clay was offered the Department of State — Western support and the Speaker’s influence translated into the first place in the Cabinet. Calhoun’s circle read the arrangement as an opposition system against Jackson.
Bargain charge and sequel
Jackson men named a democratic principle violated: Adams had been beaten in the popular and electoral sense, yet took the presidency by House coalition with Clay. The “corrupt bargain” charge became the campaign language of the next four years. In 1828 Adams was beaten 178–83; Clay was politically crippled and left the Democratic name for the National Republicans. The House election of 1824 thus seeded the party realignment that made Jackson’s victory feel like a people’s rebuke.
Chronology

Autumn 1824: Electoral votes cast; no majority for President.
9 Feb 1825: House elects Adams; Clay to State.
1825–28: Bargain charge sustains Jackson’s canvass — see election-of-1828.

events/election-of-1828.title: Election of 1828
events/election-of-1828.content:
Election of 1828
The presidential election of 1828 turned John Quincy Adams out and brought Andrew Jackson in — with John C. Calhoun again Vice President. Supporters treated the result as the people’s rebuke of the House election of 1825 (see election-of-1824-house). It closed the Adams presidency and installed the executive of Bank War and nullification proclamation. It also sat beside the Tariff of Abominations that opened the road toward nullification-crisis-1832-33.
Canvass
The years 1825–28 filled with Jackson electioneering, newspaper wars, and a Post Office under McLean that seemed ambiguous or Calhoun-leaning. Georgia nominated Crawford for Vice President while the legislature was already for Jackson as President — a remnant of old Crawford politics inside the Jackson triumph. The bargain charge of 1825 was the opposition’s constant text. Adams and Rush ran as a free-state ticket against Jackson and Calhoun.
Result
On 11 February 1829 the electoral count stood: Jackson President, Calhoun Vice President. The figures were Jackson 178, Adams 83; Rush equal with Adams on the ticket; Calhoun nearly equal with Jackson (Georgia’s shortfall remembered). The paradox mattered: an Adams–Rush free-state ticket against a Jackson–Calhoun slaveholding ticket, yet a large Northern vote for Jackson — framed as repudiation of the House coalition of 1825 rather than as a simple sectional census.
Aftermath
Jacksonian democracy claimed triumph over caucus and bargain. Martin Van Buren’s organizational role in New York and the national canvass helped build the party that would fight the Bank and the Sub-Treasury years (see martin-van-buren and democratic-party-jackson-to-buchanan). The same season’s high tariff and South Carolina’s Exposition and Protest pointed toward the nullification crisis. On 4 March 1829 Jackson was inaugurated; Adams retired from the White House toward the House career that would later center on petitions and the gag.
Chronology

1825–28: Bargain charge; Jackson canvass.
1828: Jackson and Calhoun elected.
4 Mar 1829: Jackson inaugurated; Adams leaves the presidency.

events/election-of-1840.title: Election of 1840 (Log-Cabin Campaign)
events/election-of-1840.content:
Election of 1840 (Log-Cabin Campaign)
The presidential election of 1840 — the Log-Cabin and Hard-Cider campaign — turned Martin Van Buren out of office and brought William Henry Harrison and John Tyler in on a whig-party tide. Behind the pageantry lay unfinished Bank War politics: Sub-Treasury versus national bank, hard money versus paper confidence, and the political cost of the panic-of-1837.
Hard times and party argument
After 1837, Van Buren’s Independent Treasury (sub-treasury) became the Democratic answer to divorcing bank and State. Whigs answered that destroying the second-bank-of-the-united-states and relying on “pet” deposit banks had produced the distress, and that a restored national bank and a change of men would restore confidence. Hard times after surplus and currency disorders of 1836–7 translated into votes. Democrats treated the Whig appeal as demagogic theater — log cabins and hard cider as substitutes for argument — yet the show had electoral power.
Log cabin and hard cider
Mass meetings, the cabin emblem (turned from a Democratic taunt into a Whig badge), barrels of cider, and songs made Harrison — the hero of Tippecanoe — a people’s candidate against the allegedly aristocratic Van Buren. The campaign perfected a new style of presidential canvassing: spectacle, emblem, and slogan over caucus manifesto. Whig victory reshaped House and Senate majorities that would greet the new administration.
Harrison, Tyler, and the sequel
Harrison’s triumph was brief. His death in April 1841 left Tyler President, and the Whig program of bank recharter soon collided with Tyler’s vetoes — the quarrel told on john-tyler. For this page, 1840 is the electoral verdict on the Panic and the Sub-Treasury fight: the moment Bank War alignments seized the presidency by popular festival.
Chronology

1837–39: Panic aftermath; Independent Treasury politics.
1840: Log-Cabin campaign; Harrison and Tyler elected.
1841: Harrison inaugurated and dies; Tyler succession; bank veto quarrel begins.

events/embargo-and-drift-to-war-1807-12.title: Embargo and Drift to War (1807–1812)
events/embargo-and-drift-to-war-1807-12.content:
Embargo and Drift to War (1807–1812)
Between the Chesapeake outrage of 1807 and the declaration of war in 1812, the United States tried to defend its ships and sailors without fighting — by shutting its own ports. The Long Embargo, Non-Intercourse, and related acts crushed New England commerce, fed smuggling into Canada, divided the country, and still failed to make Britain or France respect neutral rights. Under Madison the diplomacy sputtered through the Erskine arrangement and its collapse, Western war fever rose after Tippecanoe, and Congress finally chose war. This page holds that road. The campaigns, Ghent, and New Orleans live on war-of-1812.
Sailors’ rights and the Chesapeake
Britain’s war with Napoleon made American merchant ships valuable and American sailors suspect. British warships stopped American vessels and impressed men claimed as subjects. In June 1807 H.M.S. Leopard fired into the U.S. frigate Chesapeake off the Virginia capes, forced her to strike, and removed sailors. The country flared with anger. Jefferson demanded reparations and kept a gun-boat navy for harbor defense, but he would not declare war. Britain’s Orders in Council and Napoleon’s Berlin and Milan Decrees both treated neutral trade as a weapon; American ships were squeezed between the two.
The Long Embargo
In December 1807 Congress laid a general embargo: American vessels were forbidden to sail for foreign ports. Collectors’ messengers raced north; in New York at dawn, half-laden ships fled the harbor without clearances before boats could stop them. Coasters at first escaped the tightest bonds, so owners hastily turned registered foreign-traders into coasters and slipped goods toward Halifax and other British ports. Congress answered with Force Acts, bonds, and inspections that reached into warehouses and farm districts. New England called the policy ruin; flour piled up; sailors walked the streets; smuggling across the lakes and the Maine border became a way of life. State legislatures and town meetings talked of State interposition against the Force Act — language that later compact fights would echo. Jefferson left office with the embargo repealed in favor of lighter restrictions; the experiment had hurt America more visibly than it had bent London or Paris.
Non-Intercourse, Erskine, and Macon’s Bill
Madison inherited a quarrel half settled. Non-Intercourse forbade trade with Britain and France but opened other foreign ports. The British minister Erskine negotiated an arrangement that briefly raised hopes of Orders withdrawn; Canning disavowed the terms Erskine had exceeded, and the arrangement collapsed. Macon’s Bill No. 2 offered to restore trade with whichever belligerent first repealed its decrees and to keep restrictions on the other. Napoleon’s maneuvers and Britain’s persistence left Madison’s cabinet looking weak. Robert Smith at State gave way in practice to the President’s own pen; Gallatin held the Treasury as the one indispensable fiscal mind.
Tippecanoe and the war message
In the West, settlers blamed British agents in Canada for arming Tecumseh’s Indian coalition. William Henry Harrison’s fight at Tippecanoe in 1811 hardened the “War Hawk” mood in Congress. Clay and others argued that honor and western safety required a decision. In June 1812 Madison sent a war message; Congress declared war on Great Britain in a divided vote, with New England heavily opposed. The country entered the fight short of trained troops, ships, and money — the same shortages that would haunt the war-of-1812 campaigns and push postwar leaders toward a new national bank.
Chronology

Jun 1807: Chesapeake–Leopard.
Dec 1807 – Mar 1809: Long Embargo and Force Acts; repeal as Jefferson leaves.
1809–11: Non-Intercourse; Erskine fiasco; Macon’s Bill No. 2.
Nov 1811: Tippecanoe.
Jun 1812: War declared — continues on war-of-1812.

events/first-bull-run-1861.title: First Bull Run (1861)
events/first-bull-run-1861.content:
First Bull Run (1861)
The First Battle of Bull Run (First Manassas), fought on 21 July 1861, was the war’s first great field clash in Virginia. Irvin McDowell advanced from Washington against P. G. T. Beauregard at Manassas; the Union army was driven back; panic filled the roads toward the capital; and George B. McClellan was brought east to rebuild what became the Army of the Potomac. The fight sat between the firing on fort-sumter-1861 and the peninsula-campaign-1862 — the opening eastern proof that the rebellion would not be put down by a single summer parade.
Plans, Anaconda, and the three-months’ clock
Winfield Scott’s “Anaconda” plan and the need to use the 75,000 three-months’ militia before enlistments expired framed the July advance. Primary objects — capital safe, Baltimore open, Ohio line protected — had been substantially achieved in the first weeks; where to march and when to fight rose again with imperative demand. Scott did not intend the short-term militia to idle while three-years’ armies perfected organization for a fall and winter campaign. Arlington Heights, Harper’s Ferry, and pressure toward Manassas filled the interim programme. West Virginia’s mountain division of Virginia already showed that Alleghany geography could split a State; Bull Run would test whether a raw federal column could break the Confederate military league gathering south of the Potomac.
McDowell’s advance
It had been arranged that McDowell’s advance against the enemy at Manassas should begin 9 July; by extraordinary exertions he was ready and issued marching orders on 16 July. Organization was very imperfect and preparations far from complete. Many regiments reached him but two days before, some only on the day he moved. He started with barely wagons enough for ammunition and hospital supplies; tents, baggage, and rations were to follow. Utmost caution was enjoined to avoid another Vienna or Big Bethel disaster. Three things his marching orders held unpardonable: to come upon a battery or breastwork without knowledge of its position; to be surprised; to fall back. The army was a new, untried machine; men unused to fatigues and privations of a march made progress slow. With a cumbersome movement it felt its way toward Fairfax Court House and Centreville, enemy outposts retiring with time enough to spare.
Tyler commanded the first division (four brigades); Hunter the second (two); Heintzelman the third (three); Miles the fifth (two). Runyon’s fourth division stayed to guard communications. Aggregate strength about 34,320; marching column proper a little less than 28,000 including artillery — forty-nine guns — and a single battalion of cavalry.
Bull Run line and Blackburn’s Ford
On the morning of 18 July Tyler reached Centreville and found the enemy everywhere retired behind Bull Run — a winding, sluggish stream flowing southeasterly toward the Potomac, about thirty-two miles southwest of Washington, fordable in many places but often with steep, sometimes precipitous and rocky banks and wooded heights on the west. Three miles beyond lay Manassas Junction on a high open plateau where the railroads from Richmond and the Shenandoah Valley meet. Slight field-works with fourteen or fifteen heavy guns and about 2,000 men protected the junction. Beauregard, in command since 1 June, had gathered nearly 22,000 men and twenty-nine guns; Holmes from Aquia Creek raised the force above 23,000 and thirty-five guns. Instead of holding only the earthworks, Beauregard posted the army close down to Bull Run along some seven miles from the Manassas railroad to the stone bridge on the Warrenton turnpike, guarding the intermediate fords.
Tyler, ordered to observe roads but not bring on an engagement, followed toward Blackburn’s Ford near the center of Beauregard’s line. Lured by easy approach, reconnaissance became skirmish and skirmish a preliminary battle: sixty men fallen, two field-pieces extricated with difficulty, one regiment retreated in confusion, three others deployed for a new charge before McDowell’s restraint closed the day. The lesson of imperfect organization and over-eager advance was written before the main battle.
Battle, reverse, and panic
The main action of 21 July turned McDowell’s flanking movement against the Confederate left into a hard fight on the plateaus and fords west of Bull Run. Joseph E. Johnston’s Valley troops, arriving by the Manassas Gap Railroad, stiffened Beauregard at the decisive hours — the junction’s strategic meaning made real when two Confederate armies met on the same field. Union partial successes of the morning gave way to afternoon reverse; the new machine broke under counterattack and the disordered retreat toward Washington became panic on the roads among soldiers and civilian spectators who had come out as to a spectacle. Ninety-day men and early three-year volunteers mixed under imperfect staff work; ammunition wagons and hospital trains could not steady a column that had been forbidden to fall back and then fell back in confusion. The meaning for Lincoln’s Administration was plain: three-months’ war was over; a long war of three-years’ armies had begun. Congress in special session, already meeting under the April call, faced a war of years rather than a summer’s correction of rebellion.
Aftermath: McClellan and the Army of the Potomac
On the day after the battle McClellan was ordered to Washington. He arrived 26 July and next day assumed command of the division of the Potomac — troops in and around Washington on both sides of the river. His later report recalled about 50,000 infantry, less than 1,000 cavalry, and 650 artillerymen with nine imperfect field batteries of thirty pieces when he took charge. Tens of thousands of infantry gathered for the long Virginia war. Special session of Congress, the contraband question, Frémont in the West, and organization of the Army of the Potomac filled the weeks that followed. European neutrality already disappointed Northern expectation that England and France would favor the Union; Bull Run’s reverse deepened the need for a disciplined eastern army before foreign recognition questions hardened. Bull Run thus stands between Sumter’s uprising and the Peninsula bid of 1862 — the first eastern field where raw courage met imperfect organization and found that courage alone did not take Manassas.
Chronology

May–Jun 1861: Call to arms; Anaconda; three-months’ clock; West Virginia rising.
16 Jul 1861: McDowell’s marching orders.
18 Jul: Centreville; Blackburn’s Ford reconnaissance-skirmish.
21 Jul: Battle of Bull Run / First Manassas; Union reverse and retreat.
26–27 Jul: McClellan arrives and assumes command about Washington.

events/fort-sumter-1861.title: Fort Sumter (1861)
events/fort-sumter-1861.content:
Fort Sumter (1861)
The Fort Sumter crisis — from Major Robert Anderson’s move into the brick fort in Charleston harbor through the bombardment of April 1861 — opened the Civil War as both a local possession fight and a national summons to arms. Lincoln’s cabinet debated bread versus war; Alexander H. Stephens argued South Carolina’s right after secession and a Northern “breach of faith”; the North rose to muster when the first gun spoke; the people’s road to war closed at the fort’s fall.
Anderson and the Star of the West
About 26 December 1860 Anderson secretly transferred his garrison from Fort Moultrie to Fort Sumter; South Carolina commissioners reached Washington the same day. After John B. Floyd’s departure the Cabinet régime stiffened; the relief steamer Star of the West was fired on in January; Anderson’s threatened retaliation was referred to Washington. Through the secession-winter-1860-61 Sumter and Pickens remained the twin symbols of federal presence inside claimed Confederate territory — a truce of exhaustion more than a settlement.
Lincoln’s decision and the Fox expedition
Lincoln’s Cabinet debated Sumter on 29 March 1861 amid advice from Gustavus V. Fox, Stephen A. Hurlbut, and an unexpected attitude from Winfield Scott. The policy that issued was to send bread to Anderson — relief framed as humanity and holding the fort, not as invasion rhetoric — with notice to Governor Francis W. Pickens. Fox’s expedition sailed; parallel reinforcement went toward Pickens. P. G. T. Beauregard opened fire; Sumter surrendered after bombardment; the North rose. On 15 April Lincoln called for 75,000 militia. Ulysses S. Grant later remembered the country’s answer to that gun as the start of Northern mustering.
Two readings of the first shot
Stephens insisted that once South Carolina had seceded she held Sumter by right of a sovereign State, that Northern failure to evacuate was a breach of understanding, and that the 15 April proclamation was usurpation driving Virginia, Arkansas, Tennessee, and North Carolina out. Lincoln’s government treated the firing as rebellion’s choice of war against a government still offering peaceable relief. Both readings stayed on the table; the event is the fort, the expedition, the bombardment, and the call to arms.
Chronology

26 Dec 1860: Anderson to Sumter.
Jan 1861: Star of the West fired on.
Apr 1861: Fox expedition; bombardment; surrender; 75,000 called.

events/fremantle-tour-confederacy-1863.title: Fremantle’s Tour of the Confederacy (1863)
events/fremantle-tour-confederacy-1863.content:
Fremantle’s Tour of the Confederacy (1863)
In the spring and early summer of 1863 a British Coldstream Guards officer on leave, Arthur James Lyon Fremantle, crossed into the Confederacy from Mexico and rode, staged, and railed his way from the Rio Grande cotton trade to Longstreet’s headquarters at Gettysburg. His published diary — Three Months in the Southern States — is the fullest outsider’s walk through the Southern war that year: blockade cotton, Texas society, the swamp road past Grant’s Vicksburg operations, Johnston and Bragg, Charleston’s forts, Jefferson Davis at Richmond, three days with Lee’s army in Pennsylvania, and a Northern exit through the New York draft riots. This page follows that itinerary. The battle of Gettysburg itself is told on gettysburg-1863; Vicksburg’s siege spine stays on vicksburg-campaign-1863.
Why he went, and how he entered
At the war’s outbreak he had felt nearly indifferent, with a slight English leaning toward the North from dislike of slavery. Admiration for Southern gallantry and anger at what he called Northern bullying reversed that feeling. He published the day-by-day diary because the blockade made Southern news arrive in Britain mainly through Northern papers. He did not hide rough manners in the “wilder” country, yet he ended convinced that such unanimity and courage marked a people destined for independence.
He left England in the mail steamer Atrato, passed St Thomas and Havana, and reached the Rio Grande bar on 1 April among some seventy merchantmen. Cotton that sold for six cents a pound in Galveston fetched thirty-six at the mouth. Within hours of landing he saw Lynch law: a man’s body under a mesquite with the rope still on it. Brownsville and Matamoros lived on cotton, consuls, and armed riders in flannel and lone-star hats. From there the road ran inland by stage and Mexican saddle across mesquite desert to San Antonio and the new railroad to Houston.
Texas: Houston, Galveston, Sam Houston
Houston was crowded with Galveston refugees, officers, and cotton men. At General Scurry’s mess the company drank the Queen’s health, preferred shot-guns and revolvers to sabres, and treated the scattered white population as a rough aristocracy. In the cars sat Sam Houston — old San Jacinto hero, former president of Texas, deposed as anti-secession governor — talkative and vain. Stages pushed east through Huntsville and Marshall toward the Mississippi, already half closed by Federal gunboats above and below Vicksburg.
Across the river into Johnston’s theatre
The left bank was flooded. Passage meant yawls and skiffs through Log Bayou and Lake Concordia — alligators, snakes, ten days without proper sleep — to Vidalia and Natchez. A hired driver named Nelson, a slave paying weekly hire to work on his own account, said he did not want to see Yankees or be freer than he was. News came that Jackson would fall and that Joseph E. Johnston had taken command. Fremantle reached the wrecked capital, ate at Johnston’s mess, and watched the general judge Grant’s vigour: the Federals had crossed below Vicksburg, seized Jackson, and invested a garrison of about twenty thousand with perhaps seventy-five thousand. Johnston blamed Confederate combinations wrecked by straggling and by political officers who would not punish. He walked the last miles into ruined Jackson carrying his guest’s cloaks. The diary’s Vicksburg pages are a visitor’s snapshot beside Grant’s campaign narrative on vicksburg-campaign-1863.
Bragg’s army, then Charleston
From Mobile and Montgomery the tour turned to Chattanooga and Bragg’s camps around Shelbyville and Wartrace. Leonidas Polk talked Murfreesborough and Shiloh; Colonel St Leger Grenfell — French lancers, Turkish service, Morgan’s adjutant — inspected cavalry in a red forage-cap. Patrick Cleburne, once a private in the British 41st, reviewed Arkansas troops in homespun. Open-air preaching drew thousands. The press still attacked Davis and generals in print. Liddell’s weak regiments showed how thin some brigades had grown.
Then Atlanta, Augusta, and Charleston. At Fort Sumter the guest counted scores of guns, heard of the Keokuk’s eleven-inch piece fished up after the ironclad fight, and looked out to a bar crowded with blockaders. Beauregard and Ripley showed the harbor war that still held the city in mid-June.
Richmond
Petersburg and Richmond brought the civil face of the Confederacy. Secretary Seddon, Judah P. Benjamin, and Jefferson Davis received the visitor. Davis spoke of British neutrality and of the military schooling of Confederate generals; the mood in the room felt heavy. Captured flags hung in the capitol. Drewry’s Bluff guarded the James. For Davis as president across the whole war, see jefferson-davis and confederate-states-government; this stop is the diary’s closest look at Richmond in June 1863.
With Lee to Gettysburg — and out through New York
From Culpeper the British guest rode with Longstreet’s corps into Pennsylvania. Introduced to Lee on 30 June near Chambersburg, he watched the three days at Gettysburg from the Confederate side — Lee’s calm, Longstreet’s laugh after the failed assault, Lee’s words that it was he who had lost the fight. Those hours belong on gettysburg-1863 and robert-e-lee; they are the climax of the tour, not a second full battle narrative here.
The retreat carried him to Hagerstown and across into the North. Philadelphia and New York looked rich beside Richmond. Broadway showed recruiting bounties; then the draft riots of mid-July filled the streets with fire and mob cries. He sailed for England on the China. A postscript still asked how such a people could be subjugated.
What the tour adds to this wiki
Campaigns and cabinets elsewhere in this wiki tell what armies and governments did. Fremantle’s summer adds the texture of travel: cotton prices at the Rio Grande, Lynch law on the border, Sam Houston in a railroad car, swamp skiffs under Vicksburg’s shadow, Johnston’s mess talk, Sumter under blockade, Jefferson Davis in a quiet Richmond interview, and the shock of New York’s riot after Gettysburg. It is one British officer’s journey — not a complete history of the Confederacy — but the densest single outsider’s walk through the Southern war in 1863.
Chronology

2 Mar–1 Apr: Approach via Atrato, Havana, Rio Grande bar.
2–30 Apr: Matamoros/Brownsville; stages to San Antonio and Houston.
1–17 May: Houston/Galveston; Sam Houston; swamp crossing to Natchez.
18–24 May: Johnston, Jackson ruins, Vicksburg investment.
25 May–5 Jun: Mobile–Montgomery; Bragg’s army.
6–15 Jun: Charleston and Fort Sumter.
16–19 Jun: Richmond — Davis, Benjamin, Seddon.
20 Jun–9 Jul: Lee’s army; Gettysburg; retreat to Hagerstown.
10–15 Jul: Northern cities; New York draft riots; voyage home.
