events/gettysburg-1863.title: Gettysburg (1863)
events/gettysburg-1863.content:
Gettysburg (1863)
The battle of Gettysburg (1–3 July 1863) and Lincoln’s November address at the soldiers’ cemetery form the eastern hinge of mid-war: Robert E. Lee’s invasion of Pennsylvania stopped; George G. Meade holding the field; a British officer watching from James Longstreet’s side; the President defining the war’s meaning months later. The same Fourth of July that saw Lee turn south also saw Vicksburg surrender on the Mississippi — a dual Northern jubilee even though the two Union armies never met.
Invasion and Meade
After Chancellorsville, Joseph Hooker found himself again on the north bank of the Rappahannock and began to think of crossing; as he recovered, he saw that despite three days’ slaughter he had as yet fought no battle. Lee moved into Pennsylvania. Hooker thought of re-crossing; command passed to Meade on 28 June. Meade’s assumption order showed a plain confidence — free from humility and bluster — acknowledging an eminent predecessor while relying on companions in arms. To Halleck he simply acknowledged receipt.
Arthur Fremantle, a British officer riding with Longstreet’s corps on a Southern tour (the longer journey is on fremantle-tour-confederacy-1863), was introduced to Lee on 30 June before marching from Chambersburg. He found Lee almost the handsomest man of his age he had ever seen — fifty-six, tall, broad-shouldered, thorough soldier, courteous, few enemies, no small vices. That evening Longstreet told him Hooker had been disrated and Meade appointed — honourable and respectable, though perhaps not so bold as Hooker. Officers expected battle on that road rather than a march to Harrisburg; Ewell’s movements and the concentration toward Gettysburg closed the invasion’s open phase.
First of July
Hill’s and Ewell’s troops drove the Union advance through and beyond the town. Fremantle’s corps brought up the rear through a South Mountain pass after Hill’s corps and part of Ewell’s had passed Greenwood; he made acquaintance with Colonel Walton, chief of artillery to Longstreet. The enemy was driven into a strong position whose right appeared to rest on a cemetery on a high ridge to the right of Gettysburg as the Confederates looked at it. Hill, unwell and delicate, reported two divisions engaged, the enemy driven four miles, many prisoners, cannon, and colours taken. At supper Longstreet spoke of the enemy’s position as “very formidable” and expected strong intrenchments overnight. Universal feeling in the army was profound contempt for an enemy beaten so constantly under so many disadvantages. John Reynolds fell on the Union side — the first day’s price of the stand that held Cemetery Ridge for the army gathering behind it. Thousands of prisoners filled Confederate reports; the night closed with Meade’s army filing onto the ridge the invaders already called formidable.
Second of July
Fremantle’s party rose at 3.30 a.m.; Lawley insisted on riding despite illness. By 5 a.m. they held the commanding position of the day before; Fremantle climbed a tree with Captain Schreibert of the Prussian army. Below sat Lee, Hill, Longstreet, and Hood in consultation — Longstreet and Hood assisting deliberations by whittling. Councils and delay stretched toward a late-afternoon assault on the Union left and the Round Tops–Cemetery axis. Fighting won ground at fearful cost; evening left the Confederate line short of the ridge that still looked down on the open approaches. The dead and mortally wounded of both sides covered the contested ground Fremantle would ride over at dawn of the third.
Third of July and retreat
At 6 a.m. Fremantle rode the ground won the evening before; dead were being buried, many mortally wounded still lying about — including Federals in bad imitations of Zouave costume whose glazed eyes opened in a painfully imploring manner. Lee and Longstreet’s staff reconnoitred under sharpshooter and shell fire. Pickett’s division, just up and weak (under 5,000) for want of two brigades, was to bear the brunt of Longstreet’s attack with Heth and Pettigrew of Hill’s corps across the open distance between the lines. At noon Longstreet’s dispositions were made — troops deployed and lying in the woods, batteries ready; the General dismounted and slept a short time. The assault failed. Fremantle found Longstreet at the edge of the wood, calm, laughing: they had attacked and been repulsed — look there — Confederates slowly and sulkily returning in small broken parties under heavy artillery. Lee met a brigadier almost crying over the state of his brigade, shook hands, and said cheerfully that all this had been his fault — “it is I that have lost this fight, and you must help me out of it in the best way you can.” Fremantle saw him reanimate dispirited troops and magnanimously take the whole weight of the repulse.
The Army of Northern Virginia retreated toward the Potomac. Meade did not destroy it in a Napoleonic pursuit — a controversy that outlived the campaign. On 4 July Fremantle woke to thefts by stragglers who would later swagger as heroes of Gettysburg; Longstreet was in high amusement at a Federal flag of truce announcing, among other things, that Longstreet was wounded and a prisoner.
Address and dual jubilee
The Fourth of July paired Gettysburg with vicksburg-campaign-1863: the Mississippi opened as Lee turned south. Port Hudson’s fall shortly completed the river’s freedom. Care of the dead and wounded fell largely to Pennsylvania’s military and local authorities. Governor Curtin gave the duty thoughtful attention; the design of a permanent cemetery where remains of fallen heroes might be gathered was conceived and begun. Citizen soldiery from seventeen loyal States filled the field. On 19 November the cemetery dedication brought Lincoln’s Gettysburg Address — short words that stood as the war’s civic statement beside Everett’s longer oration. Meade’s later Rapidan operations and the Mine Run campaign of autumn 1863 did not destroy Lee; the Army of the Potomac held the strategic fruit of July without a Napoleonic pursuit. Defeat of the peace party at the autumn polls of 1863 owed much to Gettysburg and Vicksburg together.
Chronology

Jun 1863: Lee invades Pennsylvania; Meade takes command (28 Jun).
1 Jul: First day — Reynolds killed; Cemetery Ridge held.
2 Jul: Second day — assaults on the Union flanks.
3 Jul: Pickett–Pettigrew charge fails; Lee’s “I have lost this fight.”
4 Jul: Dual jubilee with Vicksburg; Confederate retreat begins.
19 Nov 1863: Gettysburg Address.

events/hampton-roads-conference-1865.title: Hampton Roads Conference (1865)
events/hampton-roads-conference-1865.content:
Hampton Roads Conference (1865)
The Hampton Roads conference of February 1865 brought Abraham Lincoln and William H. Seward together with Confederate commissioners Alexander H. Stephens, John A. Campbell, and R. M. T. Hunter aboard a steamer in the Roads — a peace meeting that produced no reunion terms and left Jefferson Davis and Lincoln in contrasted tempers afterward. Grant arranged the commissioners’ passage through the lines; Stephens met him at City Point before the conference proper.
Blair’s feelers
Francis P. Blair, Sr., visited Richmond with feelers that included a Monroe Doctrine / Mexico strand — reunion energy turned against foreign occupation of Mexico. The Blair visits opened the path to City Point. The commissioners reached the Union lines about 29 January claiming an understanding with Grant; Edwin M. Stanton blocked; Lincoln sent Thomas T. Eckert. Stephens’s first meeting with Grant at City Point preceded the conference.
The conference
Aboard the River Queen (and the Hampton Roads meeting that gives the event its name) the parties found no agreement on the terms of restored Union. Lincoln would not treat with the Confederacy as a coequal nation; the commissioners could not accept submission without guarantees their government would ratify. Messages of Davis and Lincoln framed the meeting; afterward Davis’s wrathful public reaction contrasted with Lincoln’s intensified conciliation — the temper that runs into the second inaugural.
Not the false peaces
The conference is distinct from the Greeley Niagara talks and the Jaquess–Gilmore mission of 1864 — earlier false or partial peaces. Hampton Roads is the last serious table before appomattox-and-end-of-confederate-arms-1865: war continued; armies, not protocols, closed the rebellion.
Chronology

Jan 1865: Blair in Richmond; commissioners to the lines.
Feb 1865: Hampton Roads conference; no terms.
Mar–Apr 1865: Second inaugural; Appomattox sequel.

events/hartford-convention.title: Hartford Convention
events/hartford-convention.content:
Hartford Convention
The Hartford Convention was a meeting of New England Federalists at Hartford, Connecticut, in December 1814 and early January 1815, while the war-of-1812 still burned along the coast and the lakes. Delegates from Massachusetts, Connecticut, and Rhode Island — with a few men from New Hampshire and Vermont counties — sat in secret for three weeks and issued a report that blamed the Republican administration for ruinous war, demanded constitutional amendments to protect commercial States, and threatened further resistance if abuses continued. Peace news from Ghent and the victory at New Orleans arrived soon after. The convention did not dissolve the Union, but Republicans branded it as disloyal, and the Federalist party never recovered nationally.
Why New England called a convention
From the Embargo years through 1814, New England’s shipping interest paid the heaviest price for commercial warfare with Britain. Militia disputes, conscription talk in Congress, blocked ports, and unpaid national debts convinced many Federalists that the Constitution, “under the persons then in power,” had failed to secure the rights the commercial States expected. The Massachusetts legislature debated a conference of New England States and, over fierce minority protests that warned of separate peace or civil war, chose twelve delegates to meet at Hartford on 15 December 1814. Connecticut and Rhode Island accepted, limiting their men to measures consistent with membership in the Union. Vermont declined; New Hampshire’s council blocked a full State delegation. Republican newspapers jeered that a “new federal edifice” of three legs would tip over.
Secret sittings and the report
Twenty-three gentlemen organized in the Council Chamber of the State House with George Cabot in the chair. Doors closed. Outside, rumors ran wild: neutrality like Nantucket’s, a separate New England confederation, even a new constitution. Some radical writers demanded that the convention stop the war and reopen commerce at once; a few towns talked of withholding national taxes. Inside, the majority was cautious. The public report, released when the body adjourned in early January 1815, urged patience before open resistance. It traced the country’s misery to bad administration — lust of power, patronage, waste, heavy taxes, and an unjust war — and argued that a change of rulers might cure what was not yet proved permanent. If combinations of men or States went on monopolizing power and trampling commercial rights, then separation might become better than forced union. For the present the convention proposed constitutional amendments: limits on embargo powers, changes in representation and admission of new States, restraints on successive presidents from the same region, and other checks aimed at Virginia’s long hold on the executive. Commissioners were to carry the proposals to Washington.
Aftermath
Before those commissioners could accomplish anything, the Treaty of Ghent and Jackson’s victory at New Orleans transformed the political weather. What might have looked like a hard bargain in wartime looked like defeatism in peacetime. Republicans used “Hartford” as a synonym for disloyalty for a generation. Federalists who had opposed the war on constitutional and commercial grounds found themselves unable to elect a national ticket. Later States’-rights movements sometimes remembered Hartford as an early protest against conscription and commercial ruin; Unionists remembered it as a warning against sectional conventions in wartime. The military and diplomatic close of the war remains on war-of-1812; the commercial road that made New England desperate begins on embargo-and-drift-to-war-1807-12.
Chronology

Oct–Nov 1814: Massachusetts call; Connecticut and Rhode Island join.
15 Dec 1814 – early Jan 1815: Hartford sittings; report published.
Feb 1815 onward: Ghent and New Orleans news; Federalist national collapse.

events/john-brown-harpers-ferry.title: John Brown and Harpers Ferry (1859)
events/john-brown-harpers-ferry.content:
John Brown and Harpers Ferry (1859)
In October 1859 John Brown led a small band against the federal armory at Harpers Ferry, Virginia (today West Virginia). His aim was to seize weapons and spark a slave uprising. The raid failed within days. Brown was captured, tried, and executed. Even so, the episode struck many contemporaries as the dramatic climax of a decade of political shocks since 1852. In the South it hardened fear and fury on the road to the election of 1860. This page holds that political catastrophe — the man, the raid, and the sectional reaction — rather than a novelistic siege diary.
Who John Brown was
Brown was born in Connecticut in 1800, of Puritan descent. When he was five, his family moved to Ohio, then still a comparative wilderness, and he grew up a strong boy of the woods. Contemporaries found him hard to classify: devout, violent, and driven by a hatred of slavery that did not fit ordinary party politics. Before Virginia, he had already appeared in the Kansas territorial war. The kansas-nebraska-and-bleeding-kansas struggle — including the Pottawatomie killings associated with his name — foreshadowed the Ferry without explaining it fully. Kansas was a guerrilla fight over whether a Territory would enter as slave or free. Harpers Ferry was something else: an attempt to turn federal arms into the tools of a slave insurrection inside a slave State.
The raid
Brown and his followers seized the armory and held it briefly, hoping enslaved people in the neighborhood would rise and join them. They did not gather the rising he expected. Local militia and federal forces closed in. The raid collapsed. Brown survived the fighting long enough to face Virginia justice; several of his men were killed or taken. The tactical story in the sources used here is thinner than the political meaning: what matters for the national crisis is that a Northern abolitionist had struck a United States arsenal on Southern soil in the name of ending slavery by force.
Southern reaction and the path to 1860
In the South the raid was read as proof that Northern antislavery politics could end in massacre. Newspapers and politicians treated Brown not as a lone madman only, but as the logical extreme of a sectional movement that denounced slavery as a sin and organized against its extension. Fear of further raids mixed with anger at Northern sympathy for Brown after his capture. That reaction fed the temper of the secession-winter-1860-61 even before ballots were cast for Lincoln. The Ferry sat among the post-1852 shocks — Kansas, Dred Scott, Lecompton, the debates — that made ordinary elections feel like preludes to disunion.
Northern responses were divided. Some condemned the violence while still calling slavery wrong. Others treated Brown as a martyr once he faced the gallows. Republican leaders, including Abraham Lincoln in later public speeches such as Cooper Institute, had to distance their party from Brown’s methods while holding their ground against slavery’s expansion. That distancing belongs on Lincoln’s entity and the 1860 canvass more than as a second raid narrative here. The point for this page is simpler: Harpers Ferry made the slavery quarrel feel physical and immediate to people who had previously argued it mainly in Congress, courts, and Territories.
What the sources do not settle
Minute marine assault command names, full trial transcripts, and scaffold speeches are not dense in the digests behind this wiki. The attested core is clear enough without them. Brown tried to arm a slave rising from a federal arsenal; the rising failed; the South’s reaction deepened the sectional breach as the country moved toward 1860. Together with the dred-scott-decision and the lincoln-douglas-debates-1858, the Ferry helps explain why the presidential election of the next year arrived with so little trust left between sections.
Chronology

1856: Kansas violence (prelude).
October 1859: Harpers Ferry raid; capture and trial follow.
1860: Election and secession winter sequel.

events/kansas-nebraska-and-bleeding-kans.title: Kansas–Nebraska and Bleeding Kansas (1854–1858)
events/kansas-nebraska-and-bleeding-kans.content:
Kansas–Nebraska and Bleeding Kansas
The Kansas–Nebraska Act of 1854 opened the northern plains to settlement under popular sovereignty and tore up the old Missouri Compromise geography that had kept slavery out of that latitude. Civil strife in Kansas followed — Border Ruffians, a bogus legislature, free-state resistance, and national spectacle through 1856. The crisis nationalized Abraham Lincoln and later split Stephen A. Douglas from James Buchanan over the Lecompton constitution. Northerners called the Act a repeal of the Missouri line; Alexander H. Stephens and other Southern readers insisted it merely applied the Compromise of 1850’s abandonment of territorial partition.
The Act and two names for it
Douglas’s Nebraska bill organized territories and opened them under popular sovereignty; the Missouri line of 36°30′ fell for those lands. The North exploded; Republican organization was born in the wreck of the old party system. Stephens insisted 1854 carried out 1850’s abandonment of territorial partition and Congressional restriction — not a “repeal” in his sense — and pointed to Senate composition and Franklin Pierce’s mandate. The quarrel of names was a quarrel of principle: whether Congress had ever had power to draw a free-soil line, and whether 1850 had already surrendered that power.
Bleeding Kansas
Border Ruffians crossed from Missouri. Hundreds of bona fide Kansas votes faced thousands of Missourians for a bogus legislature that wrote proslavery statutes into a “legal despotism.” The Topeka free-state constitution answered. The sack of Lawrence and the Pottawatomie killings followed; civil war in the territory became a national spectacle through 1856 conventions and scenes of “congressional ruffianism” in Washington. John Brown’s later raid at Harper’s Ferry grew from this decade’s violence.
Lecompton and Douglas’s revolt
Buchanan backed the Lecompton constitution; Douglas revolted in the name of popular sovereignty; Kansas voters rejected Lecompton in the contests of late 1857 and early 1858. That revolt set the Illinois Senate stage for the lincoln-douglas-debates-1858 and sat beside the dred-scott-decision’s judicial blow. Stephens marked Buchanan’s departure from the 1850–54 grammar as proximate trouble. The decade’s violence pointed on toward Harper’s Ferry without closing the Union’s quarrel.
Chronology

1854: Kansas–Nebraska Act.
1855–56: Bogus legislature; Topeka; Bleeding Kansas.
1857–58: Lecompton; Douglas revolt; popular rejection.

events/lincoln-douglas-debates-1858.title: Lincoln–Douglas Debates (1858)
events/lincoln-douglas-debates-1858.content:
Lincoln–Douglas Debates (1858)
In 1858 Abraham Lincoln and Stephen A. Douglas met in a series of joint debates across Illinois while competing for a United States Senate seat. Douglas was the incumbent Democrat and the famous author of popular sovereignty — the idea that settlers in a Territory should decide slavery for themselves. Lincoln was the Republican challenger, less known nationally, arguing that slavery’s expansion must be stopped and that the dred-scott-decision threatened free soil in the Territories. The debates nationalized Lincoln’s name and forced Douglas to explain how popular sovereignty could survive after the Supreme Court had seemed to protect slavery in the Territories. Full town-by-town transcripts are not itemized in the digests used here; Ottawa and Freeport carry the attested historical weight.
Why Illinois became a national stage
Douglas had broken with President Buchanan over the Lecompton Constitution — a pro-slavery frame for Kansas that many free-state settlers rejected. That revolt split Democrats and drew national eyes to Illinois. At the same time Republican strength was rising after Kansas and Dred Scott. The Senate race therefore felt larger than one State’s legislature choosing a senator. It became a referendum on Territories, the Court, and the future of the Democratic party.
Some influential Republican voices, including Horace Greeley’s circle, wished Illinois Republicans to adopt Douglas as the anti-Lecompton champion rather than fight him. Lincoln insisted the Republican cause must be trusted to its own undoubted friends — men who truly cared for free-soil results, not temporary Democratic allies. That choice set up the joint debates. The canvass ran through counties from the antislavery north of Illinois toward the more conservative southward districts, with each man answering the other before crowds that newspapers reported across the country.
Ottawa and Freeport
At Ottawa, in the northern or antislavery part of the State, Douglas pressed Lincoln with creed questions. He read a set of strong antislavery resolutions and wrongly claimed Lincoln had helped frame and pass them, then demanded whether Lincoln stood by each article. The aim was to pin Lincoln as an extreme abolitionist before Illinois voters who might accept free-soil limits but fear racial equality or disunion talk.
At Freeport Lincoln turned the pressure around. He asked whether the people of a Territory could lawfully exclude slavery before statehood despite the Dred Scott ruling. Douglas answered that they could still do so in practice: if territorial legislatures withheld local police protection and cooperation, slavery could not take root even if the Court said Congress could not ban it. That answer — later called the Freeport Doctrine — is the main historical incident of the debates in the sources behind this page. It pleased many Illinois Democrats who wanted local control without open war on the Court. It angered Southern Democrats who wanted the Court’s territorial protection made real, not hollowed out by “unfriendly” local legislation. The doctrine thus helped Douglas at home and hurt him later in the fractured Democratic conventions of 1860.
Outcome and aftermath
Douglas won re-election to the Senate. Lincoln lost the seat. Yet Lincoln gained a national reputation. Speeches in Ohio and elsewhere after the canvass carried his arguments beyond Illinois. The debates sit inside the same struggle that buried Lecompton and kept Kansas from entering as a slave State under that constitution. They did not decide the presidency of 1860, but they made Lincoln a Union figure Southern and Northern audiences already knew when the secession winter arrived. Douglas’s Freeport answer, meanwhile, remained a wound inside the Democracy: Northern popular-sovereignty men and Southern Court men could no longer pretend they wanted the same territorial future.
This page holds the 1858 encounter itself. Cooper Institute, the Chicago nomination, and the election of Lincoln belong on his entity and on secession-winter-1860-61. Harpers Ferry the next year belongs on its own event page. Together those episodes show how fast the late 1850s moved from courtroom doctrine and Senate debate toward open rupture.
Chronology

1858: Joint debates; Freeport Doctrine; Douglas re-elected senator.
1859–60: Cooper Institute and nomination — see Lincoln entity / secession winter.

events/louisiana-purchase-and-governance.title: Louisiana Purchase and Governance (1803– )
events/louisiana-purchase-and-governance.content:
Louisiana Purchase and Governance
In 1803 the United States bought Louisiana from France — New Orleans and a vast western country whose exact inland borders no one could yet draw on a finished map. The purchase doubled the republic’s claimed domain overnight, settled the fear that a strong France might close the Mississippi, and forced Congress to invent territorial governments for people who had lived under Spanish and French law. Governing that prize, arguing with Spain over West Florida, and calming Northern fears that the new West would swamp the old States filled Jefferson’s remaining years and Madison’s early ones. The burr-conspiracy grew out of the same unsettled dominion.
Purchase and delivery
Robert Livingston and James Monroe closed a treaty in Paris when Napoleon suddenly offered not only New Orleans but the whole of Louisiana. Jefferson had doubted whether the Constitution allowed such a purchase, yet he submitted the treaty and the Senate consented. French prefect Laussat received the province from Spain and soon delivered New Orleans to American commissioners; the flag change on the Place d’Armes ended European rule at the mouth of the river. School histories of the day taught the stroke as the great act of Jefferson’s presidency; fuller narratives add his constitutional scruples and the scramble to staff customs houses and courts.
Pierre Samuel du Pont, then advising from the French side of the Atlantic friendship with Jefferson, urged buying New Orleans rather than fighting for it — a diplomatic footnote that sits also on the early e-i-du-pont-de-nemours-and-company story. The practical American problem was simpler: how to rule a Creole city and an Indian and settler hinterland without Spanish cooperation on the Florida border.
Governance and boundaries
Congress split the purchase into territories (Orleans toward the mouth; Louisiana / upper districts inland) and debated slavery and the slave trade in the new domain. The Mobile Act and related measures brushed Spanish West Florida; Madrid talks under Monroe and Pinckney failed to fix a clean eastern boundary. Northern politicians feared the balance of power: more slaveholding or western States might outvote New England. Projects for a new State, talk of secession, and the Ely Amendment against slave representation showed how quickly a land deal became a Union quarrel. Aaron Burr’s western schemes fed on that anxiety — told fully on burr-conspiracy.
In the Senate, Federalists such as Timothy Pickering argued over whether Congress had a right to legislate for Louisiana as it pleased, or only an expedient power that might set dangerous precedents. John Quincy Adams’s early diary preserves that constitutional shadow beside the celebration of empire.
Why it matters here
Louisiana is the precondition of the missouri-compromise-1820 and of every later fight over slavery in the lands of the cession. It also explains why the Mississippi Valley seemed, to adventurers and diplomats alike, a prize that might still change hands. Benton, decades later, still measured Florida and Texas treaties against Jefferson’s purchase. For the commercial road that followed Jefferson into embargo and war, see embargo-and-drift-to-war-1807-12.
Chronology

1803: Treaty with France; delivery of New Orleans and Louisiana.
1804–07: Territorial organization; West Florida disputes; Burr crisis.
1812: Orleans Territory toward statehood as Louisiana.
1819–21: Missouri crisis on the same cession — missouri-compromise-1820.

events/march-to-the-sea-and-franklin-nas.title: March to the Sea and Franklin–Nashville (1864)
events/march-to-the-sea-and-franklin-nas.content:
March to the Sea and Franklin–Nashville (1864)
November–December 1864 split the western war into two simultaneous strokes: William T. Sherman cutting a belt from Atlanta to Savannah while John Bell Hood invaded Tennessee against George H. Thomas and John M. Schofield. Politically the season sealed Lincoln’s reelection year — Atlanta had already answered Chicago’s “war failure” platform; Savannah as a Christmas gift and Hood’s army dispersed in Mississippi closed the western rebellion’s power of offensive. The arc bridges chattanooga-and-atlanta-1863-64 to the Overland–Petersburg pressure and appomattox-and-end-of-confederate-arms-1865.
After Atlanta: Hood north, Sherman’s choice
Sherman saw it was not worth attacking Hood’s intrenchments at Lovejoy’s Station — front well covered by parapets, flanks by streams. Turning them would carry him too far from his base; he was not yet prepared for a long journey. He went back to Atlanta to rest the army and reflect. Atlanta as a military post, correspondence with Hood, Wheeler’s cavalry in the rear, and an abortive attempt at conference with Alexander H. Stephens and Joseph E. Brown fill the preliminaries. Jefferson Davis visited Hood’s army at Palmetto and Macon (20 and 22 September) and spoke; Beauregard was placed over Hood and Taylor. Hood moved on Sherman’s rear; Allatoona was fought; Hood’s eccentric movements continued. Sherman declined to follow him into Tennessee. Grant’s anxiety was real; then Sherman resolved on the march to the sea and Grant acceded. Thomas was left to defend Tennessee. Possession of Atlanta narrowed Confederate territory and cut off one of two remaining east–west rail lines. Davis’s speeches after relieving Joseph E. Johnston and appointing Hood — who had at once taken the initiative — belong to the same September that made the march conceivable.
The March to the Sea and Savannah
The march began; last communications cut; order of march fixed; little opposition met; enemy proclamations answered nothing material. Sherman arrived before Savannah; Hardee secured a line of retreat; Fort McAllister fell; correspondence between Grant and Sherman closed the investment. Savannah was evacuated. Sherman offered the city as a Christmas gift to the President; Lincoln’s letter of thanks answered. The plan of the March to the Sea was Sherman’s own. His columns cut a belt of destruction through Georgia’s war resources while Hood was already across the Tennessee. Little opposition met the columns; the enemy’s proclamations could not stop foraging and railroad wrecking on the scale Sherman intended. Once following Hood promised only to lengthen the war in the mountains, the sea march was the logical use of Atlanta — and the western half of the reelection year’s military seal.
Hood’s invasion: Columbia, Spring Hill, Franklin
While Sherman planned the sea march, Hood devised a counter scheme of invasion. In spite of rebuffs since replacing Johnston, hope and courage had not diminished. He had come west imbued, he said, with the spirit of Lee and Jackson, thinking flank attacks would destroy the National army. Courage and energy equalled any demand; mental capacity was so limited that the dream of conquest outran means. Hood succeeded in crossing the Tennessee between Muscle Shoals and the lower shoals at the end of October 1864. Thomas sent Schofield with the 4th and 23d corps and three brigades of Wilson’s cavalry to Pulaski to watch him. On 17 November Hood started and moved so as to avoid Schofield, turning his position. Hood had three infantry corps — Stephen D. Lee, Stewart, Cheatham — with cavalry about 45,000; Schofield about 30,000 of all arms. Thomas ordered Schofield to watch but not fight a battle if avoidable until concentration at Nashville.
Forrest’s raid on Johnsonville, Hood at Tuscumbia, the crossing, and the move for Columbia put Schofield racing to arrive first. Hood attempted to flank at Spring Hill and failed; Schofield reached Franklin. Hood attacked; the Battle of Franklin was a Confederate repulse with heavy losses. Schofield retired to Nashville; Hood followed and sat down before Thomas’s works.
Nashville and the dispersal of Hood’s army
Thomas prepared to attack. Grant’s impatience grew; he resolved to supersede Thomas and even started west before weather and Thomas’s readiness made the blow possible. A spell of bad weather intervened. On 15 December Thomas attacked; the Battle of Nashville drove Hood eight miles. The fight of the 16th routed Hood’s army; pursuit drove him into Mississippi and dispersed the force as an offensive instrument. From Grant’s chair the same sequence was Schofield’s delaying mission, Franklin’s slaughter of Hood’s assaulting columns, and Thomas’s deliberate blow when weather and preparation allowed. The western Confederacy’s last great army was broken in the same weeks Sherman’s men looked on Savannah’s wharves.
Political meaning
Atlanta in September had already given the lie to the Chicago declaration that the war was a failure. The March to the Sea and Franklin–Nashville translated that military fact into irreversible geography: Georgia crossed, a major port taken and presented to Lincoln at Christmas, Hood’s invasion smashed, Tennessee held. Reelection in November rested on that western news as on Sheridan’s Valley victories and Mobile Bay. From the hour of Lincoln’s reelection the Confederate cause was doomed — cheering in the trenches heard inside Richmond and Petersburg — even while Hood still dreamed of conquest on the Tennessee. Petersburg still pinned Lee; the road from Savannah north through the Carolinas would bring Sherman toward Grant’s left in 1865, the movement that ended in Johnston’s surrender after Appomattox. Grant kept the dual western problem on his desk through the autumn: Weldon Railroad fights, Early in the Valley, Sherman pushing through Georgia with detachments left as road guards. Hood’s dream of conquest ended in Mississippi mud while Sherman’s Christmas gift closed the Georgia chapter opened at Chickamauga’s gate.
Chronology

Sep–Oct 1864: Atlanta secure; Davis visits Hood; Hood crosses Tennessee (late Oct).
Nov 1864: Sherman marches from Atlanta; Hood turns Schofield; Franklin (30 Nov).
Dec 1864: Savannah falls (Christmas gift); Nashville (15–16 Dec); Hood driven into Mississippi.

events/mexican-american-war.title: Mexican-American War (1846–1848)
events/mexican-american-war.content:
Mexican-American War (1846–1848)
The Mexican-American War — from the Rio Grande clashes of 1846 through Guadalupe Hidalgo in 1848 — was James K. Polk’s expansion war. Ulysses S. Grant, then a junior officer, marched from Corpus Christi to the Halls of the Montezumas; John Quincy Adams led House opposition in the temper of an “apoplexy of the Constitution”; Thomas Hart Benton quarrelled in the Senate over cause and cession; campaigns, the Wilmot Proviso, the treaty, and Free Soil filled the politics of the war years.
Causes, occupation, and the Rio Grande
Grant’s path ran from Jefferson Barracks and Camp Salubrity through the Army of Occupation at Corpus Christi — seven companies of the 2nd dragoons, light artillery, five infantry regiments and one artillery regiment acting as infantry, not more than three thousand men under Zachary Taylor. Early in September the regiment left New Orleans for Corpus Christi; landing over the shallow channel at Shell Island was slow work. Preparations consisted largely in securing unbroken mules. On 8 March 1846 Taylor advanced toward the Rio Grande in brigades a day apart — strange caution, Grant later thought, beside the masses moved in the rebellion. Taylor forbade plundering and treated the Mexicans as the aggrieved party so far as Washington’s instructions allowed. At the Little Colorado, Mexican bugles opposite raised the fear of a large force; there were probably few troops. Fort Brown rose under siege while Taylor marched to Point Isabel for supplies; artillery at the fort could be heard from the seashore camps, and the young second lieutenant who had never heard a hostile gun felt sorry he had enlisted.
Palo Alto and Resaca de la Palma relieved the garrison; Major Jacob Brown was killed and the fort took his name. War existed, the Press and Washington announced, by the acts of Mexico; Taylor crossed and occupied Matamoras as the Army of Invasion. Benton charged the war’s cause partly on John C. Calhoun’s Texas course and noted that war was declared and peace intrigue begun the same day. Adams’s House resistance continued while Polk’s rainy inaugural and texas-annexation already behind him slide the Twenty-Ninth Congress into Oregon notice and Mexican War measures.
Monterey, Buena Vista, and the “political war”
From Camargo the advance on Monterey began 5 September in four columns a day apart. At Walnut Springs, within three miles of the city, Black Fort commanded the plain; detached hills were fortified. Garland’s charge on the lower batteries was ill-conceived or badly executed; Quitman reached the eastern suburbs under cover of houses; Worth’s movement was meant to be decisive. After surrender, quiet camp life returned; Grant thought the great majority of Mexican people regretted the departure under Taylor’s humane policy as much as they had regretted the coming. Educated and wealthy inhabitants abandoned homes; they were a small percentage.
Grant judged that the administration treated the contest as party capital. Winfield Scott, Whig and professional head of the army, submitted plans disapproved; on 27 May 1846 he answered that if a soldier’s plans were not supported, success could not be expected; four days later he was notified he need not go to Mexico. Taylor, Whig but supposed without ambitions, was left in command until after Monterey the Whig papers began to speak of him for the Presidency. Buena Vista — Taylor’s third complete victory — demoralized Santa Anna’s army before it could march south to meet Scott. Volunteers associated with disciplined men became soldiers almost at once; Mexican private soldiers, Grant wrote, were picked up from the lower class, poorly clothed, worse fed, seldom paid — yet some made as brave stands as he ever saw.
Vera Cruz to the City of Mexico
Scott’s Vera Cruz landing, siege, and occupation of city and San Juan de Ulloa (about five thousand prisoners and four hundred pieces of artillery; sixty-four Union casualties) opened the road inland. Scott had less than twelve thousand men to penetrate two hundred and sixty miles — far fewer than he claimed the administration had promised — and yellow fever threatened the coast. Cerro Gordo broke Santa Anna’s mountain position; Jalapa, Perote, and Puebla followed. Scott and Taylor contrasted as commanders: Scott precise in language and proud of rhetoric, seeing through staff eyes; Taylor plain on paper, seeing for himself. Both, Grant held, were true, patriotic, and upright.
From Puebla over Rio Frio mountain the army flanked El Peñon by the south of Lake Chalco to St. Augustin Tlalpam. Contreras, Churubusco, Molino del Rey, Chapultepec, and the aqueduct roads to the garitas San Cosme and Belen filled September 1847. Worth stopped at the Alameda; Quitman took the Palace — the Halls of the Montezumas. Liberated convicts and hostile citizens fired from housetops; Garland was wounded; Sidney Smith of the 4th infantry mortally, and by his death Grant rose to first lieutenant — having entered Palo Alto a second lieutenant and entered the capital sixteen months later with the same grade after a regiment that lost more officers than it ever had present at one engagement. Scott’s orders for the conquered city Grant called wise and discreet. The acquaintance formed in Mexico — Robert E. Lee, the Johnstons, Holmes, Hebert on one side; McCall, Mansfield, Phil Kearny and others on the other — Grant later counted immense service in the rebellion.
Wilmot, Guadalupe Hidalgo, and Adams’s death
Hostility to the war, conquering a peace, and the Free-Soil movement carried the political sequel. The Wilmot Proviso opened the slavery-extension fight over any Mexican cession; that fight ran into Free Soil politics of 1848. Nicholas Trist’s troubled negotiation and Polk’s treatment of him closed the war with Guadalupe Hidalgo — California and the Southwest in the cession. The treaty was signed early in February 1848; delay for ratification left an army anxious to go home while bull fights amused those who would pay fifty cents.
Adams died in the House, 21–23 February 1848, during a vote of thanks to Mexican War officers — seized with convulsion, carried to a committee room, dead the evening of the 23d. He had already dated his “decease” for useful purposes from the Boston seizure of 20 November 1846; the Quincy tablet later paired Ghent (24 December 1814) with death at his post. The cession’s political settlement became the crisis of compromise-of-1850.
Chronology

1845–46: Annexation; Army of Occupation; Rio Grande; Palo Alto / Resaca; declaration.
Sep 1846: Monterey.
1847: Buena Vista; Vera Cruz; Cerro Gordo; valley battles; City of Mexico.
1848: Guadalupe Hidalgo; Free Soil canvass; Adams dies (21–23 Feb).

events/missouri-compromise-1820.title: Missouri Compromise (1820–1821)
events/missouri-compromise-1820.content:
Missouri Compromise
The Missouri Compromise of 1820–21 settled — for a generation — the admission of Missouri as a slave State by pairing Maine as a free State and drawing the line of 36°30′ across the remaining Louisiana cession north of which slavery was prohibited. The bargain of Maine, Missouri, and the parallel kept sectional peace on the map until the 1850s reopened the territories in kansas-nebraska-and-bleeding-kansas.
Restriction and deadlock
Late in 1819 and into early 1820 the House tried the Tallmadge restriction, which would have limited slavery in Missouri. The Senate struck the restriction; the bill failed. Rufus King championed restriction in the Senate. John Quincy Adams, then in Monroe’s Cabinet, doubted whether Congress might constitutionally restrict slavery in Missouri under the Louisiana Treaty, yet loathed the bluster of slave-state members. The Sixteenth Congress also handled Alabama and Maine beside the Missouri fight, so admission politics stacked on admission politics.
The settlement of 2 March 1820
On 2 March 1820 the compromise stood complete: Maine separated; Missouri without the restriction; slavery prohibited in the remaining Louisiana cession north of 36°30′; House vote 90–87. Adams privately called it a law for perpetuating slavery, smuggled into the Union’s legislation. The Cabinet wrote opinions: Congress may prohibit slavery in the Territories (recorded as unanimous), while Crawford, Calhoun, and Wirt strained for textual ground. Southern senators later treated the settlement as largely their work; the Pinkney–King exchange over published Missouri speeches remained part of the memory of the fight.
Admission and aftermath
Missouri’s final admission in 1821 closed the immediate crisis; Monroe’s re-election followed. The line of 36°30′ remained the map of sectional peace until Kansas-Nebraska repealed its logic. Later compact and centralist arguments would reread Missouri; the event itself is the attested bargain of Maine, Missouri, and the parallel — and the private judgment that the bargain perpetuated what it pretended to limit.
Chronology

1819: Tallmadge restriction; deadlock.
2 Mar 1820: Compromise terms agreed in Congress.
1821: Missouri admitted; crisis closed for the time.

events/monroe-doctrine.title: Monroe Doctrine (1823)
events/monroe-doctrine.content:
Monroe Doctrine
The Monroe Doctrine is the set of principles announced in President Monroe’s message of December 1823. The United States would not meddle in Europe’s wars, and Europe must abstain from new colonization or the subjugation of independent states in the American hemisphere. John Quincy Adams, as Secretary of State, shaped the dual rule inside Monroe’s Cabinet. The message was a presidential declaration, not a treaty — aimed at rumors that the Holy Alliance might restore Spanish authority in Latin America, and at Russian claims on the Northwest Pacific coast.
Canning, Cabinet, and the dual rule
In 1823 Britain’s George Canning proposed a joint Anglo-American declaration against European intervention in Spanish America. Adams drafted instructions for Minister Rush and opposed a pledge that would bar the United States from Texas or Cuba while yielding little in return. After Cadiz fell to French arms, Calhoun pressed alarm; Monroe briefly despaired of South America; Southard stood with Adams. The formula Adams pressed was dual: no American entanglement in Europe’s internal wars; no European extension of the colonial system or forcible control over independent American states. The annual message followed that line, though the wording was Monroe’s.
Recognition and the hemisphere
The public face of the policy sat beside years of debate over recognizing the Spanish-American republics and advice from elder statesmen such as Jefferson. Non-colonization and non-intervention were the twin pillars. The United States claimed a special interest in the Western Hemisphere without promising to police Europe’s quarrels. Later, when Clay’s Panama mission reopened the question of American congresses abroad, opponents of entanglement still cited the 1823 exposition as the safe rule.
Later echo
The doctrine returned whenever Texas, Oregon, or European mediation touched American politics. For this page the event is the 1823 message and its Cabinet making — the moment a cabinet dual rule became a public presidential statement.

events/nullification-crisis-1832-33.title: Nullification Crisis (1832–1833)
events/nullification-crisis-1832-33.content:
Nullification Crisis (1832–1833)
The Nullification Crisis was South Carolina’s attempt to declare the protective tariffs of 1828 and 1832 null and void within her limits, and the federal government’s response by proclamation, Force Bill, and compromise. Andrew Jackson answered with “Our Federal Union: It must be preserved”; John C. Calhoun stood as the doctrine’s apostle; Henry Clay’s compromise tariff and the Force Bill closed the winter without battle; Thomas Hart Benton and John Quincy Adams watched the Senate and House fights; Alexander H. Stephens later read the episode as a chapter in the long compact controversy between federation and consolidation.
Jefferson Day toast and the doctrine named
On Jefferson’s birthday (13 April 1830) the doctrine received its public unveiling before the ordinance. A subscription dinner at Washington, ostensibly to honor Jefferson as founder of the political school of the subscribers, issued twenty-four regular toasts that savored of the new doctrine of nullification. Many broke off and refused to attend further; the company remained numerous. When the regular toasts were over, President Jackson gave the volunteer that electrified the country: “Our Federal Union: It must be preserved.” Calhoun’s next toast did not allay suspicion: “The Union: next to our Liberty the most dear” — liberty before union, State rights, inequality of burthens and benefits. Connecting with Robert Y. Hayne’s speech and South Carolina publications, the day revealed nullification as a distinct doctrine with Calhoun for apostle. Benton held that Madison’s Virginia resolutions of 1798–99 never supposed a right in a State, of its own motion, to annul an act of Congress; Madison in retirement recoiled from the South Carolina interpretation and from being made its pedestal.
The tariff of 1828 marked the era from which nullification takes its origin and from which a serious division dates between North and South — the work of politicians and manufacturers begun for woollens and swollen by other interests until all manufacturing interests needed to carry the bill were included. Hayne’s moderation in later tariff debate — sorrow more than anger, loyalty to the Union — had no effect on the protective majority. The presidential canvass of 1832 put the American system in issue; the issue was found against it; South Carolina alone refused to wait for regular extinction of the system under the approaching Congress.
Ordinance and proclamation
On 24 November 1832, a fortnight after the election that decided the tariff’s fate, South Carolina issued her ordinance of nullification. It declared the tariff acts — especially those of 29 May 1828 and 14 July 1832 — unauthorized by the Constitution, null and void, and no law; forbade enforcement of the duties within the State; required the legislature to give the ordinance full effect; cut off appeals to the Supreme Court in related cases; and threatened that any federal act closing her ports or coercing her otherwise than through civil tribunals would absolve her from the Union and authorize a separate government. Ordinance, proclamation, gathering of force, and the political theater in which Webster–Hayne echoes still framed the nature of the Union filled the next weeks.
Jackson answered on 10 December with a proclamation denying the right of a single State to annul an act of Congress, asserting the Union’s perpetuity, and preparing military and naval enforcement. The ordinance reached him in early December. In his annual message the President had hoped reduction of duties after extinction of the public debt would compose the question; when proceedings continued — organization of troops, collection of arms, declarations hostile to the Union — he sent Congress in January the promised communication asking powers the exigency demanded. Adams’s December 1832 diary records Major Hamilton, through J. W. Taylor, bringing the proclamation; George McDuffie jocularly reporting that they had nullified the Tariff Act of last summer; Adams answering that ordinance and proclamation must fight it out. Adams offered a resolution calling for copies of proclamation and ordinance; the House refused consideration 106–64. The message against nullification was later referred to Judiciary under Bell of Tennessee; 25,000 copies ordered printed.
Force Bill, Verplanck, and Clay’s compromise
Gulian C. Verplanck’s bill from Ways and Means promised larger reduction after the election’s verdict against the American system. On 12 February Clay asked leave to introduce his own “compromise” measure, prefacing that whether rightfully or wrongfully the tariff stood in imminent danger and must fall at the next session if not preserved by some means not now visible. Clay’s bill swept like a hurricane: engrossment 105–71, final passage 119–85. The Revenue Collection bill — Force Bill to its friends, Bloody Bill to the nullifiers — was taken up amid disorderly struggle. Wilkins of Pennsylvania, reporting it for Judiciary, insisted it revived previous laws and contained nothing novel but contingent authority to remove the custom-house from one building to another — to put it out of harm’s way after 1 February without using force. Calhoun’s resolutions on the powers of the government restated the compact and each State’s equal right to judge infractions and the mode of redress. Unionist majority and Jackson men’s determination that nullification should not stand as a working remedy even where they spoke state-rights language on other questions carried the Force Bill.
A hollow truce between Clay and Calhoun — early and long rival aspirants, united only against Jackson and Martin Van Buren — underwrote the compromise winter. Years later they quarrelled in open Senate over which had been master of the other in 1833: Calhoun declared he had Clay on his back; Clay retorted he would not own him for the meanest of his slaves. “Compromise legislation” was a popular misnomer without foundation in the Constitution — agreements of mutual consent, not votes binding future Congresses. South Carolina, faced with compromise on the tariff and force in reserve, withdrew the ordinance; the crisis closed without battle.
Constitutional meanings
To Jackson and Benton, nullification was incompatible with a government that could operate on individuals and collect a common revenue. To the Carolina theorists — and later to Stephens — the tariff fight was an instance of compact remedy; Stephens listed no president from Jefferson to Lincoln elected who did not hold the government a compact of sovereign states, explained Jackson’s proclamation, and quoted the farewell’s call to maintain unimpaired the sovereignty of the states, while still separating that language from secession “in disregard of her obligations.” Adams, no Jackson man, nonetheless sat through Force Bill and compromise as a Union measure against a State veto of federal law. The crisis thus remains both a practical settlement (compromise tariff + Force Bill + withdrawal) and an unresolved argument about where paramount authority resides — an argument Stephens would reopen after Appomattox.
Chronology

13 Apr 1830: Jefferson Day dinner; Jackson’s Union toast; Calhoun’s reply.
1832: Tariff of 1832; Jackson re-elected; SC ordinance (24 Nov); proclamation (10 Dec).
Jan–Feb 1833: Message on SC proceedings; Verplanck and Clay bills; Force Bill debates.
1833: Clay compromise tariff; ordinance withdrawn.

events/overland-campaign-1864.title: Overland Campaign (1864)
events/overland-campaign-1864.content:
Overland Campaign (1864)
The Overland campaign of May–June 1864 — Ulysses S. Grant against Robert E. Lee from the Rapidan to the James — replaced the old pattern of fighting and falling back with continuous pressure that ended in the Petersburg lines. Wilderness, Spotsylvania, and Cold Harbor filled the march; Jubal Early’s raid on Washington that summer belonged to the same season as the Confederate counterstroke while Grant held south of the James.
Plan and Rapidan
As lieutenant-general Grant set a coordinated clock: himself against Lee in Virginia, William T. Sherman against Joseph E. Johnston in Georgia. On the night of 3–4 May 1864 the Army of the Potomac crossed the Rapidan. The Wilderness (5–6 May) Grant treated as a successful crossing and a binding of the armies together rather than as a retreat to the old bases; when the columns moved south toward Spotsylvania, troops cheered that the road led toward Richmond, not back to Washington.
Spotsylvania to Cold Harbor
Spotsylvania and Emory Upton’s assault, Philip Sheridan’s raid, and the concentration near Cold Harbor filled late May. On 3 June assaults at Cold Harbor failed; Grant stopped further attacks after taking corps opinions toward midday — his own stop-order, not a later legend. The left-flank march to the James (14–15 June) placed an army still roughly 115,000 after six weeks opposite Petersburg. The long siege that followed is the sequel; the Overland march ends at that crossing.
Early’s raid
While Grant fastened on Petersburg, Jubal Early moved down the Valley against Washington. The raid threatened the capital and pulled attention from the James, then receded. Citing it here keeps the 1864 Valley flank inside the Overland season; Sherman’s Georgia war is told on chattanooga-and-atlanta-1863-64.
Chronology

3–4 May 1864: Rapidan crossed.
5–6 May: Wilderness.
May–early Jun: Spotsylvania to Cold Harbor.
14–15 Jun: James crossed; Petersburg lines begin.
Jul 1864: Early against Washington.

events/panic-of-1819-and-hard-times.title: Panic of 1819 and Hard Times
events/panic-of-1819-and-hard-times.content:
Panic of 1819 and Hard Times
The Panic of 1819 and the hard times that followed were the first great peacetime crash of the new national market: postwar speculation in land and goods, a swarm of State banks issuing far more paper than they could redeem, collapse of manufactures under British auction goods and disordered currency, sheriffs’ sales across the interior, and State “relief” systems that fought the Bank of the United States as readily as they fought creditors. Congress also voted relief for public land debtors in the same generation. The panic-of-1837 was larger and more famous; 1819 taught the pattern first.
Flush years and the bank swarm
With peace in 1815 came flush times that anticipated the country’s growth by years. The currency disorder that had helped justify the Second Bank in 1816 taught no lasting lesson: by 1818 some three hundred and ninety-two banks did business in twenty-three States and Territories — Pennsylvania and Kentucky with fifty-nine each, more than rich New York’s forty-two. Banks forced notes into circulation by distant specie deposits, usurious devices, and every trick of keeping paper afloat. Manufacturers and traders felt the pinch first; by early 1818 the people felt it too.
Crash, sales, and anti-bank politics
From New York and Pennsylvania west to the Mississippi and south to Tennessee, general bankruptcy followed. Emigration belts had borrowed from neighbors and banks; banks had issued five times what they could redeem; depreciation destroyed commerce and left debtors unable to pay. At Carlisle the sheriff advertised twenty-seven tracts at once, each owner bank-debted; at Lancaster and Bedford meetings pledged to refuse notes not at par in Philadelphia and Baltimore unless heavily discounted. Eastern and Southern States that received fewer emigrants escaped the worst; the interior did not.
Hard times in Kentucky and Missouri bred relief systems — stay laws, replevin, and State banks of a new sort — and fierce taxation or outlawry aimed at branches of the national Bank (second-bank-of-the-united-states, McCulloch v. Maryland, Ohio’s forcible tax). Pauperism rose on the seaboard; the 1820 census showed Delaware almost static and coastal growth slowed while Western States swelled. Temperance and debt-imprisonment reform (temperance-and-moral-reform-movements) answered the social wreckage; land debtor relief (public-lands-speculation-and-frontier-credit) answered the frontier’s forfeitures.
Aftermath
Manufactures that hard times and British auctions had nearly destroyed revived in the early 1820s and fed the industrial map of labor-factories-and-workingmen. Politically, anti-bank feeling and relief wars trained the generation that later fought Biddle in the Bank War. Credit theorists would still be explaining American confidence failures in 1838; 1819 was the first people’s crash those theories had to account for.
Timeline

1815–17: Postwar flush; State bank multiplication; Second Bank chartered (1816).
1818: Hard times reach the people; ~392 banks in operation.
1819–21: Suspensions, sheriffs’ sales, State relief and anti-Bank measures; McCulloch (1819).
1821–23: Slow revival; manufactures recover toward the mid-1820s boom.

events/panic-of-1837.title: Panic of 1837
events/panic-of-1837.content:
Panic of 1837
The Panic of 1837 was the commercial and banking collapse that opened Martin Van Buren’s presidency: banks stopping payment in hard money (specie), broken credit, unemployed workmen, and a special session of Congress called to deal with the public revenue and the divorce of government from banks. It closed the monetary sequel of the bank-war-and-removal-of-deposits and opened the long fight over the Independent Treasury (sub-treasury).
From boom to break
Late Jackson years mixed speculation, surplus distribution, and busy state deposit banks after the federal deposits left the second-bank-of-the-united-states. Land sales and internal improvements rode a wave of confidence; paper money multiplied. A contemporary credit treatise of 1838 argued that American personal credit could be extensive and productive when property was secure, but that the disorders of 1836–7 sprang from surplus-revenue operations and currency mismanagement rather than from free banking alone — a point set beside English crises of 1825 and 1836 and French hoarding under low confidence. Hard-money Democrats and bank Whigs both grew louder in that atmosphere.
Suspension and distress
In 1837 banks suspended specie payments across wide districts. Works stopped; wages felt the pressure; political fury turned against banks and against the administration that had destroyed the national Bank without securing a stable substitute. Hard-money men treated suspension as the fruit of a paper system divorced from discipline, and as the occasion for an Independent Treasury that would keep public funds out of corporations of discount. Whigs answered with bank and credit arguments that would feed the Log-Cabin campaign of election-of-1840.
The special session of 1837
The Twenty-Fifth Congress opened under the shadow of the panic. Sub-Treasury debates filled the House: some members against the project, others for it, still others challenging opponents to propose a new Bank of the United States. Papers were called for on Mexico, Texas, and the Northeastern boundary, and for printing State acts on specie suspension. When moves appeared to suspend the call of the States for petitions, John Quincy Adams and his allies assailed them as abridging the right-of-petition-and-gag-rule — so that the panic session was both a fiscal crisis and another round of the gag war. Van Buren’s message and the Independent Treasury bill set the Democratic remedy.
Why it mattered
The Panic was the people’s hard-times verdict on the years after the Bank War. It made the Sub-Treasury the Democratic fiscal test, kept Whig hopes for a national bank alive, and translated suffering into the electoral language of 1840.

events/peninsula-campaign-1862.title: Peninsula Campaign (1862)
events/peninsula-campaign-1862.content:
Peninsula Campaign (1862)
The Peninsula campaign of spring–summer 1862 was the Union’s great eastern bid while Grant fought in the West. George B. McClellan advanced up the York–James peninsula toward Richmond; Thomas J. (“Stonewall”) Jackson diverted Union strength in the Shenandoah Valley; Robert E. Lee struck in the Seven Days battles; and McClellan withdrew to Harrison’s Landing on the James. Richmond stayed the Confederate capital. This page is the eastern counterpart to donelson-and-shiloh-1862.
Plans, Manassas evacuated, and the water move
About 1 December 1861 Lincoln had suggested to McClellan, then general-in-chief, a plan of campaign the President thought wise; McClellan kept the memorandum ten days and returned it with a hurried pencil note showing little impression. Manassas was evacuated; Sunday 9 March brought Hampton Roads news of the Merrimac’s havoc and, in the afternoon, the Monitor’s arrival and victory — emotions reversing from depression to astonishment at the Executive Mansion. McClellan chose the Peninsula route himself. He arrived at Fort Monroe the morning of 2 April 1862 to begin the campaign against Richmond. By his own report he had next day ready to move 58,000 men and 100 guns besides division artillery — flower of the volunteer army, Sykes’s regulars, Hunt’s artillery reserve, cavalry — with almost equal numbers on the way. The Administration intended to dispatch all of McDowell’s corps to reinforce him as soon as northern Virginia allowed; Franklin’s division was so dispatched in time for Yorktown, though McClellan made no use of that fine body until the place was evacuated.
Yorktown to Williamsburg
McClellan besieged Yorktown. The evacuation took him so completely by surprise that valuable time was lost in hurried preparation to pursue. Franklin’s division, after a fortnight’s delay on the transports, had been disembarked and was hastily returned to the boats. Hours were consumed provisioning commands for the march. Evacuation was discovered at dawn; noon passed before the first column started. Joseph E. Johnston by then had taken his entire command to Williamsburg and posted a strong rear-guard under James Longstreet to protect his trains. Stoneman’s cavalry collided about dark and was repulsed, losing one gun. Sumner, Heintzelman, and Keyes came up overnight — illustrative of McClellan’s relations with corps commanders that none had orders for the inevitable battle, and even which of them commanded was in serious doubt. Sumner had been ordered to take command in the general’s absence; Heintzelman had not been told and thought the control his. Confusion of roads followed. Williamsburg was fought; pursuit lagged; the Confederates withdrew toward the Chickahominy and Richmond.
Fair Oaks and the Valley diversion
Fair Oaks (Seven Pines) followed on the approaches to Richmond — McClellan’s army astride the Chickahominy, Jackson’s Valley campaign holding McDowell’s remaining corps from joining. Preparations were vigorously made for McDowell’s march toward Richmond; Shields’s division, one of Banks’s best, was ordered to reinforce him. The most important results were expected from an officer of McDowell’s ability striking the left flank of the Confederate forces before Richmond; that attack was never made. Jackson’s Valley campaign deranged the Government’s plans: while Franklin had already gone unused at Yorktown, the remainder of McDowell’s corps was held to cover Washington against Jackson’s blows. His brilliant successes, early death, and religious enthusiasm later made him both champion and saint in Southern memory. After Fair Oaks as before it, McClellan kept up continual cry for reinforcements. The hallucination that the enemy’s force was double his own had become fixed; all plans were poisoned by that fatal error.
Reinforcements and the weather
Lincoln resolved to give McClellan absolute control of all troops on the Peninsula. Knowing Wool would never consent to serve under him — the veteran having spoken with characteristic severity of the junior’s insatiable demand — the President removed Wool to Baltimore, transferred Dix to Fort Monroe under McClellan’s direct command (greatly displeasing Dix, who yielded under protest), and saw Dix at once send ten of the best regiments. Kind and complimentary messages accompanied troops and guns gathered from every quarter. A few days after Fair Oaks, McCall’s division of McDowell’s corps — about ten thousand men and five batteries — was dispatched; McClellan telegraphed delight on 7 June that he would be in perfect readiness to move forward and take Richmond the moment McCall reached and the ground admitted artillery. McCall arrived 11–13 June; weather turned good; roads dried; Keyes reported White Oak Swamp fordable in many places by the 15th. That night rain began again — which would “retard our movements somewhat.” McClellan had a habit of regarding bad weather as exclusively injurious to himself, never to the other side; Lincoln once said he seemed to think, in defiance of Scripture, that Heaven sent rain only on the just. Johnston had not allowed the storm of 30 May to stop Seven Pines; Grant in the West used weather both ways.
Seven Days and Harrison’s Landing
Lee struck in the Seven Days before Richmond. Gaines’s Mill (Chickahominy) forced McClellan to change base to the James; battles at Savage’s Station, Glendale, and Malvern Hill followed — the last a Confederate defeat on the field — yet McClellan once more retired to Harrison’s Landing. Greatly agitated by Gaines’s Mill and the forced departure for the James, he sent from Savage’s Station on 28 June an extraordinary dispatch to the Secretary of War that showed how far his attitude toward the Government had soured. Lincoln replied; reinforcements went; McClellan’s letter from Harrison’s Landing marked the beginning of a political career of censorious letters of which William T. Sherman later spoke. The President visited the army at Harrison’s Landing; correspondence about absentees followed; Halleck was sent; it was resolved to withdraw the Army of the Potomac from the James. McClellan protested and asked for reinforcements; he delayed obeying. The Peninsula bid to take the Confederate capital ended without capture; Second Bull Run and the Maryland campaign followed on the road to antietam-and-emancipation-proclamation. Alexander H. Stephens, looking back as Confederate Vice President, named the Seven Days beside Second Manassas among the eastern summer’s fights — the season that left Richmond still the seat of Jefferson Davis’s government while Donelson and Shiloh had already broken the Tennessee line in the West.
Chronology

Mar 1862: Manassas evacuated; Monitor–Merrimac; Peninsula chosen.
2 Apr: McClellan at Fort Monroe; advance begins.
Apr–May: Yorktown siege and evacuation; Williamsburg; Fair Oaks.
May–Jun: Jackson’s Valley diversion; McDowell held back.
Late Jun–Jul: Seven Days; Harrison’s Landing; order to withdraw from the James.

events/secession-winter-1860-61.title: Secession Winter (1860–1861)
events/secession-winter-1860-61.content:
Secession Winter (1860–1861)
The secession winter — from Abraham Lincoln’s election in November 1860 to his inauguration on 4 March 1861 — was the season in which seven cotton States left the Union, formed a provisional Confederacy at Montgomery, and left the Charleston forts as an unresolved powder magazine. Conspiracy and cabinet struggle in Washington, failed compromise schemes, and the compact claim that a State may resume delegated powers all filled the same months.
Gist, Cabinet cabal, and Anderson
Before a single ballot had been cast for Lincoln, Governor William H. Gist of South Carolina sent a secret circular to Cotton-State executives inaugurating rebellion a full month before the election — repeating in bolder form Governor Henry A. Wise’s consultation talk of the Frémont campaign. Very soon the Charleston local conspiracy was in communication with the central secession cabal at Washington. James Buchanan’s Cabinet divided: Howell Cobb, John B. Floyd, and Jacob Thompson on the Southern side; Lewis Cass of Michigan at State; Isaac Toucey, Joseph Holt, and Jeremiah Black among those who would stiffen the régime after Floyd’s fall. Non-coercion doctrine, adopted as early as 20 November in the Attorney-General’s opinion, satisfied neither coercionists nor secessionists.
Major Robert Anderson reached Fort Moultrie and assumed command 21 November 1860, after interviews with President, Secretary of War, and Lieutenant-General Winfield Scott. The Charleston secession celebration of the 17th had already lit bonfires and palmetto flags; Gist’s message and the Convention bill of the Legislature were not yet statutory offenses after twelve years of disunion talk. Anderson’s transfer from Moultrie to Sumter on 26 December — planned with discretion and executed the same afternoon the South Carolina commissioners Barnwell, Adams, and Orr reached Washington — changed the fort question overnight. Cabinet struggle followed; Floyd retired; the Union section of the Cabinet gained the upper hand from 31 December. The relief steamer Star of the West was fired on in January; Anderson’s threatened retaliation became a truce of referral to Washington. Sumter and Pickens remained the twin symbols of federal presence inside claimed Confederate territory — a truce of exhaustion more than a settlement.
Buchanan’s message pleased neither camp; Senate and House raised the Committee of Thirteen and the Committee of Thirty-three; a December manifesto of Southern senators marked open planning for secession. Cass retired when concession brought only further demands. The forty muskets episode and paralyzing instructions from Washington discouraged the garrison while Charleston manufactured scaling-ladders and waited for “delivery” of arsenal and forts.
South Carolina ordinance and the cotton cascade
Delegates to the South Carolina Convention were elected 6 December and organized at Columbia 17 December; epidemic drove both convention and Legislature to Charleston. Elected under a furor that tolerated no opposition, the convention was practically unanimous. The ordinance and Declaration of Causes — full of ambiguous phrases and vague generalities — made the first formal exit. Mississippi, Florida, Alabama, Georgia, Louisiana, and Texas followed the same stages: Governor’s initiative, office-holders’ junto, Legislature, convention, ordinance, withdrawal of congressional delegations.
At Montgomery the seceded States framed a provisional government, electing Jefferson Davis President and Alexander H. Stephens Vice President. Stephens had spoken for Union delay at Milledgeville against Georgia’s rush; his November–December letters with Lincoln turned on the expediency of compromise, and he insisted that secession was the compact remedy, not rebellion against a consolidated nation. He opposed secession’s timing yet went with Georgia; he later explained the seceding states, Montgomery, and what he called Sumter’s “breach of faith.” Crittenden’s plan, the Peace Conference, and the formation of the Confederacy filled the people’s crisis — seizure of federal property, Buchanan’s policy, failure of Crittenden, Lincoln’s inaugural, march toward war.
Crittenden, Peace Conference, and compromise failure
The House Committee of Thirty-three labored under discouragement: extreme Southern members had announced futility in advance; the central cabal’s secession manifesto of 14 December showed open contempt of the Dunn resolution. A few meetings made failure evident. The Senate Committee of Thirteen likewise opened under Thomas L. Clingman’s prediction that Lincoln’s organization would soon control the entire Government and change its character without abolishing forms — and that a number of States would secede within sixty days. John J. Crittenden’s plan and kindred border-state proposals were the last great effort to draw a settlement line the cotton republics would accept; they would not. Constitutional amendment efforts and other propositions might have restored harmony had the Cotton-State movement not been controlled by men bent on rebellion as prime object. The Washington Peace Conference likewise failed to reunite the cotton States. Hopes of compromise still seemed propitious to a great majority while agitation had taken virulent form in fewer than half a dozen States; in most a decided majority still deprecated disunion — until the cascade made the minority’s work irreversible.
Lincoln’s journey and the inaugural
Lincoln as president-elect faced importuning for public statements to quiet the South from Republicans and Bell–Everett unionists alike. Legislatures of Indiana, Ohio, Pennsylvania, New York, New Jersey, and Massachusetts invited him to their capitals; municipal authorities and railroads tendered hospitalities and special trains. On the morning of 23 February the country was surprised that the president-elect, after a long public journey, had abandoned his programme and made a secret night journey through Baltimore to the capital — smuggled in, with little doubt he would have been assassinated had he travelled openly throughout. Installed at Willard’s, he paid the customary visits to Buchanan and Cabinet, the Houses, and the Supreme Court. The inaugural of 4 March left Sumter and Pickens still held by federal garrisons inside a Confederacy that claimed them. Cabinet formation had been largely sketched on election night; the Sumter question versus the “rebel game” of Montgomery commissioners seeking recognition closed the winter where bread or war in Charleston harbor begins.
Chronology

Oct–Nov 1860: Gist circular; Lincoln elected; secession agitation.
Nov–Dec: Anderson to Moultrie; Cabinet cabal; Committees of 13 and 33.
26 Dec 1860: Anderson to Sumter; SC commissioners in Washington.
Dec 1860–Jan 1861: SC ordinance; Star of the West; cotton republics.
Feb 1861: Montgomery; Crittenden/Peace Conference failure; Lincoln’s secret journey (23 Feb).
4 Mar 1861: Lincoln inaugurated.

Sources

events/texas-annexation.title: Texas Annexation (1845)
events/texas-annexation.content:
Texas Annexation (1845)
The annexation of Texas as a State of the Union — treaty rejected, then joint resolution carried at the close of John Tyler’s term and into James K. Polk’s — was the expansion stroke that set the Rio Grande army and the mexican-american-war in motion. Secret intrigue and Senate fights, House agitation, Clay–Van Buren letters against annexation at this time, Tyler’s last push, and the military sequel on Texas soil fill the same story.
Treaty and rejection
Thomas Hart Benton’s long memory ran to the Florida treaty that had “given away Texas”; recognition of Texan independence filled earlier years. Under Tyler and John C. Calhoun a treaty of annexation went to the Senate and failed amid cries Benton recorded as “Texas or Disunion.” John Quincy Adams watched the agitation rise in the House; Henry Clay and Martin Van Buren both wrote against immediate annexation in the canvass of 1844, while Democrats made expansion their mandate and elected Polk.
Joint resolution and admission
After the election Tyler still drove annexation — to preserve the administration from oblivion, critics said — while Anson Jones held the Texan presidency. Congress turned to joint resolution and legislative admission of Texas as a State as the Tyler term ended and Polk took the oath. Polk complained of French interference against annexation. The map change was political before it was military.
Sequel on the Rio Grande
Ulysses S. Grant’s Army of Occupation at Corpus Christi and the advance to the Rio Grande treated the annexed soil and the disputed boundary as the war’s first ground. Annexation thus belongs with the Mexican War as cause and stage: the State in the Union, the army on the river, the declaration to follow.
Chronology

1844: Treaty fails; Polk elected on expansion.
1845: Joint resolution; Texas admitted; Polk inaugurated.
1846: Rio Grande crisis and war — see Mexican War page.
