events/vicksburg-campaign-1863.title: Vicksburg Campaign (1862–1863)
events/vicksburg-campaign-1863.content:
Vicksburg Campaign (1862–1863)
The Vicksburg campaign — Grant’s long effort to take the Mississippi fortress and open the river — ended on 4 July 1863 with the surrender and parole of Pemberton’s army, the same day Meade’s victory closed at Gettysburg. The campaign ran from failed bayous to Bruinsburg, Jackson, Champion’s Hill, and the siege; Washington watched the same season with rising hope. A British visitor at Johnston’s mess while the investment tightened left a side view of Confederate weakness and Grant’s unexpected vigour — part of fremantle-tour-confederacy-1863.
Failed approaches
Vicksburg sat as the last high-ground link of the Confederacy across the Mississippi. Holly Springs’s raid, Sherman’s Chickasaw failure, the canal, Lake Providence, Yazoo Pass, and the bayou experiments consumed the winter of 1862–63 without placing an army south of the fortress on dry ground with a supply line. Grant persisted through a season that tested Northern patience with western operations.
Running the batteries and the interior march
Army steamers ran the batteries; volunteers from the ranks manned boats. From Grand Gulf the army crossed at Bruinsburg on 30 April 1863 while Sherman feinted at Haines’ Bluff. When Banks was delayed, Grant cut loose from his base and marched the interior: Raymond, Jackson, Champion’s Hill, Big Black — driving Pemberton into the works. Investment began mid-May; assaults on the 19th and 22nd failed; a regular siege followed; McClernand was relieved after a press order quarrel. In those same May days Johnston concentrated among Jackson’s ruins, too weak to strike Grant’s investing army, and talked of straggling as the Confederacy’s chief evil — the visitor’s window on fremantle-tour-confederacy-1863.
Surrender and the open river
On 4 July Pemberton surrendered; Grant preferred paroles to a cartel tangle Halleck feared; some 31,600 prisoners passed out of the works. Port Hudson fell afterward; the Mississippi was opened. Grant’s retrospect pairs the day with Gettysburg’s jubilee. Vicksburg is the western half of the war’s mid-point — Grant restored from Shiloh’s eclipse to the command that would later take him east.
Chronology

Winter 1862–63: Failed bayous and canals.
30 Apr 1863: Bruinsburg crossing.
May 1863: Interior battles; investment.
4 Jul 1863: Surrender; river opened after Port Hudson.

events/war-of-1812.title: War of 1812
events/war-of-1812.content:
War of 1812
The War of 1812 was the United States’ conflict with Great Britain from 1812 to 1815. It grew out of impressment, blocked trade, and western frontier anger described on embargo-and-drift-to-war-1807-12. Once declared, it mixed disasters on the Canadian border with startling ship duels, the burning of Washington, New England’s hartford-convention, Andrew Jackson’s victory at New Orleans, and a Christmas Eve peace at Ghent that restored territory without settling the sailors’-rights quarrel that had helped start the fight. Many later called it a second war of independence; others called it a needless commercial ruin. Both readings appear in the contemporary record.
Declaration
In June 1812 President Madison asked for war; Congress agreed in a divided vote. Henry Clay in the House and James Monroe in the Cabinet were remembered as the two men without whom the declaration might not have passed. New England Federalists protested loudly; Baltimore saw riots against anti-war editors. The country entered the war short of regular troops, skilled officers, and money, with no national bank to steady the currency.
Frontier and lake war
The northern campaigns opened badly. William Hull’s advance on Canada ended in the surrender of Detroit. Niagara and the upper St. Lawrence saw advances and retreats haunted by militia limits and divided command. Oliver Hazard Perry’s victory on Lake Erie restored the lake; the Battle of the Thames followed and broke Tecumseh’s power in the Northwest. In the South, Jackson’s Creek War opened land for later white settlement. Prisoner retaliations and burned border towns marked how bitter a thinly settled frontier war could become.
Ship duels, privateers, and the Chesapeake
At sea the small American navy won duels that kept morale alive — Constitution, United States, Wasp, and others — while privateers hurt British trade. Britain’s blockade tightened; in 1814 Chesapeake raids became invasion. Bladensburg failed; Washington’s public buildings burned. Baltimore held, and the defense entered popular song as the Star-Spangled Banner. Specie payments stopped; New England banks buckled; the federal Treasury ran toward emptiness.
New Orleans, Hartford, and Ghent
Jackson’s defense of New Orleans — fought after the treaty was signed but before the news crossed the ocean — became the popular seal on the war. At the same season New England Federalists met at Hartford to protest conscription talk and commercial ruin; their report and the political ruin of their party are told on hartford-convention.
Diplomacy had already moved. Russian mediation brought American commissioners toward Europe; at Ghent, Clay, Gallatin, John Quincy Adams, and their colleagues faced British demands over fisheries, the Mississippi, and Indian buffer states. Ceremony quarrels opened the talks; hard bargaining closed them. On 24 December 1814 the treaty restored the old boundaries and left impressment unsettled. Adams called Christmas Day fit for proclaiming peace on earth. Astoria and the Columbia later showed how silence on Pacific claims could reopen questions — see pacific-fur-trade-and-astoria-enterprise.
After the guns
Peace unlocked the postwar settlement: the second-bank-of-the-united-states, the tariff of 1816, and the quarrel over internal-improvements. Benton later called the war bravely fought and honorably concluded — a short war that still changed how the world treated the American flag. The Missouri crisis soon proved that the Louisiana empire the war had helped secure was not at peace with itself — missouri-compromise-1820.
Chronology

1807–11: Causes — see embargo-and-drift-to-war-1807-12.
1812: Declaration; Detroit; early naval duels.
1813: Lake Erie; Thames; Creek war; Russian mediation.
1814: Washington burned; Baltimore; hartford-convention; Treaty of Ghent (24 Dec).
1815: New Orleans; peace news; Algiers sequel.

United States 1800–65 Wiki
A narrative-research knowledge base on American history from the turn of the nineteenth century through the end of the Civil War — Jeffersonian and Madisonian republicanism, the War of 1812 and the postwar settlement, the market and transportation revolutions, Jacksonian democracy, westward expansion, the deepening sectional crisis over slavery, and the war for the Union through 1865.
Total pages: 126
What follows is the map of the wiki — people, events, and concepts — then the source library on which every claim rests. Entity, event, and concept pages are built from those sources under a contemporary lens, without modern editorial framing.

sources/adams-diaries-vol1.title: [source] John Quincy Adams: Diaries, Vol. 1, 1779–1821 (Library of America)
sources/adams-diaries-vol1.content:
John Quincy Adams: Diaries, Volume 1 (1779–1821)
Author: John Quincy Adams (1767–1848)
Editor: David Waldstreicher
Published: 2017 — Library of America (volume #293); eISBN 978-1-59853-523-5 in extract
Working text: LOA EPUB via Anna’s Archive (ISBN13 9781598535204; hash 5d3a8437740a89a243da4b1039388f1a)
Raw extract: wiki/raw/adams-diaries-vol1.txt (pandoc plain from EPUB)
Extract stats: 30,163 lines · ~296,648 words (includes chronology, notes, and index after the diary chapters)
Overview
This Library of America volume is the first of two selected editions of John Quincy Adams’s diary. It presents entries from November 1779, when the twelve-year-old Adams sailed again for Europe with his father, through March 1821, at the close of President James Monroe’s first term, when Adams was secretary of state. The editor’s preface describes the full diary as extending over fifty-one manuscript volumes and more than fourteen thousand pages, with an unbroken daily string of twenty-six years; this volume is a selection, with daily entries given in full when possible and recurring meteorological, social-call, and bill-paying matter sometimes cut (breaks marked ≈).
Adams’s diary records public and private life: cabinet meetings, diplomatic interviews, congressional debates, dinner conversation, character sketches of presidents and princes, family anxieties, sermons and books, verse and translation, theater, and natural observation. For the wiki’s period (c. 1800–1865) the later chapters are especially dense — Senate and Boston years, the Russian mission during the Napoleonic wars, Ghent and the peace with Britain, the London legation, and the State Department years that frame the Transcontinental Treaty with Spain and the American System / hemispheric policy of Monroe’s cabinet.
The extract opens with LOA copyright and front-matter images, then Contents, then the editor’s Preface. Body diary chapters run I–VII; Chronology, Note on the Texts, Notes, and Index follow (not digested as narrative chapters below). Bracketed month/year labels in the LOA text mark editorial groupings within chapters.
Full Chapter-by-Chapter Breakdown
Preface (editor)
“Have you kept a regular Journal? If you have not, you will be likely to forget most of the Observations you have made. If you have omitted this Usefull Exercise, let me advise you to recommence it, immediately. Let it be your Amusement, to minute every day, whatever you may have seen or heard worth Notice. One contracts a Fondness of Writing by Use. We learn to write readily, and what is of more importance, We think, and improve our Judgments, by committing our Thoughts to Paper.” John Adams to John Quincy Adams, May 14, 1783 JOHN QUINCY ADAMS’s diary is one of the most extraordinary works in American literature. Begun in 1779, when Adams was twelve, it was maintained more or less faithfully until his death almost seventy years later, and extends over fifty-one manuscript volumes and more than fourteen thousand closely written pages, including an unbroken string of daily observance spanning a remarkable twenty-six years. Its entries, which range from five hundred to five thousand words or more, record the events of Adams’s public and private lives, including detailed accounts, sometimes verbatim transcripts, of cabinet meetings, diplomatic interviews, congressional debates, dinner conversations, and social calls; incisive character sketches of presidents and princes; painful confessions of anxiety about his own shortcomings, and about the welfare of his family; reflections on sermons he heard and books he read; experiments in verse and translation; theater reviews; and scientific and natural observations.
The Note on the Texts in this volume offers more information on the history of the diaries and on the textual policy followed in this edition. A NOTE ON IDENTIFICATION: Adams’s diary records his interactions with or reflections on a very large cast of characters. Where these individuals are referred to by surname, identification is provided in the Index. Chapter I — 1779–1793 — Europe — Harvard — Boston

[November 1779] A Journal A Journal by Me J Q A Vol: 1st. Friday 12th. this Morning at about 11 O’Clock I took leave of my Mamma my Sister & Brother Tommy and went to Boston with Mr. Thaxter in order to go on board the Frigate the Sensible of 28 twelve Pounders. we arrived at Boston at about 1 O’Clock; dined at my uncle Smiths’, we expected to go on board in the afternoon but We could not conveniently till to morrow. Saturday 13th. to day at about 1 O’Clock Pappa, & my Brother Charles, came to town, and at about 5 O’Clock we all came on board and took our lodgings. My Brother Charles is to lodge with My Pappa and I with Mr. Thaxter. Sunday 14th. this morning a great number of Gentlemen came on board, and amongst others col Johonnot with a son of his who is going to France with us. there are a great number of Passengers and the Frigate is very well mann’d. col Johonnot introduced me to his son, with whom I hope I shall form an acquaintance, which will be very agreable to me and I shall endeavour to make myself agreable to him. this afternoon Capt’n tucker, came on board, and told us that he saw a day or two agone two ships and a brig off Cape Ann: we were very glad he told us of it, so that now we can take proper Measures for shunning them. [June 1794] On the 3d day of June, 1794. When I returned to my lodgings at the close of the Evening; upon opening a Letter from my father, which I had just before taken from the post office, I found it contained information that Edmund Randolph, Secretary of State of the United States had on the morning of the day, when the Letter was dated called on the writer and told him that the President of the United States had determined to nominate me to go to the Hague as Resident Minister from the United States. — This intelligence was to me very unexpected and indeed surprizing. I had laid down as a principle that I never would solicit for any public office whatever, and from this determination no necessity has hitherto compelled me to swerve. From the principles of the same nature which my father has always rigidly observed, I knew that no influence, nor even a request of any kind from him could have occasioned this intention of the President. And yet I was very sensible, that neither my years, my experience, my reputation nor my talents, could entitle me to an office of so much respectability. It is however of no service to indulge conjecture upon the subject. On the 5th: day of June 1794. I received further Letters from my father; informing me, that the nomination had been made; and had received, the advice and consent of the Senate without a dissenting voice. It was the most tempestuous Night we have had upon the passage; of which I had some expectation from the dark clouds flashing with lightening to the leeward of the ship, the brightness of the Stars above the horizon, and the shooting of several of those atmospheric meteors commonly called falling Stars. Great part of the Night the ship was scudding under close reefed top-sails with the wind baffling between S.W. and W — By the tossing and pitching of the vessel, my bed was sliding under me, so that I scarcely slept an hour the whole Night. When I rose I found the weather had moderated. The air was at 64, but feeling rather cool. Water at 70, importing that we are yet within the verge of the gulph-stream — A brig Eastward bound passed within sight of us before Noon. Our latitude was 41:36, Reckoning Longitude 69:40, but really about 64. The day was moderate and cool, but a heavy swell all the Morning, and the weariness which always succeeds a sleepless night prevented me from writing more than the journal of yesterday. I passed the afternoon from dinner till dusk as usual at Chess with Mr. Otis, and had various success. The greatest danger is of the application of remedies worse than the disease — Paper money; and prohibitions — The political empyrics are already as busy as Spiders in weaving their tangles for Congress and the National Executive. ≈ Immediately after dinner, Mr. Poletica, who arrived this day came and paid a visit to Mrs.
King, to such a degree, that in his Speech to the New-York Legislature he recommended King to their choice, not indeed by name, but designating him in terms not to be mistaken. The republican opposition took also the same direction, and King who after ten trials last Winter could not get so many as twenty votes out of 150 now came in by an unanimous vote of the Senate, and by all but three in the House of Assembly. Shortly before the Meeting of Congress, he published at the request of a Missouri-question Meeting at New-York, the substance of his two Speeches last Winter in the Senate on that Bill, which was then lost by the disagreement between the two Houses on the restricting clause — This publication has largely contributed to kindle the flame now raging throughout the Union, on that question, and which threatens its dissolution.
In coming to this passage, if he too should have spent a large portion of his days in studious idleness, let him solace himself with the conclusion which is my principal comfort, that he can be no other than what God and nature have made him; and that although not gifted with Genius, his mediocrity has not been without usefulness in the World — Not all can have the Wisdom of the Serpent — All can be harmless as the Dove. [June 1820] 4. V:15. ≈ I received a very large Mail, but no new despatches of importance. There were Letters and Packets enclosed for Mrs. Forsyth, Baron Stackelberg, and Mr. Poletica; which after dinner I rode round with Mrs. Adams, and delivered at their respective houses. Among the Letters received this day was one from Josiah Quincy, corresponding Secretary to the American Academy of Arts and Sciences at Boston, announcing to me that the Society had at their annual meeting on the 30th of last Month, elected me their President — I answered the Letter and
At this Moment standing on the Isthmus between the past and the future, I look back with satisfaction solid and pure at what has been accomplished of public service, with humility and regret, that more has not been effected, and with unbounded Gratitude to the disposer of all results — Forward, the prospect is beset with difficulties and dangers — Let me advance cheerily to meet the dispensations of Time; pursuing with singleness of Soul the path of duty; imploring for the faculty to will and to do — “to move in Charity, to rest in Providence, and to turn on the Poles of Truth.”
Key Data Points

















































AttributeDetailAuthorJohn Quincy Adams (1767–1848)EditorDavid WaldstreicherTitleJohn Quincy Adams: Diaries, Volume 1: 1779–1821SeriesLibrary of America #293 (2017)Manuscript basisAdams Family Papers, Massachusetts Historical Society; some 1779–1788 selections also from Diary of John Quincy Adams, 1779–1788 (MHS, 1981)Raw filewiki/raw/adams-diaries-vol1.txtLines / words30,163 lines · ~296,648 words (whole EPUB plain text)Diary chaptersPreface + Chapters I–VII (body through ~line 21,262 before Chronology)CoverageNov 1779 – Mar 1821 (selection)SignificanceContinuous first-person record of American diplomacy and national politics from the Revolutionary generation through the early Monroe years
Relationship to the Wiki
For a wiki scoped 1800–1865, this volume is a primary spine for Jeffersonian and Madisonian politics, the War of 1812 settlement, and the Monroe administration as seen from inside the State Department. Chapters III–VII (Boston and Washington; St. Petersburg; Ghent and Paris; London; Secretary of State) carry the heaviest period weight; Chapters I–II supply formation and early diplomatic apprenticeship. Companion LOA volume 2 (not yet in this wiki) continues beyond 1821. Entity and event pages on Adams, Ghent, the Florida / Transcontinental negotiation, and cabinet politics should cite chapter and date ranges from this source page rather than modern summaries.

sources/adams-diaries-vol2.title: [source] John Quincy Adams: Diaries, Vol. 2, 1821–1848 (Library of America)
sources/adams-diaries-vol2.content:
John Quincy Adams: Diaries, Volume 2, 1821–1848 (Library of America)
Author: John Quincy Adams (1767–1848)
Editor: David Waldstreicher
Published: Library of America — Diaries Vol. 2 (LOA #294); eISBN 978-1-59853-524-2
Working text: EPUB via Anna’s Archive (hash eaf47dd7ef8640e700fa28d914772542), pandoc plain extract
Raw extract: wiki/raw/adams-diaries-vol2.txt
Extract stats: ~31,925 lines · ~308,723 words
Overview
This is Volume 2 of the Library of America John Quincy Adams: Diaries, spanning 1821–1848, the companion to LOA Vol. 1 (1779–1821) already on this wiki. It is not Charles Francis Adams’s Lippincott Memoirs and not an Adams Papers letterpress Diary volume. Waldstreicher’s selection presents continuous reading texts of diary entries grouped in seven long chapters, with Chronology, Notes, and Index after the body.
Body chapters in this extract:













































Ch.YearsRunning titleVIII1821–1825Secretary of StateIX1825–1829PresidentX1829–1831RetirementXI1831–1835Twenty-Second and Twenty-Third CongressesXII1835–1838Twenty-Fourth and Twenty-Fifth CongressesXIII1839–1843Twenty-Sixth and Twenty-Seventh CongressesXIV1843–1848Twenty-Eighth, Twenty-Ninth, and Thirtieth Congresses
Prefer LOA volume + chapter + diary date for citation when using this selection; for parallel CFA Memoirs wording on the same days, compare the matching Lippincott volume without conflating slugs (adams-diaries-vol2 vs adams-memoirs-vol*).
Full Chapter-by-Chapter Breakdown
Chapter VIII — Secretary of State (1821–1825)
Opens on the interregnum day before Monroe’s second inauguration: official oath postponed, “no person qualified to Act as President.” Church at the Treasury building; visitors; evening writing. 5 March arrangements at the House hall; heads of departments accompany Monroe; reserved seats for diplomatic corps and members.
The chapter covers the second Monroe term at State: South American recognition and neutrality toward Spain’s colonies; cabinet discussions of Canning’s proposals and Holy Alliance fears (Calhoun “stimulates the panic” after Cadiz falls; Monroe appears briefly to despair of South America); draughts of message minutes and Rush instructions; foreign ministers and domestic patronage. Mid-span entries show Adams pressing written answers to Baronial notes and finding Monroe unsettled. Closing stretch runs through the House election aftermath of 1824–25: Webster committee notification of Adams’s election; written answer modeled on Jefferson’s precedent; invitation to Crawford to remain at Treasury; Military Ball with Monroe, Lafayette, Calhoun. Conversations with G. Sullivan report Calhounite threats—that Clay as Secretary of State would organize opposition under Jackson’s name; a preferred Calhounite cabinet slate (Poinsett, Cheves, McLean, Southard). Adams treats the intimidation as forewarning of systematic opposition. 3 March 1825 closes the Eighteenth Congress and Monroe’s administration: sleepless nights, State Department pressure, wife’s alarming health, Clay in the evening, proof of the inaugural Address from the National Intelligencer.
Chapter IX — President (1825–1829)
4 March 1825: Mrs. Adams desperately ill through the night; Adams’s prayer for country and name; escorted to the Capitol with Southard and Wirt; Monroe follows; Calhoun already sworn as Vice-President; inaugural from the Speaker’s chair; oath administered by Chief Justice Marshall from a volume of the Laws.
Administration years in this selection include foreign settlements (e.g. joy at Gallatin’s convention with Huskisson and Addington ending the Ghent slave-carrying controversy by a British payment over $1.2 million), cabinet business, internal improvements and Indian questions, and the rising Jackson opposition. Clay discusses the next presidential contest. Closing weeks of the term: Jackson avoids personal calls; newspaper explanations (publications against Mrs. Jackson; desire to avoid Clay) are recorded and denied as to Adams’s privity; Meridian Hill removal; Giusta retained by Jackson; inventory delays. 3 March 1829: last messages and bill signings; joint committee announces adjournment; Adams leaves the President’s House for Meridian Hill; accepts resignations of Rush, Porter, Southard, and Wirt—close of the Twentieth Congress and of his presidential public life in this framing.
Chapter X — Retirement (1829–1831)
4 March 1829: Andrew Jackson inaugurated. The leisure years at Quincy and occasional Washington passages: classical and literary study, family economy, correspondence, Anti-Masonic and local political soundings, and the path back toward elective office. The selection bridges defeat and the Plymouth-district return to the House (treated more fully as election machinery in the CFA Memoirs House volumes).
Chapter XI — Twenty-Second and Twenty-Third Congresses (1831–1835)
House service resumes. Committee labor, petitions, tariff and Bank politics, and personal parliamentary combat fill the span. Near the chapter end (30 January 1835), Adams attends the funeral of Warren Ransom Davis of South Carolina—Preston says Adams has lost a devoted friend; Davis’s near-last House words had asked God’s forgiveness for opposing Adams in 1828. Descending the eastern steps of the Capitol, Adams hears a pistol snap “like a squib”: the insane Lawrence’s attempt on President Jackson; both pistols miss fire; the funeral proceeds; sparse return to the House; adjournment on Adams’s motion.
Chapter XII — Twenty-Fourth and Twenty-Fifth Congresses (1835–1838)
Opens in foul winter weather with broken diary threads repaired as far as possible. Adams compares his public position to 1807–08: forced unanimous support for a resolution as counterpart to forced town-meeting politics after the Chesapeake, then Federalist vengeance; now he expects struggle without living to see reparation. French indemnity and Jackson’s possible rashness, presidential succession, and slavery-petition warfare dominate. Mid-chapter literary digressions (Gray, Plato) alternate with committee and library hours.
A set-piece of parliamentary defiance: on a call of yeas and nays Adams refuses to answer, declaring the proceedings unconstitutional; Speaker and two-thirds cry “Order!”; he completes “A direct violation of the Constitution of the United States” and sits; Waddy Thompson’s silvery sarcasm; laughter; vote 185–6 with Wise also refusing. Select committee on the duelling bill; presidential message on Pennsylvania’s call for aid against the Harrisburg mob that blocked legislative organization—Adams reads the refusal of federal aid as ominous precedent, fraud and violence triumphant, and a template by which servile insurrection might later meet the same non-assistance.
Chapter XIII — Twenty-Sixth and Twenty-Seventh Congresses (1839–1843)
Accepts, with extreme repugnance, the New-York Historical Society invitation to address the fiftieth anniversary of Washington’s inauguration—age, reputation, and decaying faculties warn him off; obligation prevails. Fragment delivery plans for a large church at noon. Political gossip (Clay, place-hunting) continues.
Amistad-related legal threads appear (discharge of Africans; Judge Thompson). Patronage seekers meet the limits of Adams’s influence (“Porter at the gate of Heaven”). Church-going and slavery’s absence from conventional sermons are noted. February 1843: Leavitt and Giddings discuss underhand movements for Texas annexation and a possible free-state address; Adams will concur but distrusts firmness of free-state members. Foreign Affairs committee on Cushing’s Ashburton report—boundary parts acceptable; slave-trade compromise sections full of “bad temper and absurd reasoning”; Adams warns Cushing of a coming global war of freedom against slavery headed by Britain, and conjures him not to commit to slavery’s side. Great Latimer petition of Massachusetts blankets his table; fifty-three petitions presented including dissolution-of-the-Union prayers; resolutions on slave-holding disproportion on the Supreme Court bench are blocked when the House flees into Committee of the Whole.
Chapter XIV — Twenty-Eighth, Twenty-Ninth, and Thirtieth Congresses (1843–1848)
Opens with reading of Prigg v. Pennsylvania—seven judges, every one dissenting from the others’ reasoning, all concluding the “transcendent omnipotence of Slavery” under the fugitive clause. Illness, lost days, and self-reproach at idleness recur (“I’ve lost a day”).
Texas annexation fever, Polk’s rise, and nativist–Irish Catholic riots in Philadelphia enter the political field of vision. Campaign and House work parallel the denser CFA Vol. XII narrative for 1844–46. Late entries follow the 20 November 1846 Boston seizure and slow convalescence (amanuensis-marked passages); return via Philadelphia and Baltimore to F Street on Louisa’s birthday 12 February 1847; autumn 1847 travel that feels like the “last great journey”; December 1847 scripture and lighthouse patronage at the Treasury with Secretary Walker—“every word henceforth… last words and dying speech.” Final dated verse lines 20 February 1848 (“Fair Lady, thou of human life…”) stand at the edge of the fatal House seizure the next day. Chronology, Notes, and Index follow the body in the LOA apparatus.
Notes on Using This Source

Edition tradition: Library of America Diaries Vol. 2 (Waldstreicher), slug adams-diaries-vol2. Do not confuse with CFA Memoirs Vol. II (adams-memoirs-vol2) or with “John Adams” (the father).
Companion: LOA Vol. 1 on this wiki covers 1779–1821 (adams-diaries-vol1). Together they are the LOA selected diary arc; CFA Memoirs remain a separate twelve-volume selection with different cuts and editorial bridges.
Overlap: Presidency, nullification-era House, gag rule, Texas, and Mexican War years also appear in CFA Memoirs Vols. VI–XII; use both traditions deliberately rather than merging quotes.
Extract: Pandoc plain from EPUB; ornamental chapter rules appear as [orn.jpg]; section date headers in brackets; ≈ often marks diary paragraph joins in the LOA text encoding.

sources/adams-memoirs-vol1.title: [source] Memoirs of John Quincy Adams, Vol. I (Charles Francis Adams, ed.; AMS reprint 1970 of Lippincott 1874)
sources/adams-memoirs-vol1.content:
Memoirs of John Quincy Adams, Volume I (Lippincott 1874; AMS reprint 1970)
Author: John Quincy Adams (1767–1848)
Editor: Charles Francis Adams (1807–1886)
Published: Lippincott Philadelphia edition 1874–77; this working text is the AMS Press, New York, 1970 reprint of Vol. I (title page: AMS PRESS NEW YORK; reprint note: Reprinted from the edition of 1874–77, Philadelphia; First AMS edition 1970)
ISBN / catalog: Complete set 0-404-00330-3; Volume 1 0-404-00331-1; LCCN 71-134915
Working text: Page-OCR ZIP via Anna’s Archive (hash 0df4c09f0dc01a4a4989f42a06677bba)
Raw extract: wiki/raw/adams-memoirs-vol1.txt (page-sorted OCR, 574 leaves)
Extract stats: 24,309 lines · ~222,203 words
Overview
This is Volume I of Charles Francis Adams’s multi-volume Memoirs of John Quincy Adams, Comprising Portions of His Diary from 1795 to 1848, not the Library of America Diaries series and not an Adams Papers scholarly Diary volume. The AMS reprint front matter identifies the text as reprinted from the Philadelphia Lippincott edition of 1874–77; chapter structure and continuous chapter numbering match the original Memoirs series.
Volume I contains six body chapters:

Chapter I — Birth and Education
Chapter II — The Mission to Holland
Chapter III — The Mission to Holland (Continued) (continuous diary from 1 March 1795)
Chapter IV — A Mission to Great Britain — Appointment to Portugal
Chapter V — Marriage, and the Mission to Prussia
Chapter VI — I. The Senate of Massachusetts — II. The Senate of the United States

The book runs from birth (11 July 1767) and early formation through the first diplomatic missions, marriage to Louisa Catherine Johnson, the Prussian mission, return and Massachusetts service, the United States Senate years, and closes as Adams receives the mission abroad again in 1809 (instructions and farewell Harvard lecture), with END OF VOL. I.
OCR is Hathi-style page files; library bookplate/scan noise appears on early leaves. Prefer diary date + chapter when building event pages; cite as CFA Memoirs Vol. I (AMS reprint of Lippincott). This volume fills the early end of the Memoirs set on this wiki (later volumes II–IX and XII already registered or in process).
Full Chapter-by-Chapter Breakdown
Chapter I — Birth and Education
Charles Francis Adams opens by doubting whether any man left more abundant materials for a life from cradle to grave. John Quincy Adams, eldest son of John and Abigail Adams, was born 11 July 1767 and baptized the next day at the instance of his maternal grandmother, naming him for her father John Quincy (then near death in his seventy-ninth year). CFA sketches the elder Quincy’s colonial public service—popular assembly, council, Indian negotiation—and contrasts that narrow scale with the great-grandson’s career as an illustration of the century’s social and political revolution in America.
Twelve days before the birth, Charles Townshend’s American policy in the Commons marks Burke’s “fourth period” of Anglo-American measures. The chapter draws on family papers and early notebooks rather than the later formal diary: childhood, wartime education, European travel with his father, schooling, and the formation of habits of study and public service that precede the diplomatic appointments of the 1790s.
Chapter II — The Mission to Holland
Materials come from two small paper books written by Adams, predecessors of the more formal diary—covering the unexpected appointment on a public mission to Holland through the eve of the continuous journal. The chapter treats the Hague posting under the Washington administration: arrival, diplomatic society, Batavian politics, correspondence with the Department of State, and the young minister’s self-training in languages, international law, and republican representative manners.
Chapter III — The Mission to Holland (Continued)
At this point the continuous diary begins, drawn from the first of nineteen quarto volumes (about five hundred pages each of fine writing). CFA prints the author’s own title-page for the manuscript diary: Greek motto; Diary of John Quincy Adams from 1 March 1795 to 31 December 1802; Bacon on Truth; the Seven Sages’ maxims (Know thyself; Look to the end of a long life; Watch opportunity; The many are evil; To industry, all; Measure is best; Suretyship…).
Entries from March 1795 onward record Hague business, European war news, American neutrality problems, colleagues and visitors, reading, and self-examination. Breaks occur when public pressure made daily writing impossible; CFA selects portions that illustrate public events or the writer’s character. The Holland continued chapter carries the mission through the mid-1790s until the British special assignment of Chapter IV.
Chapter IV — A Mission to Great Britain — Appointment to Portugal
After Jay’s treaty of 1794 is accepted, ratifications must be exchanged. Thomas Pinckney is in Spain negotiating; Washington’s government calls Adams across the Channel. Instructions include conferring with the British ministry on matters essential to good understanding under the treaty. Adams is to reach London by 25 October or the duty falls to W. A. Deas, secretary of legation. Travel vexations consume twenty-eight days instead of eleven to spare; on arrival Deas has already exchanged ratifications, so that labor is void—but other pending questions keep Adams in negotiation.
The chapter follows London diplomacy, social observation, and the subsequent appointment to Portugal, with the design of proceeding via London and marriage arrangements toward Lisbon.
Chapter V — Marriage, and the Mission to Prussia
On 31 June 1797 (diary/editorial dating as printed) Adams leaves the Hague after nearly four years, intending Portugal via London and marriage to Miss Johnson. In England the first news is another change of destination. Washington, days before leaving office, writes John Adams (20 February 1797) urging that the son not be withheld from merited promotion because he is the father’s son: “Mr. Adams is the most valuable public character we have abroad” and will prove “the ablest of our diplomatic corps.”
Marriage to Louisa Catherine Johnson (26 July 1797 in the series’ later monumental summary) and the mission to Prussia occupy the chapter: Berlin court, commercial and political reporting, Frederick William’s monarchy, and the domestic establishment of the young couple. CFA interlaces official letters with diary narrative of travel, presentation, and literary/diplomatic self-culture.
Chapter VI — The Senate of Massachusetts — The Senate of the United States
Recalled after eight years abroad by the political revolution at home, Adams resumes the legal profession under the disadvantage of long absence. Judge John Davis names him a bankruptcy commissioner; Jefferson’s administration, under a new statute transferring appointments to the Executive, replaces him—an act Abigail and the family read as personal ill will; Jefferson later disavows any such intention or even knowledge of the specific removal.
Adams enters the Massachusetts Senate, then the United States Senate. The long chapter is the densest political narrative in the volume: Jeffersonian measures, embargo and non-importation debates, party pressure, Adams’s independent course that alienates Federalist friends, committee work (including minute recording of sub-committee resolutions on commercial retaliation), Tracy and Anderson and Smith alignments, and the personal cost of leading without a party. Year-headers and diary dates run heavily through 1803–1809.
The volume closes in 1809 as he receives a major mission “totally unsolicited” and confirmed by every Senate vote except personal enemies and two who opposed the mission rather than the man. He prays for clearness of intellectual vision, courage, fortitude, and temperance. Senior and junior classes at Harvard request publication of his lectures; he consults Judge Davis and hesitates. A republican public dinner is declined for want of time. On the twelfth wedding anniversary he receives instructions (credentials still to come from the President in Virginia). At Cambridge he reads his twenty-fourth lecture with leave-taking thoughts; chapel crowded with strangers; leave-taking at President Webber’s—END OF VOL. I.
Notes on Using This Source

Edition tradition: CFA Memoirs Vol. I. This working file is the 1970 AMS reprint of the Lippincott text, not a new edition and not LOA Diaries Vol. 1 (which is a different selection covering 1779–1821).
Not Vol. XI: Title page and chapter map (Birth → Holland → Britain/Portugal → Prussia → Senate) identify Vol. I only. A separate Vol. XI ZIP was not present in the batch that produced this extract.
Continuity: Vol. I ends on the 1809 foreign-mission threshold; Vol. II of this wiki’s set opens the Russian mission (Ch. VII).
OCR / reprint: Early pages include Cornell/library charge-slip noise; body text is continuous Lippincott-style memoir with CFA editorial bridges before pure diary stretches.

Overview
This is Volume X of Charles Francis Adams’s multi-volume Memoirs of John Quincy Adams, Comprising Portions of His Diary from 1795 to 1848, not the Library of America Diaries series and not an Adams Papers scholarly Diary volume. Title page: Memoirs of John Quincy Adams… Edited by Charles Francis Adams. Vol. X. Philadelphia, J. B. Lippincott & Co., 1876. Chapter numbering continues from Vol. IX, which left Chapter XIX (Twenty-Fifth Congress) unfinished.
Volume X contains three body chapters:

Chapter XIX (Continued) — The Twenty-Fifth Congress (from 1 June 1838; TOC)
Chapter XX — The Twenty-Sixth Congress (TOC p. 109)
Chapter XXI — The Twenty-Seventh Congress (opens in this volume; TOC p. 439; continued in Vol. XI)

Running-header years in the OCR cluster on 1838–1841. Prefer diary date + chapter when building event pages; cite as CFA Memoirs Vol. X.
Full Chapter-by-Chapter Breakdown
Chapter XIX (Continued) — The Twenty-Fifth Congress
Opens 1 June 1838. Completes the Van Buren-era House session left open at the end of Vol. IX.
June 1st, 1838.—House business opens with Great Lakes survey resolutions (Erie, Huron, Ontario, Michigan, Superior, Champlain) and amendments. The session continues the petition and slavery-floor fights that dominated Vol. IX: Atherton of New Hampshire’s anti-petition resolutions, gag procedure, and Adams’s recorded resistance on the right of petition. Banking and Sub-Treasury legislation, Texas agitation, and Indian/territorial business recur in the diary’s running comment. Dense keyword field in this volume overall: petitions, gag, Bank, Sub-Treasury, Atherton, slavery.
Chapter XX — The Twenty-Sixth Congress
Covers the 1839–1841 Congress under Van Buren’s close and the Harrison–Tyler transition’s approach.
Diary density rises on Amistad: Spanish ship taken into New London with African captives and Cuban claimants; murder/piracy charges; Judge Smith Thompson and the knotty questions that will reach the Supreme Court—Adams follows as a matter of law and conscience. Smithsonian bequest: Rush recovers about half a million dollars; college interests lobby Adams against applying the fund to a national university destructive of existing colleges; Adams records the Act of Congress and his own views of the trust. Petition and gag fights continue (Atherton resolutions, suspensions of the rules). Electoral politics of 1840—Harrison, Clay, Van Buren—fill visitor and floor notes. China trade and Smithsonian fund administration appear among recurring topics.
Chapter XXI — The Twenty-Seventh Congress (opening)
Begins in this volume (TOC p. 439) and continues in Vol. XI from 1 September 1841.
Harrison’s election and the brief opening of the new administration; early Tyler succession after Harrison’s death; Webster at the State Department; carry-over of Amistad, Smithsonian, and petition business into the special and regular sessions. The chapter break into Vol. XI falls in autumn 1841, with Fletcher Webster already bringing State Department notes to Adams for advice.
High-value passages / topics

Atherton gag / anti-petition resolutions — suspension of the rules; yeas and nays; previous question; Adams’s running protest for the right of petition.
Amistad — capture, New London, Spanish claimants, judicial knot, Adams’s later argument trajectory (carries into Vol. XI / XII era).
Smithsonian bequest — Rush’s recovery of the fund; college lobbying; Adams’s stewardship concern.
Sub-Treasury / Bank politics under Van Buren’s last Congress and the Whig succession.
1840 election and Harrison–Tyler opening of the Twenty-Seventh Congress.

Notes on use

Completes the gap between Vol. IX and Vol. XI.
OCR is Archive.org _djvu.txt (not Hathi page-ZIP); expect soft hyphens, spaced letters, and occasional garble. Verify quotations against neighbouring lines.
Lens: Adams’s own diary as selected by CFA; contemporary-lens paraphrase only.

Memoirs of John Quincy Adams, Volume XI (1876)
Author: John Quincy Adams (1767–1848)
Editor: Charles Francis Adams (1807–1886)
Published: 1876 — J. B. Lippincott & Co., Philadelphia
Working text: Internet Archive / University of Toronto (memoirsofjohnqui11adamuoft) plain OCR (_djvu.txt)
Raw extract: wiki/raw/adams-memoirs-vol11.txt
Extract stats: 24,691 lines · ~214,491 words
Deposit copy: Memoirs of John Quincy Adams Vol XI -- Charles Francis Adams -- Lippincott 1876 -- memoirsofjohnqui11adamuoft_djvu.txt
Overview
This is Volume XI of Charles Francis Adams’s multi-volume Memoirs of John Quincy Adams, Comprising Portions of His Diary from 1795 to 1848, not the Library of America Diaries series and not an Adams Papers scholarly Diary volume. Title page: Memoirs of John Quincy Adams… Edited by Charles Francis Adams. Vol. XI. Philadelphia, J. B. Lippincott & Co., 1876. Continues Vol. X’s Chapter XXI without renumbering; Vol. XII will continue Chapter XXII and close the series.
Volume XI contains two body chapters:

Chapter XXI (Continued) — The Twenty-Seventh Congress (from 1 September 1841; TOC p. 3)
Chapter XXII — The Twenty-Eighth Congress (TOC p. 335; continued in Vol. XII)

Running-header years cluster on 1841–1844. Prefer diary date + chapter; cite as CFA Memoirs Vol. XI.
Full Chapter-by-Chapter Breakdown
Chapter XXI (Continued) — The Twenty-Seventh Congress
Opens 1 September 1841.
September 1st, 1841.—Fletcher Webster calls to ask whether Adams is satisfied with the State Department note to Spanish Minister Argaiz (closing correspondence on a claim after the Supreme Court’s decision—Amistad aftermath). Adams advises against reopening merits if Spain will treat the note as final. Tyler administration patronage and nominations fill the diary: Sandwich Islands commissioner; Everett talked of for China; Wise thrice rejected for France; Cushing thrice rejected for Treasury then Spencer confirmed by one vote; Irwin to Denmark; English vacancy after Everett’s China appointment.
Lord Ashburton (Alexander Baring) arrives on special mission; Adams on Foreign Affairs notes the baggage and the committee meeting with Everett, Stuart, Shepperd, Caruthers. Webster–Ashburton boundary and related diplomacy become a running thread. Creole: brig from Norfolk to New Orleans with tobacco and ~135 slaves; mutiny 7 November; one trader and one mutineer killed; mutineers force course to a British port—Adams records the official narratives and the diplomatic storm. Gag and petition fights continue (Atherton and allies; tariff reference battles with Ways and Means / Manufactures). Smithsonian fund: Adams briefs a new Secretary who receives the history with courteous indifference; promises a statement of the fund’s condition.
Chapter XXII — The Twenty-Eighth Congress
Opens in this volume (TOC p. 335); Texas, Oregon, and Smithsonian threads intensify and carry into Vol. XII.
House years under Tyler’s later term: Texas annexation agitation rises sharply in diary frequency; Oregon appears among territorial/diplomatic notes; China mission and commercial openings recur; petition/gag warfare remains Adams’s signature floor struggle; censure attempts and personal collisions with Southern members continue the pattern of Vols. IX–X. Banking and tariff fights under Whig–Tyler rupture appear alongside foreign-affairs committee work. The volume leaves Chapter XXII unfinished for Vol. XII’s continuation through annexation, Oregon, and the Mexican War run-up.
High-value passages / topics

Amistad aftermath — memorial to transport the Africans to Africa in a public ship; Adams presses Webster and the President.
Webster–Ashburton — special mission; Foreign Affairs committee; northeastern boundary settlement context.
Creole mutiny — slave-brig narrative; Anglo-American friction over asylum and property claims.
Tyler nominations — Wise, Cushing, Spencer, Everett/China, Irwin/Denmark as diary barometer of the Whig split.

Texas / Oregon / gag — bridging into Vol. XII’s terminal chapters.

Overview
This is Volume XII of Charles Francis Adams’s multi-volume Memoirs of John Quincy Adams, Comprising Portions of His Diary from 1795 to 1848, not the Library of America Diaries series and not an Adams Papers scholarly Diary volume. The title page of the extract reads Memoirs of John Quincy Adams… Edited by Charles Francis Adams. Vol. XII. Philadelphia, J. B. Lippincott & Co., 1877. Chapter numbering continues across the series without renumbering.
Volume XII contains two body chapters plus closing editorial apparatus:

Chapter XXII (Continued) — The Twenty-Eighth Congress (opens 2 April 1844; TOC)
Chapter XXIII — The Twenty-Ninth Congress (opens 4 March 1845, Polk inauguration)

The continuous diary carries through the close of the Twenty-Eighth Congress, Polk’s rainy inaugural, Oregon and Texas policy, the Mexican War debates, and Adams’s re-election nomination for the Thirtieth Congress. After a break, a posthumous memoir in Adams’s own hand dates his “decease” for useful purposes from the Boston seizure of 20 November 1846; Charles Francis Adams then narrates the final return to Washington, the last diary/letter threads into early 1848, and death in the House on 21–23 February 1848, with tablet and Hiram Powers bust notes closing the volume before the Index.
Running page headers preserve month and year. OCR is Hathi-style (----- PAGE N -----); soft hyphenation and occasional garbled words appear. Prefer diary date + chapter when building event pages; cite this book as CFA Memoirs Vol. XII. This is the final volume of the Lippincott Memoirs series.
Full Chapter-by-Chapter Breakdown
Chapter XXII (Continued) — The Twenty-Eighth Congress
The chapter resumes 2 April 1844 with the select committee on the Massachusetts Legislature’s resolves of 23 March 1843 meeting in the Manufactures committee room. Morse reads a long report; Sample’s motion to append petition lists divides the committee; Adams is instructed to report that the proposed constitutional amendment ought not to be recommended and that the committee be discharged. The same days bring Orson Pratt and John E. Page of the Latter-Day Saints (Nauvoo / Joseph Smith) seeking interviews and presenting memorials for redress after Missouri expulsions.
Through spring 1844 the diary thickens with Texas annexation, tariff, and House politics. Walter Forward of Pittsburgh remains anxiously against annexation; Adams already sees the impulse of national aggrandizement “doomed beyond the reach of all but Almighty power.” Clay arrives from a southern tour; his letter against annexation at this time appears in the National Intelligencer. Van Buren’s letter against annexation is noted. Mexican relations remain raw: Adams declines intervening with Santa Anna for a Texan prisoner at Perote because of the state of relations. Committee work, personal explanations, and factional theatre (Brown vs White on Clay and protection) fill House days. Mormon memorials, Washington camp-chest presentation requests, and portrait sittings interleave with committee reports.
Summer and autumn 1844 turn on the presidential campaign and Adams’s self-defence against Jackson’s letter to Aaron V. Brown (published via the Globe) alleging treacherous surrender of Texas to Spain. On 7 October Adams delivers a two-hour-plus address at the Tremont Temple for the Young Men’s Whig Club of Boston, using Jackson/Brown as text; reception is enthusiastic; the manuscript goes at once to the Atlas. He prepares a further address to the Eighth District constituents. Clay campaign errands (mass-meeting invitations, printing-press addresses) are mostly declined; Langdon Cheves’s letter on tariff, Texas, nullification, and disunion consumes temper and time.
Smithsonian Fund committee sittings recur. Oregon jurisdiction bills, harbor and tariff bills, and the usual end-of-session scramble appear. The session of the Twenty-Eighth Congress closes in convulsive midnight business: Cave Johnson and Romulus Saunders rival for Postmaster-General; Adams helps defeat what he calls a “swindling Smithsonian bill”; McKay kills a Great Brewster sea-wall appropriation; Tyler vetoes a steamer-payment prohibition and is overridden in both Houses—the first law passed over the veto “precisely as midnight came.”
Chapter XXIII — The Twenty-Ninth Congress
4 March 1845 opens with Polk’s inauguration. Adams likens the day after a dying Congress to the sudden calm after typhoon or hurricane. He declines the Senate committee’s invitation to the ex-Presidents’ place in the ceremonies. Polk and Tyler ride together from Coleman’s; Dallas is sworn; Polk’s half-hour inaugural is delivered in hard rain “to a large assemblage of umbrellas”; Taney administers the oath; two inaugural balls follow (Carusi’s bipartisan; a cheaper pure-Democratic ball).
The Twenty-Ninth Congress diary centers on Texas annexation accomplished despite European interference, Oregon (“fifty-four forty” boundary talk and notice to terminate the 1827 convention with Britain), and the slide into war with Mexico. Foreign Affairs committee work, notice debates, Preston King–Rhett sparring over alleged Ashburton–Webster–Calhoun understandings, and Hilliard’s eloquent notice speech appear. Adams records Guizot’s European balance-of-power language toward the American hemisphere and Thiers’s contrary French tradition of favoring United States aggrandizement against Britain; Polk’s message had complained of French interference against Texas annexation.
Wilmot appears among minority groupings on committee ballots. House and personal life continue: private bills, Washington’s birthday adjournments, European news by steamer. Through 1846 Adams remains active on petitions, Oregon, and Mexican War measures; he comments on the “apoplexy of the Constitution” in related contexts and notes efforts to shape a declaration of war against Mexico. In October 1846 the Whig Convention of the Eighth District nominates him unanimously by ballot for the Thirtieth Congress; he accepts, remarking on Oregon and the Mexican War as subjects of animadversion. Democratic and Liberty-party nominations (Isaac H. Wright; Appleton Howe) repeat the prior canvass. Election day he deposits a Whig ticket with his own name removed; later correspondence corrects Roxbury return errors in his favor.
20 November 1846, at his son’s Mount Vernon Street house in Boston, after morning ablutions he collapses walking with Dr. George Parkman toward the Medical College—knees sinking, “unable to walk.” Physicians Bigelow and Jackson attend; he is confined for days. From that hour he dates his “decease” for every useful purpose and styles subsequent writing a posthumous memoir (paper entirely in his hand). Louisa returns from Washington via the Atlantic. Gradual convalescence: carriage rides from 1 January 1847, street walks, First Church communion with Frothingham. 8–12 February 1847 the family travels Springfield–New Haven–New York–Philadelphia–Baltimore to the F Street house in Washington; 12 February is Louisa’s seventy-second birthday.
Charles Francis Adams then bridges the thin last year: summer 1847 at Quincy including a quiet fiftieth wedding anniversary; last transfer to Washington 1 November 1847; diary by dictation to a granddaughter loses former animation; latest diary entry 4 January 1848, letters to 4 February. A New Year’s letter to his son (1 January 1848) in steady hand urges “a stout heart and a clear conscience, and never despair.” On 21 February 1848 Adams takes his House seat as usual; during a vote of thanks to Mexican War officers he is seized with convulsion; Washington Hunt stops the House; he is carried to a committee room and dies the evening of the 23d. Funeral honors, congressional escort to Quincy, and joint burial with Louisa (d. 15 May 1852) under the church portal follow. The volume closes with the Quincy tablet text (birth 11 July 1767; Ghent 24 December 1814; death at his post 23 February 1848), Hiram Powers bust provenance, acorn/oak-leaf and Α–Ω emblem notes, and Adams’s own lines on Time and to Powers—then the Index.
Notes on Using This Source

Edition tradition: CFA Memoirs (Lippincott selection 1874–77), not LOA Diaries Vol. 2 and not Adams Papers Diary. For overlapping years prefer diary date + this volume when the event is narrated here; cross-check LOA Diaries II for different selection density.
Continuity: Prior Lippincott volumes carry House career through earlier Congresses; Vol. XII is the terminal book (Ch. XXII cont. + XXIII + death apparatus).
Posthumous memoir: Distinguish Adams’s own 20 Nov 1846 “posthumous” framing from CFA’s editorial close on the February 1848 death.
OCR: Page markers and running headers aid dating; soft hyphens and misreads are common near proper names (Polk, Wilmot, Taney, Guizot).

About nine o’clock I returned to the inn, and, having breakfasted, proceeded upon. my journey. From Fors to Kärra, and from Lahall, the last stage, to Gottenburg, I took six horses. At both these places I overtook Axel, whom I had sent forward this morning to bespeak the horses, and I waited for them nearly an hour at every stage. Wherever I had six horses, there were three. peasants came with me to take them back. One of them, at one of the stages, was a woman, and it is a very common thing at the post-houses in Sweden. The women also row the boats upon the rivers, and in general perform almost every kind of labor which in other countries exclusively belongs to the male sex.
Thus far the record has given only the proceedings pre- liminary to the assemblage of the Commissioners of the two sovereign powers on the important duty of restoring peace. The details of the negotiation will be better understood if kept entirely together: hence it has been deemed best to embrace them all in the next volume. END OF VOL. Overview

The title page of the extract reads Memoirs of John Quincy Adams… Edited by Charles Francis Adams. Vol. III. Philadelphia, J. B. Lippincott & Co., 1874. Volume numbering continues the chapter sequence from Vol. II (which closed with the opening of the Ghent negotiation and deferred its full detail to this book).
Volume III contains three chapters:

Chapter IX (Continued) — The Negotiation for Peace
Running-header years sampled in OCR: 1803, 1807–1811, 1813–1815. Month labels include August through January (1814–15). Body: lines ~97–6200 (~57,500 words).
August 7th, 1814. The British Commissioners arrived last evening, and are lodged at the Hôtel du Lion d’Or. Mr. Baker, the Secretary to the Commission, called this morning, first upon Colonel Milligan, who lodges at the Hôtel des Pays-Bas, and where Mr. Baker supposed we were yet all lodged. He afterwards came and called on Mr. Bayard, and notified to him the arrival of the British Commissioners, with a proposal from them that we should meet them to-morrow at one o’clock, afternoon, at their lodgings, and exchange our full powers, and arrange the mode of proceeding between us for the future. Mr. Bayard received this notification, which he agreed to communicate to his colleagues, and promised that we would send an answer this evening. We had a meeting at noon, and were all of opinion that this first step of the British Commissioners was advancing, on their part, an offensive pretension to superiority. I referred my colleagues to Martens, book vii. chap. iv. section 3, of his Summary, where the course now taken by the British Commissioners appears to be precisely that stated there to be the usage from Ambassadors to Ministers of an inferior order. I proposed that Mr. Hughes should call in the evening on Mr. Baker, and say that we should be happy to meet and confer with the Commissioners, and exchange full powers with them, at any time which they would indicate, and at any place other than their own lodgings. Mr. Bayard and Mr. Clay made other propositions, and, after deliberating upon them about two hours, on Mr. Bayard’s proposal we adjourned, to meet again at half-past three. At this meeting, Mr. Bayard produced the case in Ward’s History of the Law of Nations, vol. ii. chap. xvi., of the Commissioners between Spain and England, at Boulogne, in 1600, which in almost every particular resembles the present, and at which the Spanish Commissioners made, and the English resisted, the pretension now advanced by the English. Mr. Bayard and Mr. Gallatin were reluctant at taking any notice of this matter; not that they felt it differently, or doubted that it was intended on the part of the British Commissioners, but from an aversion to clog the negotiation with any question of mere ceremony. We adjourned the meeting again to dine, and finally concluded to send Mr. Hughes with the message I had proposed, substituting, at Mr. Gallatin’s suggestion, instead of the expression, “at any place other than their own lodgings,” the milder terms, “at any place which may be mutually agreed upon,” and authorizing Mr. Hughes to name the Hôtel des Pays-Bas. Mr. Hughes performed his message, and about ten in the evening Mr. Baker came and informed Mr. Bayard, and afterwards all the mission, assembled in Mr. Clay’s chamber, that the British Commissioners agreed to meet us at the appointed hour, and at the Hôtel des Pays-Bas. 8th. We had a meeting of the mission at noon… At one o’clock we went, accompanied by Mr. Hughes, to the Hôtel des Pays-Bas, and found the British Commissioners already there. They are James, Lord Gambier, Henry Goulburn, Esquire, a member of Parliament and Under-Secretary of State, and William Adams, Esquire, a Doctor of Civil Laws. The Secretary to the Commission is Anthony St. John Baker.
could we possibly be said to restore to the Indians the right of trade, if we debarred those who carried it on from trading with them? As to the duties, undoubtedly provision must be made for collecting them, and no doubt that would be agreed to. Mr. Gallatin declared himself of the same opinion with me, as to the grant of the mere right of the navigation of the Mississippi; but he asked me why I had then hesitated so much about offering it as an equivalent for the fisheries. Mr. Clay, on the other hand, thought there would be a gross inconsistency in asking a specific stipulation for the fisheries, after the ground we had taken, that no article…
24th. I wrote letters to the Secretary of State and to my mother, to be prepared for Mr. Hughes, and took my last letter to the Secretary of State to Mr. Smith, for a duplicate to be made. Engaged much of the morning in preparing the copies… the six copies were signed and sealed by the three British and the five American Plenipotentiaries. Lord Gambier delivered to me the three British copies, and I delivered to him the three American copies, of the treaty, which he said he hoped would be the foundation of a lasting peace between the two nations… agreed that the signature of the treaty should not be divulged here until to-morrow noon, so that Mr. Baker may have an opportunity to carry the first information of the event to the British Government. 25th. Christmas-day. The day of all others in the year most congenial to proclaiming peace on earth and good will to men. We had a meeting of the mission at one o’clock. My draft of a dispatch to the Secretary of State had passed through the…
close the record of it with a fervent tribute of gratitude to Divine Providence for the signal favor granted to my country by the conclusion of a treaty of peace; also for the blessings it has continued to me of a domestic nature, to my parents, wife, and children, for the increased proportion of health I have enjoyed, and for the comforts of a quiet conscience. And I implore a continuance of the favor of Heaven upon my country, family, friends, and myself; and, above all, the strength and the will to discharge all my duties to my fellow-creatures and my God. January 2d, 1815. The pressure upon my time is excessive, and accidents continually occurring prevent me from retrieving it. I wrote this morning an answer to the requisition signed by Messrs. Bayard, Clay, and Russell, and presented to me on Saturday by Mr. Clay. I gave it to…
Chapter X — Paris in the Hundred Days
Running-header years sampled in OCR: 1804, 1810, 1815. Month labels include January–May 1815. Body: lines ~6201–8517 (~21,800 words).
BRUSSELS, January 26th, 1815.—I had ordered my horses at ten o’clock this morning, having yet partly to pack my trunks. Antoine came to my chamber just after I had kindled my fire, and we were both busied until eleven in finishing the preparations. I had intended to call yesterday upon Mr. Nuytens to take leave, but had not found a moment for the purpose. It was therefore necessary to write him a note, which I sent by the messenger of the hotel. Nuytens, the son, immediately came to my chamber at the hotel, and took leave of me there. Mr. Cornelissen did the same, and also Mr. Meulemeester, who brought me the music of the couplets sung by his daughter on the 4th instant; they were written by Mr. Cornelissen. At a quarter-past eleven o’clock I entered my carriage and left the Hôtel des Pays-Bas and the city of Ghent, probably never to see them again. My residence in the city has been of seven months and two days, and it has been the most memorable period of my life. I left it with the sentiments suitable to the occasion of grateful regard for its inhabitants, who have taken a strong interest in our success, and have shown us many civilities and attentions; but, above all, with gratitude to Heaven for the signal favor to my country, in which I have participated at this place. There are three stages between Ghent and Brussels—Quadrecht, Alost, and Assche. The distance is six and a quarter posts. I left my carriage only once, at the first stage, and landed at half-past five in the afternoon at the Hôtel de Flandres, in Brussels. It was the coldest day there had been this winter, and was growing colder the whole day. The ground was covered with one sheet of snow the whole way, though not anywhere three inches deep.
Mr. Bayard first mentioned to me that Bonaparte was in France. The proclamation of the King, declaring him a… us that he had been utterly ruined since he left America… Mr. Gallatin said he had heard that it was expected Bonaparte would be last night at Auxerres, and he supposed there would… Napoleon was reviewing troops… he would be glad to have a last resort, even if Louis XVIII. should come back. At bottom, there is an ardent love of his country, and a sincere desire that it should be governed by a free and liberal Constitution; but with regard to the means, he…
quietly to the victorious party, and will do nothing in support of either. If the same spirit should prevail throughout France, Napoleon will soon be overthrown. As I walked to the Tuileries, and through the Palais Royal, before dinner, I saw a multitude of pamphlets against the projected supplement to the Constitution. The caricatures, as yet, are all of one side. 7th. Mr. F. Williams called upon me this morning, with Mr. Boott, from Boston. He left London last Wednesday morning, and brought me a letter of the preceding day, the 2d of this month, from Mr. Beasley, enclosing a dispatch from the Secretary of State, dated 13th March, and which, though not marked as such, must be a duplicate. It informs me that I was appointed Minister Plenipotentiary to Great Britain, and mentions the enclosure of a commission and credentials, neither of which, however, was enclosed. We had a…
Chapter XI — The Mission to Great Britain
Running-header years sampled in OCR: 1800–1818, 1821, 1864 (editorial/cross-ref). Month labels include May 1815 through June 1817. Body: lines ~8518–24453 (~149,500 words; bulk of the volume).
May 16th, 1815. Began the day by bringing up the arrears of my journal, at which it is generally inconvenient to write in travelling. The remainder of the morning was occupied with the last preparations for departure. Mr. Erving and General La Fayette came and took leave of us, and Mr. R. Boyd saw us into the carriage. We received a multitude of letters and packages from several persons, to be carried to England. With our large quantity of baggage, they encumber us not a little. We had ordered the horses at three o’clock in the afternoon. They came at half-past three, and at twenty minutes past four we left the Hôtel du Nord, Rue de Richelieu, No. 97, where I have passed upwards of three months of leisure, too unprofitably for any useful purpose, but as agreeably as any part of my life. We travelled three stages, and arrived at Pontoise between seven and eight. We stopped to lodge at the Hôtel du Juste, and ordered horses for three o’clock to-morrow morning. My object in coming thus far this day was to have an easy day’s ride to reach Rouen to-morrow, but we find the roads so good, and the days are now so long, that we might easily have gone two stages further this evening, and have reached Havre itself to-morrow night. The country is in its early verdure, and the orchards are all in full blossom. We had green peas this day for the first time at dinner, and within these two days have seen small bunches of cherries for sale in the streets. LONDON, 25th.—We breakfasted this morning at six, and at seven left Dover with two post-chaises, Mrs. Adams and myself in one, Lucy and Charles in the other.
I wrote a note to Lord Castlereagh, informing him of my arrival with a public commission, and requesting him to appoint a time for me to call upon him… when the Prince Regent would receive my credential letter. He said if I was desirous of presenting it at an early day, the Prince would receive me at a private audience; otherwise it would be at the first levee day… It was almost three when the Prince Regent began to give private audiences. The first was to Lord Grenville… The second was to me… by the Prince Regent Envoy Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary to the United States… I received from Messrs. Robinson and Goulburn and Dr. Adams, the Commissioners appointed to negotiate with us for a treaty of commerce, a note requesting me to meet them… a sort of celebration of the battle of Waterloo, of which this is the anniversary… suggested that in each cruiser there should be an officer of each power agreeing to the principle, and that he should be present at every search… I also alluded to the misconduct of many naval British officers, to the manner in which they had taken slaves from the United States… Wilberforce was much struck by this information…
N.B. I have now completely brought up the arrears of this journal, which, during my last residence in Europe, and most especially from the time when I left St. Petersburg to attend at the negotiation of the Peace of Ghent, has occupied so large a portion of my time that I can henceforth no longer continue it with the same minuteness. On my return to my native country, a new and, for some time at least, a busy and laborious scene threatens to open before me—a scene so laborious and so full of perils and perplexities that a stouter heart than mine would be appalled at the prospect of it. From the time of my arrival in the United States my journal must be a mere abstract of loose memoranda. My whole time must be devoted to the performance of duties; and may the mercy of Heaven assist me duly to discharge them! 10th. VI. Tuesday. London, farewell! … At a quarter before one we left London in a post-chaise. For my own part, I bade adieu to London in all probability forever. We came over Westminster Bridge, and our first stage was to Kingston; we proceeded thence to Cobham, Guildford, Farnham, where we dined, and Alton, where we arrived a quarter before nine in the evening, and stopped for the night. 11th. At eleven we proceeded upon our journey to Alresford, Winchester… and to Southampton… 15th. Sunday. COWES, ISLE OF WIGHT.—At eleven o’clock in the morning I embarked with all my family on board the ship Washington, which was lying in the roads. The anchor was immediately weighed, and we proceeded upon our voyage. END OF VOL. III.
