Overview
This is Volume IV of Charles Francis Adams’s multi-volume Memoirs of John Quincy Adams, Comprising Portions of His Diary from 1795 to 1848, not the Library of America Diaries series and not an Adams Papers scholarly Diary volume. The title page of the extract reads Memoirs of John Quincy Adams… Edited by Charles Francis Adams. Philadelphia, J. B. Lippincott & Co., 1875 (with copyright entry 1874). Half-title OCR includes VOL. IV. Chapter numbering continues across the series: Vol. III closed with Chapter XI (Mission to Great Britain) and embarkation home; this book is a single continuous chapter.
Volume IV contains one body chapter:

Chapter XII — The Department of State—First Term (New York landing 6 August 1817 through February 1820; TOC lists pp. 3–533)

Running page headers preserve month and year (e.g. [August, / 1817.]). OCR is Hathi-style page files (----- PAGE N -----); soft hyphenation and occasional garbled words appear. Front matter includes a one-line table of contents for Chapter XII only.
This CFA Memoirs volume covers the first years of Adams as Secretary of State under James Monroe and continues [[adams-memoirs-vol3|CFA Memoirs Vol. III]] after the 1817 homecoming. Prefer diary date + chapter when building event pages; cite this book as CFA Memoirs Vol. IV.
Full Chapter-by-Chapter Breakdown
Chapter XII — The Department of State—First Term
Running-header years sampled in OCR: 1817–1820. Month labels run August 1817 through February 1820. Body: lines ~78–22999 (~215,000 words; the entire volume after front matter).
NEW YORK, August 6th, 1817.—Immediately after daylight this morning the ship was within three miles of the highlands of Neversink, and the new Sandy Hook light-house in full sight, as well as the two old ones; all the lights were still burning. The morning was fine, and almost all the passengers soon came upon deck. The sun rose clear, and Venus was visible more than a quarter of an hour after she had risen; air and water both at 67. There were a number of vessels in sight, and among the rest a pilot-boat schooner, from which a pilot, named Bird, came on board at six. We had a fair and light breeze, which took us up to the wharf at New York, where we landed at one in the afternoon, immediately from the ship. The approach to New York was slow, and the termination of the voyage as agreeable as could be wished. The sentiments with which, after an absence of eight full and eventful years, I touched once more my native land were of a mingled nature: of the deepest gratitude to the Supreme Disposer for all the enjoyments and preservations of that long period, and particularly for the safe and happy close of the voyage just completed, together with an anxious forecast of the cares and perils of the new scene upon which I am about to enter… nothing but a firm reliance upon Him who has ever been my preserver, and the dispenser of every blessing, supported me from despondency. 7th. We had a continual succession of visitors… In the evening, Mr. Astor, Mr. Colden, and Mr. … came as a committee… and invited me to a public dinner… 11th. … I went with them to the public dinner at Tammany Hall. There were about one hundred persons present… among them Governor De Witt Clinton… 14th. Called on Mr. Trumbull, and found him with the frame for his large picture of the Declaration of Independence… left them transhipping to the sloop Margaret… for Washington.
In Washington he finds President Monroe returned from a long eastern and western tour; the President’s House is again habitable after the British burning of 1814. Monroe directs that Richard Rush is to succeed Adams at the Court of Great Britain and that instructions for Rush be drawn. Early Cabinet meetings take up Spain, South American insurgents, and the breaking up of marauding parties at Amelia Island and Galveston. Adams avows that it is not then expedient to acknowledge the Government of Buenos Ayres; the President postpones that determination. Bagot (British), Hyde de Neuville (French), and Don Luis de Onis (Spanish) fill the diplomatic calendar; fisheries proposals, etiquette with Senators, and the daily grind of the Department open the first term.
January 1st, 1818.—In the evening, and until eleven, I was writing remarks for Mr. Middleton’s draft of a report to the House of Representatives upon Amelia Island… 3d. … At the President’s, I mentioned to him again the proposal for the fisheries, to be made to Mr. Bagot… he directed me to ask Mr. Crowninshield, Mr. Holmes, Mr. Silsbee, Mr. Nelson, and all the members from Massachusetts representing districts interested in the fisheries, to call… for a consultation… Crowninshield had received dispatches with information of the surrender to us of Amelia Island on the 23d of last month. Mr. Calhoun afterwards came in with the same dispatches, and the President appointed a Cabinet meeting… to determine what should be done with Amelia Island.
Through 1818 the diary is dominated by the Florida–Seminole crisis and Jackson’s seizure of Spanish posts. In Cabinet, Crawford argues that if the Administration does not immediately declare itself and restore Pensacola, it will be held responsible for Jackson’s having taken it and for having commenced a war in violation of the Constitution. Adams answers that to disavow and publish now would look like a disposition entirely to put down Jackson; that Pensacola might be restored and its capture still justified; that he does not believe war would follow, though he admits it might. Hyde de Neuville is extremely anxious for the preservation of peace; Adams marks on the map the boundary authorized at the President’s—the Trinity from its mouth to its source, then a line north to the Red River… then crossing to the Rio del Norte… or the summit of a chain of mountains… there stop, or take a line west to the Pacific. De Neuville offers to carry the line to Onis at Bristol. Adams says Onis will be told that Jackson had taken Pensacola without orders and upon his own responsibility; that the place would be restored, but that no blame could be admitted as attaching to General Jackson, and strong charges would be made against the Governor of Pensacola and the Commandant at St. Mark’s. Arbuthnot and Ambrister executions, Bagot’s agitation over court-martial news, and Calhoun’s orders for the surrender of Pensacola interleave with Onis’s notes.
WASHINGTON, January 1st, 1819. Friday.—Began the year by commencing the draft of a dispatch to R. Rush, London, and then finished the fifth volume of this diary… Went with Mrs. Adams to pay the New Year’s visit at the President’s… The President’s house was also more crowded than I ever saw it on a similar occasion. Mr. Daschkoff, the Russian Minister, paid me likewise a visit this morning. It is the first time he has been at Washington since I have been in office… 2d. I finished my draft of a dispatch to R. Rush… to instruct Rush to inform Lord Castlereagh that the President intended before long to recognize the Government of Buenos Ayres as independent… When I read my draft to the President, he thought it best to consult the Cabinet… They were all startled at the paragraph announcing it as the President’s intention at no remote period to recognize the Government of Buenos Ayres… Mr. Pedersen, the Danish Minister, came… upon the project of a treaty of commerce between the United States and Denmark…
Onis delivers a projet of a treaty for the cession of the Floridas by Spain to the United States, for the settlement of the western boundary, and for the adjustment of claims of indemnities… in seventeen articles; Adams promises a counter-projet. After protracted negotiation, 22d (February 1819): Mr. Onis came at eleven, with Mr. Stoughton… The two copies of the treaty made out at his house were ready… We exchanged the original full powers on both sides… I read the English side, which he collated, and he the Spanish side, which I collated. We then signed and sealed both copies on both sides—I first on the English and he first on the Spanish side… Mr. Onis took with him his executed copy of the treaty, and I went over with ours to the President’s… Brent takes the message with the treaty to the Senate; Fromentin reports it was received with universal satisfaction. The same season brings Jackson to the city, Forsyth’s appointment as Minister to Spain, and Rufus King’s long political conversations (including the British West India trade article).
Later entries turn to the Missouri question. Congress had failed at the last session to make the Territory of Missouri a State, owing to a restriction introduced by the House excluding slavery from the State and declaring free all persons to be born there after a certain period; the Senate struck out the provision, and the bill failed by disagreement. Adams records the violent agitation among members from the slave-holding States, and writes: The slave-drivers, as usual, whenever this topic is brought up, bluster and bully, talk of the white slaves of the Eastern States, and the dissolution of the Union, and oceans of blood; and the Northern men, as usual, pocket all this hectoring… Crawford… relies on the support of the slave-drivers… On this particular question I did not approve of the attempted restriction upon the State of Missouri, because I believe it not compatible either with the Constitution of the United States or with the Louisiana Treaty. But I think Crawford’s toast not remarkable for delicacy towards the Legislature, while the question is pending before them…
January 1st, 1820.—I attended at the Treasury Office a meeting of the Commissioners of the Sinking Fund, which Mr. Crawford had appointed at two o’clock… The volume closes still deep in the Missouri agitation. 27th. Called upon Mr. R. King at his lodgings at Crawford’s Hotel, Georgetown. Found him still absorbed in the Missouri slave question, upon which he has been the great champion of freedom and the Northern interest. The partisans of slavery have spread abroad the idea that he has been actuated… by motives of personal ambition… King, however, indulges hopes that it may survive the present question. END OF VOL. IV.

Full Chapter-by-Chapter Breakdown
Chapter XII (Continued) — The Department of State—First Term
Running-header years sampled in OCR: 1820–1821. Body: lines ~81–13599 (~March 1820 through the eve of Monroe’s second inauguration).
March 1st, 1820.—I was at the President’s. The Missouri slave question has come to its crisis in Congress. The majorities in the two Houses are on opposite sides, and there are Committees of Conference to effect a compromise. 2d. The compromise of the slave question was this day completed in Congress. The Senate have carried their whole point, barely consenting to the formality of separating the bill for the admission of the State of Maine into the Union from that for authorizing the people of the Territory of Missouri to form a State Government. The condition that slavery should be prohibited by their Constitution, which the House of Representatives had inserted, they have abandoned. Missouri and Arkansas will be slave States, but to the Missouri bill a section is annexed, prohibiting slavery in the remaining part of the Louisiana cession north of latitude 36° 30’. This compromise, as it is called, was finally carried this evening by a vote of ninety to eighty-seven in the House of Representatives, after successive days and almost nights of stormy debate… And so it is that a law for perpetuating slavery in Missouri, and perhaps in North America, has been smuggled through both Houses of Congress… The fault is in the Constitution of the United States, which has sanctioned a dishonorable compromise with slavery. There is henceforth no remedy for it but a new organization of the Union…
Monroe summons the Cabinet for written opinions to be deposited in the Department of State on two questions: whether Congress has a constitutional right to prohibit slavery in a Territory, and whether the eighth section of the Missouri bill (interdicting slavery north of 36° 30’) applies only to the territorial stage or also after statehood. The Cabinet unanimously agrees that Congress may prohibit slavery in the Territories, though Crawford, Calhoun, and Wirt struggle to ground that power in the Constitution’s text. Adams argues that the power to “dispose of” territory and to make “needful rules and regulations” must reach persons as well as land, and that interdiction of slavery where it does not exist is needful to “establish justice.” He records that he has favored the compromise as all that could be effected under the present Constitution and from extreme unwillingness to put the Union at hazard, yet wonders whether persistence until a convention of the States might have been wiser. In conversation with Calhoun he writes that slavery taints the very sources of moral principle and establishes false estimates of virtue and vice.
Through 1820 the diary also tracks Spain’s failure to ratify the Florida treaty within the stipulated period. Adams holds that by withholding ratification Spain has thrown away the bargain and that the United States are no longer bound by it; he weighs messages proposing postponement of reprisals, Clay’s tactics to set the treaty aside and recognize the South Americans, Southern greed for more slave territory, and Northern distaste for Florida as another slave State. Russian and French wishes for moderation, disturbances in Spain, and Forsyth’s Madrid dispatches shape the President’s course. Agents and adventurers from South America (Torres, Forsyth of Venezuela, Bolívar’s circle, privateering under Colombian and Venezuelan flags) press for recognition, arms, and letters of recommendation; Adams distrusts their coaxing as much as their earlier bullying and steers Monroe toward principal-to-principal correspondence rather than free-handed patronage.
29th (September/October season, 1820).—I received this morning a letter from Mr. Stratford Canning, informing me that he had arrived late last evening in the city, with a credential letter as Envoy Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary from the King of Great Britain… He came with Mr. Antrobus… The conversation then turned upon indifferent topics… October 2d. Mr. Canning came by appointment… and I had with him a conversation of more than two hours upon the slave-trade. He renewed and urged the proposal heretofore made by the British Government, that the United States should accede to the principles of treaties made by Great Britain with the Netherlands and Portugal, by which the vessels of either nation are allowed to be searched by the captains of the armed vessels of another, and two mixed Courts of Commissioners are instituted… We have rejected this proposal, on two grounds: one, a want of Constitutional authority to establish such a Court, and the other, as disapproving the principle of allowing the search, in time of peace, of our merchant vessels by the armed cruisers of another nation… The first was the general extra-European policy of the United States…
January 1st, 1821.—At the drawing-room at the President’s. It was more thronged with company than I ever saw it on any similar occasion… Mr. Monroe, by a vote, with a single exception unanimous, of all the electoral colleges of this Union, has just been re-elected President of the United States for a second term of four years… I received a private letter from John Forsyth, our Minister at Madrid, informing me that the Cortes, on the 5th of October, had advised in secret session the ratification of the Florida Treaty… Canning continues long conversations on the slave-trade; Adams’s substitute proposals for African-coast co-operation without mixed courts leave the British envoy unsatisfied. The chapter closes on the eve of Monroe’s second inauguration, with Florida ratification at last in view and the first-term State Department chronicle complete.
Chapter XIII — The Department of State—Second Term
Running-header years sampled in OCR: 1821–1822. Body: lines ~13600–23335 (March 1821 through early 1822; END OF VOL. V).
March 4th, 1821, Sunday.—And the commencement of the second term of the Administration of James Monroe, fifth President of the United States. But, the administration of the official oath… being postponed till to-morrow, this day was a sort of interregnum, during which there was no person qualified to act as President… 5th. Second inauguration of James Monroe as President of the United States. The arrangements were made at the hall of the House of Representatives… The President, attired in a full suit of black broadcloth of somewhat antiquated fashion, with shoe- and knee-buckles, rode in a plain carriage with four horses and a single colored footman. The Secretaries of State, the Treasury, War, and the Navy followed… On alighting at the Capitol a great crowd… Mr. Canning and Mr. Antrobus, in full Court-dress uniforms, were in the midst of this crowd, unable to obtain admission… The President took a seat on a platform just before the Speaker’s chair. The Chief Justice was seated at his right hand… the President repeating the oath in the words prescribed by the Constitution. The address was delivered in a suitably grave and rather low tone of voice… At his departure from the House there was a cheering shout from the people in the galleries, and the music of the Marine Band played both at his entrance and departure.
The second-term narrative is dominated by the practical aftermath of the Florida cession and by ordinary diplomacy. Cabinet meetings debate Jackson’s proceedings as provisional governor—Callava’s arrest, Fromentin’s writ of habeas corpus, Spanish Chargé Salmon’s protests, and whether Spanish commissioners retained diplomatic immunities after surrender of the province. Monroe fluctuates; Adams drafts letters to Jackson and Fromentin and an answer to the Spanish complaint, urging that Jackson first be heard on Salmon’s charges. Anduaga (Spanish minister) and boundary/commissioner appointments under the treaty recur; Calhoun consults on fortifications and contracts (Dauphin Island) when Congress withholds appropriations.
January 1st, 1822.—This year began, as the last had commenced and closed, with solitary meditation… Mr. Sterling… said that one hundred and ten members out of one hundred and sixty-nine had met in caucus, and fifty-seven of them had voted Mr. Lowndes as a candidate for the Presidency at the next election… It was but one-third of the whole Legislature, and was altogether a precipitate and injudicious measure… At noon we attended the drawing-room at the President’s. The crowd of company was as great as I have ever known it… Canning presses boundary and Navigation Act questions; Trimble moves calls for French-negotiation papers. Late entries turn on Hyde de Neuville’s commercial Convention projet—discriminating duties, deserting seamen, Consular Convention articles, refunding of duties under the Act of 15 May 1820—and on whether the Executive is already too far committed to break off. The President concludes to take the Attorney-General’s opinion on Dauphin Island contractor suits; Calhoun’s object, Adams notes, is to escape congressional investigation of the contract. END OF VOL. V.

Overview

Full Chapter-by-Chapter Breakdown
Chapter XIII (Continued) — The Department of State—Second Term
Running-header years sampled in OCR: 1822–1825. Body: lines ~74–22308 (2 June 1822 through the close of Monroe’s administration and the transfer of power). TOC places this chapter at p. 3.
June 2d, 1822.—General D. Parker came in, and detained me at an interview of more than three hours. Parker was brought in as Chief Clerk of the War Department by Dr. Eustis… Both the President and the Secretary of War have reasons for disliking, and, as he evidently thinks, for dreading Parker… Crawford wrote him a note (6th May)… offering him a clerkship… which he declined… This avidity of Crawford to secure Parker in his interest is easily accounted for. He knows that great use may be made of him against both the President and Calhoun… The opening of the volume is thus already a map of presidential undercurrents—Armstrong’s attacks on Monroe, Scott as a Calhoun champion, Russell’s letter and the President’s search for papers, and Adams’s insistence that he must stand upon his own support. Cabinet meetings immediately take up Porto Rico privateers and West India piracy, Creek and Florida awards, and Canning’s visits on South American recognition and the slave-trade.
Through the summer and fall of 1822 the diary tracks recognition of the South American Governments, commercial missions without exclusive advantages, and European embarrassment at the American example. Adams tells Monroe that running a race with England for special privilege would be neither wise nor honest; mutual advantage and reciprocity are all that should be asked. Canning continues long interviews on slave-trade search, boundary, and colonial trade; Hyde de Neuville and French commercial questions, Russian agents, and agents of the new republics recur. Cabinet and congressional politics harden around Crawford’s “Radicals,” Calhoun’s presidential expectations, and newspaper warfare.
July–November 1823 bring the crisis that the editor later labels the first hint of the Monroe doctrine. Adams drafts instructions to R. Rush on maritime, belligerent, and neutral law and a project of Convention on neutral and belligerent rights. Cabinet debate on Canning’s proposals for a joint Anglo-American declaration against European recolonization of Spanish America runs for weeks. Adams opposes a joint declaration that would give Britain a pledge against American annexation of Texas or Cuba while yielding little in return; Southard inclines the same way; Monroe is averse to any course that appears subordinate to Britain and suggests a special Minister to protest Holy Alliance interposition. Calhoun stimulates panic after Cadiz surrenders to the French; Monroe for a time despairs of the South American cause. Adams prepares minutes for the President’s message, drafts on communications from Baron de Tuyl, and presses a firm non-interference dual rule: the United States will not meddle in European politics, and European powers must equally abstain from subjugating any part of the American hemisphere. The final paper, though varied from Adams’s original draft, is conformable to his views; paragraphs on Greece, Spain, Portugal, and South America are drawn in the spirit he had urged.
January 1st, 1823 opens with a New Year poem and Anglo-Russian slave-convention salaries; January 1st, 1824 opens on the Richmond anti-caucus explosion (Tyler’s report indefinitely postponed 77–76) and Webster’s Greek resolution, which Adams fears will compromise quiet work at Constantinople. Through 1824 the diary is dominated by succession politics. Rufus King reports rumor of a Crawford–Adams caucus coalition for President and Vice-President; Adams says such overtures were made and rejected. R. M. Johnson relates Calhoun’s proposed arrangement (Adams President, Jackson Vice-President, Clay Secretary of State, Johnson Treasury) “not as a bargain or coalition, but by the common understanding of our mutual friends.” Clay’s friends (Letcher and others) sound Adams on Kentucky and Western votes if the election goes to the House. Adams writes “Incedo super ignes.”
January 1st, 1825.—… Richard Forrest brought me, to authenticate, an Act of Congress granting to General La Fayette a sum of two hundred thousand dollars and a township of land… Robert P. Letcher… told me… the members of the Kentucky Legislature would… recommend… General Jackson… But I might rely upon it they would have no effect. The vote of Kentucky in the House was fixed and unalterable… 9th February 1825.—May the blessing of God rest upon the event of this day!—the second Wednesday in February, when the election of a President of the United States for the term of four years, from the 4th of March next, was consummated. Of the votes in the electoral colleges, there were ninety-nine for Andrew Jackson… eighty-four for John Quincy Adams… forty-one for William Harris Crawford… and thirty-seven for Henry Clay… in all, two hundred and sixty-one… the House of Representatives immediately proceeded to the vote by ballot from the three highest candidates, when John Quincy Adams received the votes of thirteen, Andrew Jackson of seven, and William H. Crawford of four States. The election was thus completed, very unexpectedly, by a single ballot.
The next day a House committee (Webster, Vance, Archer) formally notifies him of the choice; he returns a written answer on the Jefferson precedent. He invites Southard to remain at the Navy, offers Crawford the Treasury (declined in friendly terms), and determines to offer the Department of State to Clay—due to his talents and services, to the Western section of the Union, and to the confidence of the friends who had supported him. Calhoun’s circle, Johnson’s disclosures, and Benton/Poinsett moves are read as a system of opposition to bring in Jackson under Calhoun’s auspices. Nominations and leave-taking with Monroe fill the last days of the second-term chapter as Adams prepares to enter the presidency.
Chapter XIV — The Presidency
Running-header years sampled in OCR: 1825. Body: lines ~22309–23604 (4 March 1825 through mid-May 1825; END OF VOL. VI). TOC places this chapter at p. 518.
Charles Francis Adams opens with an editorial caveat: materials for this important period are not continuous; constant interruption of visitors and imperative official duties left gaps never afterwards filled; much of what remains is minutes for a narrative rather than the narrative itself, founded largely on the visits of persons drawn to the President.
March 4th, 1825.—After two successive sleepless nights, I entered upon this day with a supplication to Heaven, first, for my country; secondly, for myself and for those connected with my good name and fortunes, that the last results of its events may be auspicious and blessed. About half-past eleven o’clock I left my house with an escort of several companies of militia and a cavalcade of citizens, accompanied in my carriage by Samuel L. Southard, Secretary of the Navy, and William Wirt, Attorney-General, and followed by James Monroe, late President of the United States, in his own carriage. We proceeded to the Capitol, and to the Senate-chamber… John C. Calhoun presiding… having been previously sworn into office as Vice-President… I repaired to the hall of the House of Representatives, and, after delivering from the Speaker’s chair my inaugural address to a crowded auditory, I pronounced from a volume of the laws held up to me by John Marshall, Chief Justice of the United States, the oath faithfully to execute the office of President of the United States… After exchanging salutations with the late President… I returned to my house… a crowd of visitors… then… to the President’s house… and in the evening attended the ball…
Early presidency business is cabinet formation and foreign and military detail. Nominations include Henry Clay Secretary of State; Richard Rush of Pennsylvania Secretary of the Treasury; James Barbour of Virginia Secretary of War; Alexander Hill Everett to Spain; chargés to the Netherlands, Portugal, Buenos Ayres, Guatemala, and Brazil; Roger Jones Adjutant-General; and batches of customs, land-office, navy-agent, Florida, and consular renominations. Adams resists a principle of rotation at the expiration of commissions that would make government a perpetual scramble for office. Clay prepares instructions for Rufus King; conversations with General Brown turn on army rank (Gaines vs. Scott) and Mackinaw troops; Southard brings the Court of Enquiry on Captain Porter (Foxardo / Porto Rico). Barbour reports Mexican designs on Cuba and the critical state of Georgia and the Creek Indians, with Crowell’s letter complaining of the Governor of Georgia. Clay urges removal of Sterret, Naval Officer at New Orleans, as a clamorous reviler of the Administration after the election; Adams accepts the principle that after decision no officer at the President’s pleasure should hold open disparagement, but insists on specific proof and delicacy in application. The volume ends as Adams renews the attempt to journalize morning and evening: END OF VOL. VI.

Opening — May–summer 1825: Creek massacre, Troup, cabinet routine
May 15th, 1825.—Chilly Mackintosh, Colonel Mackintosh, Jim Tallazan, Ben Tallazan. These four Creek Indians called on me this morning before breakfast with a letter from Governor Troup, of Georgia, and a talk sent by him to certain other Creek chiefs… announced to me the murder of the chief called General Mackintosh… It was on Saturday, the 30th of last month, that a party of about four hundred surrounded and set fire to his house, and killed him and another chief… Troup charges Crowell, the Agent, with having instigated this massacre, and vows revenge with a spirit as ferocious as ever inspired any Creek Indian. Adams directs Secretary of War Barbour to confer with the chiefs, measure disposable force for the Georgia border, and draft an answer: the United States cannot interpose in internal feuds of an Indian tribe, but will warn the Upper Creeks against further violence and permit a winter deputation. He apprehends the massacre is only the signal for a ferocious Indian war.
The same week Clay’s October letter to Hammond on objections to Crawford is discussed for publication; Adams doubts its expediency. Indian school and Seneca annuity funds under Monroe and Calhoun require regular accountability. Through summer 1825 the diary mixes Creek and Georgia papers (Gaines councils, Mackintosh party talks, Indian Springs aftermath), army brevet and rank questions, Porter court materials still in train from Vol. VI, and visitors. August brings General Lafayette to Washington: Adams declines private parties on the principle of his predecessors, visits the frigate Brandywine with Lafayette and Southard, and records the General’s leave-taking circuit. Gaps appear where visitor pressure leaves only margin lists of names.
Autumn–winter 1825–26: first annual message, Panama, New Year 1826
Preparation of the annual message fills November. Adams reads Rush the concluding part recommending internal improvement in its full extent; Rush approves though other members of the Administration will not. Sergeant accepts appointment as one of the Ministers to the Congress at Panama; Gallatin declines. Cabinet meeting of 23 November takes Pea-patch fortification claims (Delaware vs. New Jersey), Creek business, and first reading of the message. Forsyth later marks the announced Panama mission as a change of policy; Adams answers that circumstances, not policy, have changed.
December–January bring Edward Thomson’s Philadelphia custom-house failure (near a million dollars in tea duties at risk) and pressure to remove the Collector. Clay urges that the Panama nominations go to the Senate; Adams agrees to send the message on the Monday after adjournment. New Year’s Day 1826 draws two to three thousand visitors; Russian and French Ministers refuse the crowd and ask a separate ceremonial day, which Adams declines. Branch’s hostile Senate resolution and the Panama nomination fight open the session. Lloyd and Mills report the Foreign Relations Committee (Tazewell writing) will report against the mission; confirmation, if it comes, will be by a small majority after long debate.
Winter–spring 1826: Panama as first united opposition; internal improvement
February 1826.—A debate commenced this day in the House of Representatives on two resolutions calling for papers relating to the proposed mission to Panama. This is the first subject upon which a great effort has been made in both Houses to combine the discordant elements of the Crawford and Jackson and Calhoun men into a united opposition against the Administration. The House passes a modified call 124–40. Cabinet and Senate business track the nominations, instructions, and South American correspondence. Internal-improvement language and canal/road papers (including Cumberland Road routing disputes) recur alongside visitor lists and message drafts. Anderson later remarks that the late session produced four or five challenges to duels that ended in smoke, and that a public dinner to John Randolph of Roanoke produced a toast directly instigating assassination.
Summer 1826: Jubilee Fourth; deaths of Jefferson and John Adams
July 4th, 1826—the fiftieth anniversary—Adams joins the Capitol procession with Calhoun following; Joseph Anderson reads the Declaration; Walter Jones delivers the oration; Barbour and Rush solicit subscriptions for Jefferson’s relief with scant immediate success. Within days the mail brings word that John Adams’s end is approaching; Adams determines to leave for Quincy. On the road to Baltimore he learns his father died on the 4th about five in the afternoon. My father had nearly closed the ninety-first year of his life—a life illustrious in the annals of his country and of the world… The time, the manner, the coincidence with the decease of Jefferson, are visible and palpable marks of Divine favor… Funeral honors for Jefferson he leaves to the heads of Departments; his own journey becomes a chain of eulogies and processions (Storrs at Braintree; Sprague at Salem with Webster and Everett present; Wirt’s two-and-a-half-hour discourse on return). After about a hundred days partially released from Washington cares he resumes the stream of visitors and official business.
Autumn 1826–winter 1827: British negotiation; Monroe and Panama/Mexico; Creek surveys
Clay reports Gallatin’s dispatches: the British Government have assumed the new ground of refusing to negotiate upon the Colonial trade, and propose £250,000 sterling to compromise the slave-indemnity question, which Adams authorizes Gallatin to accept after reasonable effort for more. Northwestern boundary under the seventh article of Ghent (Porter and Barclay) also threatens difference. Barbour and Southard sound Monroe on a mission to the Congress of American nations now transferred from Panama to Mexico; Monroe declines on Mrs. Monroe’s health and private affairs. Creek and Georgia survey disputes continue; Indian Springs and Troup language remain live.
January–February 1827 cabinet meetings take the Creek arrest of Georgia surveyors and Troup’s troop of horse ordered to force the survey. The Act of 30 March 1802 (surveying forbidden; military conveyance of trespassers) is consulted. Clay urges force to protect Indian rights; Adams doubts expediency of sending troops against surveyors acting under State authority and prefers civil process and reference to Congress before a conflict of arms. Draft messages avoid the statement that a national–state military clash would dissolve the Union. Messages go to the Senate with Panama papers and land resolutions. Southard reports a scurrilous Jackson letter to him (criticisms at a Fredericksburg dinner) entrusted open to Houston and for the present withheld by Jackson’s friends.
1827–early 1828: electioneering, Jackson papers, McLean, New Year 1828
Through 1827 the diary records newspaper warfare, applications for Jackson court-martial orders on the six militiamen executed for mutiny (Force and Duff Green; Adams reluctant to furnish documents at printers’ request as a measure of hostility), and McLean’s ambiguous Post Office posture—devoted to Calhoun, no friendship to Clay, widely thought hostile to the Administration though he disclaims it. Electioneering language multiplies. January 1st, 1828 opens with a crowded New Year drawing-room; Krudener, Vaughan, Huygens and other ministers attend; Adams signs the release of Edward Thomson from prison and hears McDuffie (Ways and Means) on modifications of the tariff—woollens, hemp, iron, fine cottons, teas, wines. Georgia has nominated Crawford for Vice-President; the prior legislature had already nominated Jackson for the Presidency.
Spring 1828: tariff, canal subscription, cabinet on missions; close of volume
Thomas of Illinois reports the Tariff bill before the Senate: professed protection of domestic manufacturers compounded with taxation peculiarly oppressive upon New England; passage may depend on Massachusetts votes and Webster. Adams declines to interpose to fix Webster’s vote. House passage to third reading of a bill for a one-million-dollar subscription (five annual instalments) to Chesapeake and Ohio Canal stock by a majority of forty-four gratifies the District. Marks of Pennsylvania brings western newspaper tales that Adams’s wife is an Englishwoman; Adams states the facts of the London marriage to Joshua Johnson’s daughter. Barbour and Clay advise removal of McLean after Philadelphia postmaster intrigue; the Retrenchment Committee report is expected as an electioneering pamphlet.
Late May cabinet (Clay, Rush, Southard): whether to nominate ministers of plenipotentiary rank for Great Britain and Colombia now. Adams prefers postponement to the next session; the Cabinet prefer action—Barbour for England, Harrison for Colombia, Porter for War in Barbour’s place. Adams objects that Barbour’s departure would be read as abandonment of the Administration and that an all-northern cabinet (no Southern vote south of the Susquehanna save through Clay’s West) would be pernicious; he floats Gaston of North Carolina and John Williams of Tennessee for War. Concurrent opinion still prefers Porter and, for Colombia, Harrison over Robertson. Adams recalls 1823–24 communications that plenipotentiary rank in the South American States need not continue, and Colombia’s notice that it will keep only a chargé. Meeting adjourns. I sent message to Congress No. 12, with copies of the three Conventions with Great Britain, the ratifications of which were exchanged at London the 2d of last month. END OF VOL. VII.

Memoirs of John Quincy Adams, Volume VIII (1876)
Author: John Quincy Adams (1767–1848)
Editor: Charles Francis Adams (1807–1886)
Published: 1876 — J. B. Lippincott & Co., Philadelphia (Entered according to Act of Congress, 1875)
Working text: Page-OCR ZIP via Anna’s Archive (hash deb4478a8c74494e11298e3ed8eed5b5; OCLC 318369951)
Raw extract: wiki/raw/adams-memoirs-vol8.txt (page-sorted OCR, 568 leaves)
Extract stats: 23,536 lines · ~218,009 words
Overview
This is Volume VIII of Charles Francis Adams’s multi-volume Memoirs of John Quincy Adams, Comprising Portions of His Diary from 1795 to 1848, not the Library of America Diaries series and not an Adams Papers scholarly Diary volume. The title page of the extract reads Memoirs of John Quincy Adams… Edited by Charles Francis Adams. Vol. VIII. Philadelphia, J. B. Lippincott & Co., 1876 (copyright page 1875). Chapter numbering continues across the series: Volume VII closed Chapter XIV in late May 1828; this book resumes the same chapter without renumbering.
Volume VIII contains four body chapters:

Chapter XIV (Continued) — The Presidency (20 May 1828 through the close of the Administration; TOC p. 3)
Chapter XV — The Last Two Years of Leisure (4 March 1829; TOC p. 105)
Chapter XVI — The Twenty-Second Congress (4 March 1831; TOC p. 335)
Chapter XVII — The Twenty-Third Congress (4 March 1833; TOC p. 535)

Running page headers preserve month and year (e.g. [May, / 1828.] through 1833.]). OCR is Hathi-style page files (----- PAGE N -----); soft hyphenation and occasional garbled words appear. Front matter includes the full table of contents for the four chapters.
This CFA Memoirs volume covers the end of Adams’s presidency and his return to public life in the House of Representatives: the last months of cabinet business and the 1828 succession; Jackson and Calhoun declared elected 11 February 1829; the two years of leisure at Quincy with classical reading, private controversy, Anti-Masonic conversation, and the Plymouth district nomination; election to the Twenty-Second Congress (6 November 1830 returns: 1817 for Adams of 2565 votes); House committee work on manufactures; debate over the Bank of the United States; Jackson’s proclamation against South Carolina nullification; the Clay compromise tariff and the Revenue Collection (Force) bill; and the opening of the Twenty-Third Congress with Harvard’s planned LL.D. for Jackson, which Adams refuses to attend. Prefer diary date + chapter when building event pages; cite this book as CFA Memoirs Vol. VIII.
Full Chapter-by-Chapter Breakdown
Chapter XIV (Continued) — The Presidency
Running-header years sampled in OCR: 1828–1829 (body open May 1828; first 1829 ~L3808). Body: lines ~98–4464 (20 May 1828 through eve of 4 March 1829). TOC places this chapter at p. 3.
Opening — May–summer 1828: privateers, treaties, cabinet threads
May 20th, 1828.—Mr. Derrick, of the Department of State, brought a letter from N. Williams, the District Attorney of Maryland, concerning the privateer Tuncal of Baltimore and related Bolivar (New York) privateer business; Mr. Brent brought copies of the proclamation of the treaty with the Eel River or Thornton party of Miamis. Cabinet and visitor threads continue from Vol. VII: Porter and Colombia, Barbour for Great Britain, Clay answers, army brevet and Scott–Macomb command questions, blank signatures left with Brent for proclamations and commissions during absences. August travel to Baltimore records a Jackson-party popular meeting in the square by Barnum’s House while Adams dines and receives visitors; McMahon harangues three hours on the unpardonable sins of the Administration.
Autumn–winter 1828–29: Scott claims, tariff abroad, close of the term
December business includes Northeastern Boundary agents (Gallatin and Preble) and compensation; Barbour from London reports the American tariff as unpopular in England as in South Carolina and expects Huskisson retaliation. Adams finishes a long manuscript on General Scott’s claim of command over Macomb and Gaines—perilous matter, written under a sense of duty, too long for a third rewriting. Scott arrives in a quasi-arrest posture; Porter drafts answers to the Military Committee.
January 1st, 1829.—The year begins in gloom. My wife had a sleepless and painful night. The dawn was overcast, and, as I began to write, my shaded lamp went out, self-extinguished… I began the year with prayer, and then, turning to my Bible, read the first Psalm. The last New Year’s drawing-room is crowded beyond former example. Clay and Porter business continues: Captain Turner of the Erie cutting out the Buenos Ayrean privateer Federal from St. Bartholomew (to be disavowed but with complaint against harbor authorities); Webster’s reported adhesion to the new Administration; Scott memorial answers. Adams begins reply materials to the Boston confederates’ pamphlet and confides papers to Jonathan Elliot for republication.
February–March 1829: electoral count; succession
February 11th, 1829.—This day the votes for the election of President and Vice-President of the United States for four years from the 4th of March next were opened, and Andrew Jackson, of Tennessee, declared President, and John C. Calhoun Vice-President. The President elect came into the city. Adams receives Baron Krudener with the Emperor Nicholas’s letter on the death of the Empress-mother, and hears delicacy over the near close of the Administration. Nominations are expected to be postponed; claims and Indian-agency accounts are left for the successor. Chapter XIV closes as the Presidency ends.
Chapter XV — The Last Two Years of Leisure
Running-header years: 1829–1831 (open 4 March 1829 ~L4465; first strong 1830 clusters mid-chapter; House election November 1830 ~L10425–10534). Body: lines ~4465–14357. TOC p. 105.
March 1829 onward: retirement, visitors, Eaton and Jackson court
March 4th, 1829 opens the leisure chapter. Diary entries mix Quincy and occasional Washington visitors, classical reading (Cicero completed over ten months), horticulture, and political intelligence. January 1830 conversations record the Eaton–Campbell–Ely controversy over Mrs. Eaton: Ely’s letter to Jackson, Cabinet confrontation, challenges and correspondence; Adams treats reports as incomplete and not fully authentic. McLean’s presidential ambitions, Calhoun as possible Nullification candidate, and Anti-Masonic prospects appear in talks with J. W. Taylor and others; Adams discounts McLean’s assurance that Jackson will not seek re-election.
Anti-Masonry and private study
Anti-Masonic conversation multiplies: Stone of the Commercial Advertiser proposes Letters upon Masonry and Anti-Masonry addressed to Adams for the abolition of Freemasonry; Adams presses that the work not favor continuance of the order and discusses Morgan’s manuscript, Clinton, and Knapp. William Wirt and Anti-Masonic candidacy threads appear later in related electoral talk. Adams continues classical and religious reading while receiving intelligence on tariff and nullification doctrine under Jefferson’s name, Georgia, and party realignment.
November 1830: nomination and election to the House
Richardson and Lincoln inform Adams that a district meeting has selected John Quincy Adams to represent Plymouth in the Twenty-Second Congress; the other party nominates Turner of Scituate to divide the vote and hope for Anti-Masonic support. Adams acquiesces: And so I am launched again upon the faithless wave of politics. National Republican convention handbills and Hedge’s letter confirm the nomination. November 6th newspaper returns: Twenty-two towns gave 2565 votes, of which 1817 were for John Quincy Adams, 373 for Arad Thompson (Jacksonite), 279 for William Baylies (federal), and 96 scattering… I am a member elect of the Twenty-Second Congress. Reflection follows: no prior ex-President has sat in either House; refusal would have been arrogance and ridicule; the call is a misfortune that ends hope of quiet old age. Chapter XV closes toward the March 1831 opening of the new Congress.
Chapter XVI — The Twenty-Second Congress
Running-header years: 1831–1833 (open 4 March 1831 ~L14358; Bank and manufactures density 1832; nullification winter 1832–33). Body: lines ~14358–22938. TOC p. 335.
Opening and committee work
March 4th, 1831 opens the congressional chapter. Adams takes his seat and is repeatedly named Chairman of the Committee of Manufactures. Diary records petitions, resolutions, tariff paragraphs, and committee struggles over reports. Anti-Masonic and National Republican alignments in New York and elsewhere continue as side conversation (Granger, electoral tickets, McLean angling).
Bank of the United States
Through the session the Bank of the United States appears in message distribution, Ways and Means silence or debate, Biddle-related talk, and investigative motions: new attack on the Bank; charges and indictments against the Bank; motions for investigating committees; Speight and Polk moves on bank portions of the President’s message; reference sometimes denied powers to send for persons and papers. Adams tracks yeas and nays and Western members’ shifts when public-land bribes are alleged to buy off internal-improvement votes.
South Carolina nullification, proclamation, tariff and Force bill
December 1832.—Major Hamilton, through J. W. Taylor, gives Adams the President’s proclamation to and against the South Carolina nullifiers. McDuffie jocularly reports that they have nullified the Tariff Act of last summer; Adams answers that ordinance and proclamation must fight it out. Adams offers a resolution calling for copies of the proclamation and the South Carolina ordinance; the House refuses consideration 106–64 (Jackson party, Unionists of South Carolina, and some National Republicans against; most National Republicans and nullifiers for). The President’s message against nullification, with proclamation, ordinance, etc., is later presented; referred to the Judiciary Committee under Bell of Tennessee; 25,000 copies ordered printed.
February 1833.—Clay’s Compromise tariff bill moves in Senate and House; Letcher moves recommitment with instructions to report Clay’s bill totidem verbis; engrossment carries 105–71 and final passage 119–85 as it swept like a hurricane. The Revenue Collection bill, otherwise called the Force bill, or, as the nullifiers call it, the Bloody bill, is taken up amid disorderly struggle. Adams prepares a minority report for the Committee of Manufactures after the majority directs discharge; Hoffman threatens to block reception and printing. Chapter XVI closes with the compromise session’s endgame.
Chapter XVII — The Twenty-Third Congress
Running-header year: 1833 (open 4 March 1833 ~L22939). Body: lines ~22939–23509; END OF VOLUME VIII. L23510. TOC p. 535.
March 4th, 1833 opens a short closing chapter. Electoral arithmetic of the late presidential contest is noted (Anti-Masonic and other tickets; Wirt’s seven electoral votes appear in related count talk). District nomination by ballot for the Twenty-Third Congress is recorded. At Quincy, Adams confers with President Quincy of Harvard on natural-history appointments (Fisher fund; Waterhouse vs. Nuttall and Harris). Quincy reports that President Jackson will visit Boston and that the Corporation will invite him, address him in Latin, and confer the degree of Doctor of Laws, with an invitation for Adams to attend. Adams refuses: personal relations with Jackson preclude friendly intercourse; as an affectionate child of Alma Mater he will not witness her disgrace in conferring highest literary honors upon a barbarian who could not write a sentence of grammar and hardly could spell his own name. Quincy answers with precedent (Monroe) and fear of party-spirit imputation; Adams is unsatisfied—time-serving and sycophancy of learned institutions—and stays home. Nursery and horticultural entries follow (walls, cherry-stones, strawberries, elm-seeds); distant cannonading of the President’s military review in Boston gives relish to solitary tranquillity. No period of life has ever yielded me so much quiet contentment as that which I enjoy with my family… cultivating… my seedling plants and trees… “Alteri Seculo” is the motto of all my plantations; but I am yet sensible and conscious that this life of pleasure is not a life of profit. END OF VOLUME VIII.

Overview
This is Volume IX of Charles Francis Adams’s multi-volume Memoirs of John Quincy Adams, Comprising Portions of His Diary from 1795 to 1848, not the Library of America Diaries series and not an Adams Papers scholarly Diary volume. The title page of the extract reads Memoirs of John Quincy Adams… Edited by Charles Francis Adams. Vol. IX. Philadelphia, J. B. Lippincott & Co., 1876 (copyright page also 1876). Chapter numbering continues across the series: Volume VIII closed Chapter XVII in early summer 1833 at Quincy after Jackson’s Harvard LL.D.; this book resumes the same chapter without renumbering.
Volume IX contains three body chapters:

Chapter XVII (Continued) — The Twenty-Third Congress (from 24 June 1833; TOC p. 3)
Chapter XVIII — The Twenty-Fourth Congress (4 March 1835; TOC p. 214)
Chapter XIX — The Twenty-Fifth Congress (2 April 1837; TOC p. 344)

Running page headers preserve month and year (e.g. [June, / 1833.] through 1838.]). OCR is Hathi-style page files (----- PAGE N -----); soft hyphenation and occasional garbled words appear. Front matter includes the full table of contents for the three chapters.
This CFA Memoirs volume covers Adams’s House years under the later Jackson and early Van Buren administrations: the removal of the deposits and the Bank war; the Senate’s censure of Jackson and the presidential protest; French claims under the treaty of 4 July 1831; Northeastern and Ohio–Michigan boundary disputes; Anti-Masonic and district electoral politics; the flood of abolition petitions, the Pinckney select-committee report, and successive gag resolutions (including Patton’s), with Adams’s recorded protest that the gag violated the Constitution and the right of petition; Texas recognition and annexation agitation; the Lovejoy killing at Alton; the Cilley–Graves duel and House investigation; the Sub-Treasury / divorce of Bank and State; and Indian-hostility and Cherokee / New Echota debate. Prefer diary date + chapter when building event pages; cite this book as CFA Memoirs Vol. IX.
Full Chapter-by-Chapter Breakdown
Chapter XVII (Continued) — The Twenty-Third Congress
Running-header years sampled in OCR: 1833–1835 (body open 24 June 1833; first dense 1834 ~L1101 area; close early March 1835). Body: lines ~79–9172. TOC places this chapter at p. 3.
Opening — June–July 1833: Ghent anniversary; Jackson in New England
June 24th, 1833.—This day is one of those anniversaries which bring to my mind placid recollections. It is that of my arrival at Ghent… The transactions at Ghent were the most fortunate occurrences of my life. Diary continues with President Jackson’s New England tour: receptions, sickness under Dr. Warren at the Tremont House, postponed Bunker Hill and Harvard ceremonies, then the Cambridge LL.D. (Quincy address in English; senior oration in Latin), Everett’s address on Bunker’s Hill, and the ride to Salem. Dr. Waterhouse dines and reports captivation by Jackson’s manners yet extreme debility; Adams answers that four-fifths of the sickness is trickery and that a Doctorate for which an apology was necessary was a cheap honor and a sycophantic compliment. Jackson cuts short the tour and returns toward Washington via Concord and Roxbury.
Autumn 1833: removal of the deposits; Taney for Duane
Late September–October entries record President Jackson’s order to withdraw the deposits of public moneys from the Bank of the United States and place them in sundry State banks, a paper read to the Cabinet on the 18th of the month, the dismission of William J. Duane, and the appointment of Roger B. Taney as Secretary of the Treasury—upon all which Adams takes time for reflection. November conversations with Huntington (Connecticut) anticipate Stevenson’s re-election as Speaker and a bank committee that will report approving the removal; Biddle assures that the bank is prepared for the crisis. Adams tells E. Wyer he is at present neither for nor against the bank and will wait for the evidence submitted to Congress on removing the deposits. Richard Rush’s intrusion into the deposit controversy is treated as painful and ruinous to Anti-Masonry in Pennsylvania.
1834: Bank war on the floor; Senate censure and Jackson protest
Through the session the diary tracks deposit banks, committee investigations, Speakers and Ways and Means under Polk, and House–Senate conference fights over appropriations. April 1834.—The President of the United States this day sent to the Senate a protest against their resolution of censure upon him for his recent interferences with the public revenues, and he calls upon them to enter his protest upon their journals. Great excitement. Poindexter moved that it should not be received. Clay, Webster, and Preston are absent. In the House, Wise and Baylie Peyton offer competing resolutions on custody of the public moneys and on whether the Senate’s censure infringed the prerogatives of the House.
Boundary, Texas, France; close of the session March 1835
Resolutions and messages touch the Northeastern boundary negotiation with Britain, the province of Texas and the Mexican boundary under the treaty of 22 February 1819, and the French Chamber’s refusal to appropriate for the twenty-five millions of francs of the treaty of 4 July 1831. At the midnight close of the short session, Adams’s resolution on the dispute with France is carried unanimously—two hundred votes, followed by clapping of hands in the gallery (CFA editorial note: the first of the great triumphs of Mr. Adams in the House). The Fortification bill fails after the Senate disagrees to a three-million discretionary amendment and the conference report comes after midnight without a quorum; at twenty minutes past three A.M. the House adjourns without day after Bell’s thanks address.
Chapter XVIII — The Twenty-Fourth Congress
Running-header years: 1835–1837 (open 4 March 1835 ~L9173; slavery-petition density 1835–36; Texas and Pinckney May 1836; district returns November 1836; blank after early January 1837). Body: lines ~9173–14767. TOC p. 214.
Opening — March 1835: Speaker Bell; Ohio–Michigan; French news
March 4th, 1835.—Rose much exhausted… Adams retains no unkind feeling toward late Speaker John Bell after the vote of thanks, yet suspects Bell’s motive in making him chairman on the northern boundary of Ohio, Indiana, and Illinois—a service impossible honestly to perform without alienating three States. Conversation with Secretary of War Cass on the Ohio–Michigan disputed territory: Cass says the President shares Adams’s view and would dispossess Ohio by force if she took the lands; Michigan might compromise, Ohio not. Rumor circulates that the French Chamber of Deputies has rejected the appropriation for the 1831 treaty. Anti-Masonic and Whig nomination talk for Edward Everett as Governor appears in evening visits.
Petitions, slavery, Pinckney report
Jarvis of Maine, at Owens of Georgia’s request, offers a resolution that the House will not entertain any petitions for the abolition of slavery in the District of Columbia; Adams moves to lay on the table and is rejected 123–66; Wise substitutes declarations that Congress has no power to abolish slavery in the District. May 1836.—H. L. Pinckney presented the report of the select committee to whom all the abolition petitions were referred, and said that the report had the unanimous assent of the committee… It was immediately attacked with extreme violence… Waddy Thompson said that he would commit it to the flames or to the hangman. Hardin, a committee member, dissents. Related floor fights include Texas acknowledgment motions (Thompson would amend to ask the President’s opinion on recognizing Texan independence) and printing / recommitment of the Pinckney report with instructions that Congress has no constitutional authority to abolish slavery in the District.
District politics 1836; Michigan boundary; blank before Chapter XIX
November returns from the Twelfth Massachusetts district show a perilous passage: nomination by Anti-Masonic meeting; Whigs and Democrats make no opposing nomination but do not fully consolidate; Abington, Rochester, and Weymouth fragments appear in the newspapers while most Whig papers omit the district. Adams reflects that the strait will not be repeated. Extended entries denounce the congressional settlement of the Ohio–Michigan boundary as usurpation of judicial power and robbery of Michigan property, forced through by electoral arithmetic of the three Northwestern States—against which Adams alone spoke three hours and found no support. CFA records a blank in the diary extending beyond the remainder of the Twenty-Fourth Congress, regretting silence on the memorable attempt to censure Mr. Adams on the 23d of January [1837] after presentation of twenty-one petitions, some purporting to come from slaves—the first of his great struggles in that cause—and points readers to Letters from John Quincy Adams to his Constituents… (Boston: Isaac Knapp, 1837), with introductory remarks initialed by John G. Whittier.
Chapter XIX — The Twenty-Fifth Congress
Running-header years: 1837–1838 (open 2 April 1837 ~L14768; special session Sub-Treasury and petition fights; regular session gag, Texas, duel, Indian bill). Body: lines ~14768–23712; END OF VOLUME IX. L23713. TOC p. 344.
Opening — April 1837: slavery reading; Whitney libel; Taney on the bench
April 2d, 1837.—I wrote to Mr. Biddle, and read the printed letter of Gerrit Smith to the Rev. James Smylie… Smylie defends slavery as an institution sanctioned by the Scriptures… This subject of slavery, to my great sorrow and mortification, is absorbing all my faculties. Baltimore journey for the Whitney libel case against Leakin and Barnes; Circuit Court held by Roger B. Taney, now Chief Justice of the United States, and Upton Heath. Testimony is delayed; Adams returns to Washington.
Special session: Sub-Treasury, specie suspension, right of petition
Bell breaks out against the Sub-Treasury project of the message; Cambreleng supports it and challenges the opposition to propose their Bank of the United States. Adams offers resolutions calling for Mexican boundary and Texas-annexation correspondence and for Northeastern-boundary papers since Jackson’s 15 June 1836 message. He moves that the Clerk print State acts relating to the suspension of specie payments by banks. When Cushman moves to suspend the call of the States for petitions, Adams assails the resolution as an abridgment of the right of petition; Cushman withdraws after his own party calls for withdrawal. Anti-Masonic convention visitors (Denny, Middleswarth) appear at Brown’s Hotel.
Gag, Texas annexation, Lovejoy, Cilley–Graves
Patton offers a resolution that no petitions relating to slavery or the slave trade in any State, district, or Territory shall be read, printed, committed, or in any manner acted upon. Suspension of the rules carries 136–65; previous question and resolution carry. When my name was called, I answered, “I hold the resolution to be a violation of the Constitution, of the right of petition of my constituents, and of the people of the United States, and of my right to freedom of speech as a member of this House.” —amidst a perfect war-whoop of order. Adams moves that the answer be entered on the journal; after further struggle it is entered though amendment of the journal is laid on the table. Texas annexation memorials and remonstrances crowd the calendar; Adams argues for a select committee rather than Foreign Affairs alone.
November 1837 diary records the Alton, Illinois, mob that shot Lovejoy dead defending a fourth printing-press, broke the press, and threw it into the river: Such men are often fated to be martyrs; and he has fallen a martyr to the cause of human freedom. CFA editorial note inserts the Graves–Cilley duel (William J. Graves of Kentucky and Jonathan Cilley of Maine, the latter killed), which added to party and sectional excitement; Fairfield moves a committee of seven to investigate. Adams presents large batches of petitions under the gag, and occasional non-slavery petitions (women for Mexican arbitration; congress of nations) that escape to Foreign Relations.
Indian Hostility bill; Georgia and New Echota; close of the volume
Late May 1838 committee of the whole on the Indian Hostility bill: Holsey of Georgia delivers invective against Adams’s Administration and glorifies Georgia’s defiance of the Supreme Court decision on Indian lands, which Jackson prevented being executed—arguing that without Executive concurrence there is no law, and Georgia would laugh the Court to scorn. Naylor denounces the treaty so called of New Echota of December 1835 as nefarious villainy already exposed when the Senate advised and consented. Dawson of the Georgia “Indian party” justifies by Adams’s Plymouth oration and older States’ practice. Bell of Tennessee reviews Jackson-administration measures and his own defense against Jacksonite slander, then offers an amendment to apply two millions to coaxing Cherokees rather than driving them by bayonet. Horace Everett, Crary, and Turney follow amid a thin, drowsy House. Between nine and ten Adams reaches home. END OF VOLUME IX.
Key Data Points
