High-value passages

Preface — English indifference reversed; blockade and Northern news monopoly; Gettysburg already in Blackwood’s; independence prediction.
2 Apr — Rio Grande bar, seventy merchantmen, cotton 6¢ Galveston / 36¢ at the mouth; Mongomery lynched within three hours of landing.
1 May — Houston mess with Scurry; Queen’s health; shot-guns vs sabres; “aristocratic negro” John; Sam Houston in the cars (deposed anti-secession governor).
14–17 May — skiff through Log Bayou / Lake Concordia to Vidalia–Natchez; Nelson the hiring slave; Jackson evacuated; Grierson’s raid described by a farmer.
21–23 May — Johnston’s mess: straggling as the Confederate general’s chief evil; Grant’s vigour; Vicksburg ~20,000 vs Grant ~75,000; Stonewall as courage not grand strategy; Johnston carrying Fremantle’s cloaks into wrecked Jackson.
30 May–1 Jun — Polk on Murfreesborough and Shiloh; St Leger Grenfell; Cleburne from the British 41st; Bishop Elliott preaching to ~3,000; Liddell’s Arkansas brigade homespun.
9 Jun — Fort Sumter: 68 guns, Keokuk 11-inch fished up, ironclad fight 2h25m, bar nine miles out, thirteen blockaders.
17–18 Jun — Jefferson Davis interview (silent despair; Russell/neutrality; military education of Confederate generals); Seddon letters to Lee and Longstreet.
30 Jun–3 Jul — Lee’s person and manners; 1 Jul “brisk little scurry”; 2 Jul silence till 4.45 p.m.; 3 Jul Longstreet on the snake fence (“we’ve attacked and been repulsed”); Lee “this has been a sad day… it is I that have lost this fight.”
13–15 Jul — New York luxury vs Richmond; Broadway bounties; draft riot, fires, “Down with the b——y nigger”; Irish waiters drafted; Postscript on wounded recycling and “How can you subjugate such a people as this?” (Polk).

Full breakdown
Preface
At the outbreak of the American war Fremantle, like many countrymen, felt indifferent, with a slight English bias toward the North from dislike of slavery. Admiration for Southern gallantry, and the “unhappy contrast” of Northern “foolish bullying,” produced a “complete revulsion.” Returning to England he found friends hungry for Southern truth: the blockade made intelligence come mainly through Northern sources, and “nowhere is the ignorance of what is passing in the South more profound than it is in the Northern States.” He therefore publishes the diary kept day by day. The Gettysburg portion had already appeared in Blackwood’s Magazine. He has not concealed Southern peculiarities or defects in the wilder country, but thinks no generous man can fail to admire the courage, energy, and patriotism of the whole population and the skill of its leaders “in this struggle against great odds,” and that such unanimity and heroism destine the people “sooner or later, to become a great and independent nation.”
Approach (2 March–1 April 1863)
Leaves England in the royal mail steamer Atrato; St Thomas 17 March; Havana 22 March, where H.M.S. Immortalité (Captain Hancock) takes him and the Irish-Texan merchant M’Carthy toward Matamoros. 1 April: anchored three miles from the mouth of the Rio Grande / Rio Bravo del Norte among about seventy merchant vessels.
Texas border and Matamoros (2–12 April)
2 April. Cutter over the bar (3½ feet, sharks, Orlando recently lost a man) to Bagdad on the Mexican bank: wooden shanties, endless cotton bales, two shallow steamers feeding the outer fleet. Ituria’s buggy toward Brownsville; passless Fremantle taken before Duff’s cavalry officers in flannel shirts, jack-boots, and lone-star hats. Cotton schooner from Galveston: 6 cents a pound there, 36 at the mouth. Meets General Bee (brother of the Bee killed at Manassas) with beef and beer; Bee disavows the “Mongomery” killing. A few miles on, Mongomery’s corpse—slightly buried, rope still on a mesquite: Fremantle’s “first experience of Lynch law within three hours of landing.” Duff’s newly raised regiment: young men, some owning vast tracts and above a hundred slaves; Duff says the affair was wrong but the boys “meant well.” Brownsville ~3,000; ~4,000 troops under Bee.
3–7 April. Crosses to Matamoros (Good Friday; no carriages). Acting British consul Mr Zorn (“Don Pablo”) and partner Behnsen put him up; merchants, Peterhoff owner Bennet elated at capture as a case for the British government. Matamoros ~9,000, consulate riddled in 1861–2 fighting; drought eleven months; diligence robberies with blinds down. Hancock and officers visit; society, gambling, fandango.
8–12 April. Preparations to start inland with M’Carthy; Unionist interlocutor; affectionate leave of the consulate circle.
Interior Texas to Houston (13–30 April)
13–21 April. Breakfast with General Bee; letters for Magruder. Stages and Mexican saddles across mesquite desert: tics, water, horse trouble, lost animals 18 April. Hamlets and ranches; armed travellers.
24–29 April. Push to San Antonio (prettily situated on both banks of the San Antonio River). M’Carthy’s buggy; Colonel Bankhead letters. Cross Guadalupe; exhausted sleep. Alleyton, railroad terminus sprung up in three years, crammed with travellers and cotton speculators; San Antonio–Alleyton 140 miles in forty-six hours.
30 April. First Texan railroad: one class, “all aboard,” jumping on and off, no fences. Richmond on the Brazos—inclined-plane trestle shot; Judge Stockdale vs General Chambers (married soldiers to embrace families once a year). Terry plantation, cotton and corn mixed, more than 200 negroes. Houston at 4.30 p.m., Fannin House; Galveston refugees; theatre; five beds to a room, negro cleaning boots, captain’s lecture on the “genuine African.”
Houston, Galveston, Sam Houston (1–7 May)
1 May. General Scurry (ophthalmia) takes him in; Magruder’s letter. Dinner: Terrill, Pyron, Wharton, Watkins (Sabine Pass), Cook (artillery, ex-U.S. navy, Methodist preacher). Queen’s health; scattered white population as “a sort of aristocracy”; cavalry prefer shot-guns and revolvers to sabres.
2 May. Scurry sends servant John, “an aristocratic negro,” “nearly as white as myself.” In the cars: General Samuel Houston—Virginia-born, U.S. senator at thirty, Tennessee governor at thirty-six, San Jacinto 1836, President of Texas, annexation 1845, deposed as anti-secession governor in 1860; “extremely egotistical and vain.”
4–7 May. Galveston steamer delayed; Huntsville breakfast; Federal prisoners; Crockett; smaller coach at 1.30 a.m. East-Texas stages.
Trans-Mississippi to the river (8–17 May)
8–13 May. Marshall 3 a.m.; stage for Monroe; rough night; General Hebert (Creole, West Pointer) at Monroe. Three negroes from a plantation; row on board; officers and soldiers ~30.
14 May. Mississippi left bank overflowed; Federal gunboats past Vicksburg and Port Hudson; passage only by yawl and skiffs through swamps. Trinity 6 a.m.; Log Bayou; Lake Concordia; alligators and snakes; land at Mr Davis’s; Vidalia opposite Natchez; first bed and boots-off in ten days. Conscripts (Irishman and Pole) dislike the military profession but acknowledge mass enthusiasm.
15–17 May. Cross to Natchez (~6,000, high bluff). Haller Nutt’s pagoda-like house. Hire carriage 100 to Brookhaven (66 miles) with Texas contractor, wounded Missourian Douglas, soldier's wife; driver Nelson, slave paying 4½ a week to work on his own account, “didn’t want to see no Yanks, nor to be no freer than he is.” Farmwomen in “miserable uncertainty,” slaves “generally remain true.” News: Jackson to be evacuated; Johnston assumed command. 16 May: coffee of sweet potatoes; “This is the most unjust war ever waged upon a people by mortal man”; negroes run to swamps; Jackson in enemy hands; farmer’s account of Grierson (~1,500, horses, railroad, paroles, “no barbarities,” Northwestern men). 17 May: Brookhaven full of soldiers; Maxey’s brigade gone to Johnston; Fremantle “always intercepted” (Alexandria, Harrisonburg, now Jackson).
Johnston, Jackson, Vicksburg (18–24 May)
18–20 May. Civilized aspect after the swamp; Bowmont House breakfast; 3 a.m. bombardment (later learned: unsuccessful assault). Jackson wrecked; Johnston concentrating.
21 May. Johnston’s mess (Eustis, Washington). Henderson’s ~50 scouts to Grant’s camps and Pemberton. Yankee surgeon left with wounded at Jackson; Johnston refuses flag-of-truce return, sends him North via Richmond; doctors treated as non-combatants by agreement. Planter Harrold’s slave quarters: clean huts, clothes/shoes short, incurable woman kept thirteen years; Fremantle notes planters shirk the word “slave.” Johnston too weak to attack Grant; will not guess when strong enough. Johnston on titles in a republic; camp-fire hyperbole that nine (Johnston: ninety-nine) in a hundred would rather be Queen Victoria’s subjects than return to the Union—then French/Japanese emperors and even infernal regions as alternatives to “Uncle Abe.”
22 May. Heavy Vicksburg bombardment. Johnston: Confederate combinations wrecked by straggling; qualities (bravery, firearms, patriotism, confidence in Lee/Johnston/Beauregard/Longstreet) vs political officers who will not punish, knapsacks thrown away, early-war going home after a victory. Grant more vigour than expected: crossed below Vicksburg, seized Jackson, invested the fortress; army ~75,000; Vicksburg land defences little valued; garrison ~20,000. Walker to Yazoo City. Canton planter with 700 slaves. Scout: prisoner “surrendered so quick, I couldn’t kill him.” Johnston wounded ten times; senior old-army officer to join; Seven Pines.
23–24 May. Locomotive toward Jackson; Johnston on Stonewall: not a great strategist, unfit perhaps for independent large command, but courage, determination, Providence; indebted to Ewell; flower of Virginians vs Fremont and Banks. Engine wooded from the roadside; Johnston’s Seven Pines wound. Walk last four miles, Johnston carrying cloaks. Loring (one arm) ~6,000 from Crystal Springs; Evans ~3,000 from Charleston; Maxey arriving; Fremantle estimates ~25,000 between Jackson and the Yazoo. Farewell; ambulance; worst railroad; engine off the track. Meridian 7.30 a.m. five hours late; Mobile 7.15 p.m.; engineer had shot a passenger, unhitched, cut the telegraph.
Mobile to Bragg’s army (25 May–5 June)
25–27 May. Mobile disappointing; Montgomery, capital of Alabama.
28–29 May. Chattanooga 4.30 a.m. Walk with Dr Quintard; Polk’s headquarters.
30 May. Prayers; Polk on Murfreesborough (Confederate 30,000 including Breckinridge not engaged first day; losses 10,000 vs 19,000) and Shiloh (Beauregard’s retire order unfortunate; Albert Sidney Johnston’s death). Colonel St Leger Grenfell, Inspector-General of Cavalry: French lancers, Abd-el-Kader, Riff pirates, Turkish contingent, Indian Mutiny, South America, blockade-runner, Morgan’s adjutant; red forage-cap in action; Morgan “enervated by matrimony.” Young Polk on Jackson at Lexington VMI: “be slow to draw the sword in civil strife, but when you draw it, throw away the scabbard.”
31 May. Bishop of Georgia preaches and confirms. Bragg on Murfreesborough: held three and a half days, 6,000 prisoners; Rosecrans “the only man in the Yankee army who was not badly beaten.” Grenfell on Bragg, Polk, Hardee, Cleburne vs “political” generals. Baggage-car to Wartrace with Bragg and the Bishop. Major-General Cleburne: Ballincollig doctor’s son, ran away at 17, three years private/corporal in the British 41st, Arkansas lawyer, only foreigner (with Polignac) at general’s rank; white facings like the 41st. Open-air preaching ~3,000 at Wood’s camp; Bishop Elliott on colonial Church of England and Revolution. Press not gagged: attacks on Davis and generals; Chattanooga Rebel leaked Breckinridge’s departure to Johnston.
1–5 June. Review of Liddell’s Arkansas brigade at Bellbuckle: weak regiments, homespun, officers’ collar bars and branch facings. Touchiness whether Mr Mason was kindly received in England. Outposts with Richmond; leave Shelbyville 6 a.m. 5 June.
Atlanta, Augusta, Charleston (6–15 June)
6–7 June. Atlanta 3 a.m.; Augusta (~20,000).
8 June. Charleston 5 a.m. Beauregard absent in Florida. General Ripley (Northern-born “red-hot” rebel, Enfield connection, artillery reputation) commands forts. Merchant Robertson: Combahee raid by Northern armed negroes, Blake/Heyward losses, city shops shut, fire wilderness a mile by half a mile, blockade-running speculation, slave-auction ads, hotels crowded, $8 a day.
9 June. Captain Feilden (late 42d Highlanders) on Beauregard’s staff. Boat to Fort Sumter: pentagon, two casemate tiers plus barbette, 68 guns (10-inch columbiads 128-lb shot, Brooke/Blakely, Parrott, Dahlgren, 11-inch from Keokuk). Garrison 350 regulars under Colonel Rhett, many foreigners. Ironclad attack eight weeks earlier: 2h25m, one man killed (flagstaff), Keokuk disabled in a quarter hour and sank next morning, none closer than 900 yards. Harbour: Pinckney, Ripley, Moultrie/Bee/Beauregard on Sullivan’s, Johnson, Cummins Point, Wagner on Morris; bar nine miles, thirteen blockaders; Folly Island Yankees. Blockade-runners painted water-colour; Kate double-screw; Feilden shows new ironclads vs Chicora and Palmetto State. Ripley “blockade dinner.”
10–15 June. Exchange office; Colonel Rice; St Michael’s; goodbye to Beauregard; Wilmington 16 June.
Richmond (16–19 June)
17 June. Petersburg 3 a.m. Jefferson Davis via Benjamin: silent despair vs noisy grief; Grenfell’s quarrel with civil power; Confederate generals must keep popularity; black-flag talk vs men who have thrown down arms; Lord Russell and neutrality (Davis: open ports to prizes of both); Davis’s wish to have joined the army; West Point / Secretary of War as the start in generals. Winchester recaptured by Ewell; hope Milroy not taken alive. Favourable impression of Davis’s manners.
18 June. Seddon, Secretary of War: letters for Lee and Longstreet. Aides Wood, Lee, Johnston (sons of R. E. Lee and A. S. Johnston). Capitol librarian Thompson; captured silk Union colours vs Confederate bunting; 37th New York colours twice, second inscribed “Fairoaks.” Mrs S—— converted by Lincoln’s 75,000-man call. Butler King: ruin borne equably; South looks to English merchants and ships after the war.
19 June. Drewry’s Bluff: Monitor and Galena repulse; Yorktown/Patrick Henry; ironclad Richmond; 7-inch Brooke. Beauregard’s view: ironclads cannot stand plunging fire even of smooth-bores. Deserter to be shot at Chaffin’s Bluff. Johnston’s “inactivity” in Mississippi; Vicksburg given up in conversation; papers as violent as New York’s; press liberty “carried to its fullest extent.”
To Lee and Chambersburg (20–30 June)
20–27 June. Train to Culpeper; captured Chancellorsville rifles rotting; Stoneman’s raid. Sergeant Norris (Maryland gentleman now a private) rides him toward Lawley in the rain, sore-backed horses. Army already advanced after Winchester. Lawley ill; Greenwood/Chambersburg approaches. Hood introduced (33, Texan/Alabama idol). Moses requisitions three days’ rations; corporation hides keys; Lee forbids searching private houses; Union women abuse Moses.
28–29 June. No one under general into Chambersburg without Lee’s pass. Pennsylvanian women assail Fremantle until gold appears; “Yankee” a reproach there too. Lee’s non-retaliation order; troops’ forbearance vs Southern towns Fremantle has seen ravaged; “Pennsylvanian Dutch” unpatriotic, abuse Lincoln. Longstreet on Texas and polite sentries. Pendleton (artillery chief, Episcopal clergyman, surplice over uniform); Pickett (ringlets, San Juan Island).
30 June. Longstreet introduces Lee: 56, “almost without exception the handsomest man of his age I ever saw,” courteous, three stars, no arms, grey jacket, never sleeps in a house; relations with Longstreet “quite touching”; Jackson the third simple servant of the country until death. Texans destroy Chambersburg whisky under orders. News: Hooker replaced by Meade. Battle expected on this road, not Harrisburg; Ewell ordered to reunite; Stuart’s cavalry valued for raids not for charging infantry.
Gettysburg (1–4 July)
1 July. Hill’s corps passes; Stonewall Brigade (mostly Virginians) run ahead to look at Longstreet; Florida brigade: “here’s the old bulldog again.” Wounded and prisoners; Pennsylvanian colour captured. 4.30 p.m. with Lee and Hill: enemy driven to cemetery ridge; Hill unwell, two divisions in, Yankees fought with unusual determination, colour-bearer retiring last. Ewell 3.30 on the enemy’s right; Reynolds reported killed. Town occupied; ~6,000 prisoners, 10 guns; 1st and 11th Corps. Longstreet: position “very formidable,” will be entrenched. Footnote: fight came off prematurely; neither Lee nor Longstreet intended it that day.
2 July. 3.30 a.m.; Lee, Hill, Longstreet, Hood, Heth (head wound) consulting and whittling. Semicircle five to six miles; Ewell left (cupola), Hill centre, Longstreet right; only McLaws and Hood (Pickett still rear). Dead silence till 4.45 p.m.
3 July. Cannonade then Pickett (under 5,000, two brigades absent) with Heth and Pettigrew to cross a mile of open ground. Fremantle and the Austrian fail to reach Ewell’s cupola under crossfire. 2.30: stream of wounded “as great as the crowd in Oxford Street.” Longstreet on a snake fence, calm: “we’ve attacked and been repulsed: look there!” Pickett had carried the position ~20 minutes then retired when left gave way. Lee “perfectly sublime,” rallying alone: “This has been a sad day for us, Colonel”; to Willcox, “all this has been my fault—it is I that have lost this fight.” Garnett and Armistead killed, Kemper mortally; Pickett nearly all field officers hit; slaughter ~one mile square, one hour. Gunners still confident in “Uncle Robert.” Johnson said successful on the left; Hood’s Texans and cavalry. First food in fifteen hours at 10 p.m.
4 July. Moses’s trunk stolen by stragglers. Flag of truce: Federals think Longstreet wounded and a prisoner—he sends thanks. Pendleton: 12-pounder Napoleon preferred; almost all artillery captured or recast from old 6-pounders. Army to move toward Virginia that evening for want of ammunition; hoped the enemy might attack on the Fourth.
Retreat, Hagerstown, North, New York (5–15 July)
Crosses toward the Potomac; Hagerstown. 9 July: to Hancock; detained; explains himself to General Kelly as a British officer who entered via Mexico to break no blockade, Longstreet’s guest, no letters; Kelly lets him go, keeps the driver, who then talks. Farmer supper, violent Unionists. 10–12 July: Cumberland, Johnstown militia garlands, Philadelphia Confederate prisoners (one suggestion they be drowned), New York Fifth Avenue Hotel 10 p.m. 13 July: Broadway prosperity, 550 bounties, greyback posters; shops closing; fire, mob, negro chased, "Down with the b——y nigger"; citizen cavalry who cannot sit horses. **14 July:** Irish waiters drafted; Northern talk of Rebel demoralisation vs Lee's army four days earlier "as full of fight as ever"; Gettysburg + Vicksburg + Port Hudson have "turned everybody's head"; riot: telegraphs cut, tracks torn, draft suspended, 300 commutation hated. 15 July: military in the hotel; boarding the China.
Postscript
On the China, upper-class Northerners still ignorant of Southern feeling; illusions of Charleston/Mobile/Savannah/Wilmington about to fall, Lee and Bragg wrecked, Mississippi open. Fremantle on Confederate recruiting: no discharge however wounded; maimed to public labour; boys reserved until fit; negroes “a last resort” not soon contemplated. Arms: Augusta powder, Atlanta caps, Tredegar cannon, Federal generals as “indefatigable purveyors of artillery.” Northern gentlemen determined to crush the rebellion but not to fight themselves. Quotes Polk: “How can you subjugate such a people as this?” Cannot believe the nineteenth century will witness destruction of “such a gallant race.”
Notes on use

Lens: British professional officer, increasingly Confederate-sympathetic; slavery described as he met it (planter language, hiring-out, Combahee raid, New York riot hatred of negroes) without later moral frame. Independence forecast is the book’s own closing politics.
Gettysburg: eyewitness from Longstreet’s staff axis, not a complete tactical survey; 2 July fighting is mostly the morning wait; 3 July is the aftermath of Pickett as seen from Longstreet then Lee.
Names: Jefferson Davis, Lee, Longstreet, Johnston, Bragg, Polk, Beauregard, Ripley, Seddon, Benjamin, Hood, Pickett, Cleburne, Grenfell, Sam Houston, Magruder, Bee, Scurry.

sources/gates-dupont-family.title: [source] The du Pont Family (Gates, 1979)
sources/gates-dupont-family.content:
The du Pont Family
Author: John D. Gates
Published: 1979, Doubleday & Company, Garden City, N.Y. (First Edition)
Working text: PDF via pdftotext (Anna’s Archive hash 9130d08d4a9ea53ad5eca33e6890f6a5)
Raw extract: wiki/raw/gates-dupont-family.txt (pdftotext)
Extract stats: 15,031 lines · ~758 KB text
Period-Overlap Note
This source has been copied into the United States 1800–65 wiki because the du Pont family arrived in America on January 1, 1800, and their entire nineteenth-century development — the foundation of the Brandywine powder mills (1802), the War of 1812 and Mexican-American War government contracts, the early decades of explosives manufacturing, the Civil War gunpowder procurement, and the company’s rise as the dominant American explosives house by 1865 — falls within this wiki’s period. Its strongest overlap with this folder is Chapters 2–4: Pierre Samuel du Pont de Nemours’s French origins and migration, E. I. du Pont’s gunpowder venture, the early powder-mill economy, the War of 1812 contracts, antebellum expansion, and the explosives-supply infrastructure that supported the Union war effort. For the post-1865 trajectory of the Du Pont Company, General Motors, and the family holding company, see the copy at the United States 1866–1919 wiki.
Overview
John D. Gates’s The du Pont Family is an insider’s portrait of one of America’s richest and most private industrial dynasties. Gates, a du Pont in-law for many years and a Wilmington newspaper reporter, writes from a position of unusual access: several dozen du Ponts cooperated with the project, granting interviews and opening family perspectives that earlier books had not obtained. The book is explicitly anecdotal and personal rather than strictly scholarly — Gates compares his approach to Marquis James’s biography of Alfred I. du Pont — but it covers the full sweep of the family’s American history from their landing on January 1, 1800, through the 1970s.
The first half of the book is broadly chronological: Pierre Samuel du Pont de Nemours’s French origins, the family’s migration to America, the founding of the gunpowder mills on Brandywine Creek, expansion into dynamite and explosives, and the transformation of the company under Pierre S. du Pont into the world’s largest chemical corporation, with holdings in General Motors, U.S. Rubber, and other industrial giants. The second half is organized by family branch — Pierre’s relatives, T. C. du Pont, Alfred I. du Pont (the “rebel”), the heirs of “the Boss,” and various other branches — before concluding with chapters on the company itself and “a way of life.”
A central narrative thread is the decline of family control. The book opens with Irenee du Pont Jr.’s 1972 letter proposing the absorption of Christiana Securities (the family holding company, which held 28.3% of Du Pont common stock) into the Du Pont Company itself — effectively ending the family’s formal control of the enterprise. The antitrust case that forced divestiture of General Motors holdings (63 million shares) and the tax and marketability pressures on Christiana are treated as the terminal phase of a dynastic arc that began with E. I. du Pont’s powder mills in 1802.
For this United States 1800–65 wiki, the source is valuable for early American industrial chemistry, the gunpowder and explosives industry before the Civil War, the economic and political conditions that enabled a single-family powder monopoly, early federal contracting (War of 1812, Mexican-American War), and the du Pont family’s integration into the early national elite — Thomas Jefferson was their friend and correspondent.
Narrative Source Flow
Preface
Lines 157–266. Gates explains his personal connection to the du Ponts (debutante party in 1957, marriage to a du Pont descendant, nine years as a Wilmington newspaper reporter). He contrasts his sympathetic perspective with the skeptical or hostile attitudes of fellow reporters. Describes the family’s studied avoidance of publicity and the cooperation of several dozen du Ponts in the project. Notes earlier books: Gerald Colby Zilg’s Behind the Nylon Curtain, Ralph Nader’s The Company State, Alfred Chandler and Stephen Salsbury’s Pierre S. du Pont and the Making of the Modern Corporation, and Marquis James’s Alfred I. du Pont, the Family Rebel.
Chapter 1 — Now and Then: An Overview (lines 369–1500+)
Opens with Irenee du Pont Jr.’s retirement in 1978 and the 1972 letter proposing Christiana Securities’ absorption into Du Pont. Christiana held 28.3% of Du Pont common stock and was the vehicle of family control; Du Pont once owned 38% of General Motors, and the 1949 antitrust suit (Attorney General Tom Clark: “the largest single concentration of industrial power in the United States”) forced GM divestiture. The chapter frames the book’s central theme: family control as a waning reality, Christiana as an albatross rather than a pendant of power, and the transformation of the du Ponts from a commanding dynasty to a dispersed, divided family.
Chapter 2 — The Move to America (lines ~1500–)
Pierre Samuel du Pont de Nemours (1739–1817), French physiocrat and politician, his friendship with Thomas Jefferson, the family’s escape from Revolutionary France, their arrival in Rhode Island on January 1, 1800, with one of the largest libraries ever brought to America by an immigrant family. Eleuthère Irénée du Pont’s (E. I. du Pont) decision to enter gunpowder manufacturing, the purchase of land on Brandywine Creek near Wilmington, Delaware, and the founding of the powder mills in 1802.
Chapter 3 — Building the Business (~lines –)
The early decades of the powder works, competition with established powder makers, the War of 1812 and government contracts, expansion through the nineteenth century, the introduction of dynamite and smokeless powder, and the company’s rise as the dominant American explosives manufacturer.
Chapter 4 — Two Crises (~lines –)
Two critical episodes: the powder-mill explosions that periodically devastated the Brandywine works, and the financial and operational crises that threatened the company’s survival in its early decades.
Chapter 5 — Pierre: Star of the Show (~lines –)
Pierre S. du Pont (1870–1954), the central figure of the family’s modern history. His education at MIT, his reorganization and modernization of the Du Pont Company after the 1902 crisis, the creation of the modern corporate structure, the expansion into chemicals, and the acquisition of a controlling interest in General Motors.
Chapter 6 — Two Brothers (~lines –)
Pierre’s brothers Irénée and Lammot du Pont, their roles in the company and the family, the division of responsibilities, and the dynamics of the fraternal partnership that ran Du Pont for decades.
Chapter 7 — Fathers and Sons (~lines –)
Generational relationships within the family, the pressures on du Pont sons to enter the family business, and the tension between dynastic expectation and individual ambition.
Chapter 8 — Pierre’s Other Relatives (~lines –)
The broader network of du Pont cousins and relations connected to Pierre S. du Pont’s branch, their roles in company and community, and the management of extended-family interests.
Chapter 9 — T.C. and Family (~lines –)
Thomas Coleman du Pont (T.C.), a cousin who was instrumental in the 1902 reorganization and later a U.S. Senator from Delaware. His branch’s history, political ambitions, and the 1920s conflict over family control.
Chapter 10 — The Rebel and His Relations (~lines –)
Alfred I. du Pont, the “family rebel,” who contested control after the death of the senior generation, fought legal battles over the family company, and built his own independent fortune in Florida banking and real estate.
Chapter 11 — Heirs of “the Boss” (~lines –)
The descendants of Eugene du Pont (the “Boss”), who ran the company in the late nineteenth century. Their inheritance, family position, and place in the expanded du Pont network.
Chapter 12 — A Diverse Branch (~lines –)
A lesser-known du Pont branch, their businesses and fortunes outside the main company, and the diversity of paths taken by family members.
Chapter 13 — The Underrated Victors (~lines –)
A branch of the family that built substantial independent success outside the central Du Pont Company narrative — their achievements, their relationship to the main family, and the family’s internal status hierarchies.
Chapter 14 — The In-Laws (~lines –)
The du Ponts who married into the family rather than being born into it — their roles, their acceptance (or lack thereof) in the dynastic structure, and the social dynamics of marriage into a closed wealthy family.
Chapter 15 — The Company (~lines 327–)
The Du Pont Company itself: its corporate structure, research and development, product diversification (explosives, paints, plastics, synthetic fibers — nylon, rayon, cellophane), the shift from a family-managed to a professionally-managed corporation, and the position of the family in the modern company.
Chapter 16 — A Way of Life (~lines 342–)
The social world of the du Ponts: chateaux-country estates, Wilmington society, the Brandywine landscape, charitable foundations, political influence in Delaware, and the texture of daily life in a family defined by inherited wealth and a shared name.
Appendix (~line 359 onwards)
Family charts and genealogical tables.
Coverage Guide
Gunpowder and explosives industry
Chapters 2–4 are the core material on the foundation of the du Pont powder mills, the early American gunpowder market, government contracts (War of 1812, Mexican-American War, Civil War), the transition from black powder to dynamite and smokeless powder, and the company’s quasi-monopoly position in American explosives by the late nineteenth century. This is the single most important source for the explosives and munitions industry in the early and antebellum republic.
Early national elite connections
Pierre Samuel du Pont de Nemours’s friendship with Thomas Jefferson, the family’s arrival during the Adams administration, their rapid integration into the early national scientific and political elite, and the role of French emigré expertise in early American industry.
War contracting and government relations
The War of 1812 contracts that established the du Pont powder works as a major government supplier, the Mexican-American War procurement, and the Civil War powder orders that transformed the company into the dominant American explosives house.
Corporate reorganization and management
Chapter 5 (Pierre S. du Pont) and Chapter 15 (The Company) cover the 1902 crisis and reorganization, the creation of the modern divisional structure, scientific management, research, and diversification. Pierre S. du Pont’s MIT education and systematic approach transformed a family powder business into a diversified chemical corporation.
Family dynamics, intermarriage, and dynastic identity
Chapters 7, 14, and 16, supported by the individual branch chapters, treat the social and psychological dimensions of du Pont family life: cousin marriage (a repeated pattern), the pressure on sons to join the company, the management of reputation and publicity, and the internal status competition between branches.
High-Value Passages to Mine

Lines 268–359: Table of contents — full chapter structure for navigation.
Lines 157–266: Preface — Gates’s access and perspective, the family’s cooperation, the existing literature on the du Ponts.
The Chapter 2 material: E. I. du Pont’s arrival on January 1, 1800, the Jefferson connection, and the founding of the powder mills.
The Chapter 3 material: the early powder business, War of 1812 contracts, antebellum expansion.
The Chapter 4 material: early crises and explosions at Brandywine.

Suggested Future Pages

E. I. du Pont — entity page on Eleuthère Irénée du Pont, founder of the gunpowder mills and patriarch of the American du Pont family.
Du Pont gunpowder mills — entity/concept page on the Brandywine Creek powder works, the technology of early American gunpowder manufacturing, and the company’s rise as a government contractor.
Pierre Samuel du Pont de Nemours — entity page on the physiocrat, politician, and Jefferson correspondent who brought the family to America.

Related Sources

Goodrich: A History of the United States (1823) — contemporary early republic context for the du Ponts’ arrival and Jeffersonian era.
Benton: Thirty Years’ View — Congressional and political context for the du Ponts’ government contracting and early national business environment.
McMaster: A History of the People of the United States, Vol. III (1803–1812) — the Jeffersonian and Madisonian political economy in which the powder mills were founded.

Notes on Scope
This is a late-twentieth-century popular biography by an insider, not an academic monograph. It is anecdotal and personal in approach and largely sympathetic to the family. Its value for this 1800–65 wiki lies in the detailed account of the family’s first sixty-five years in America — the French origins, the Jefferson connection, the foundation and growth of the powder business, War of 1812 contracting, antebellum expansion, and the establishment of the du Ponts as a dominant industrial family by the Civil War. Chapters 5 onward (post-1865 reorganization, General Motors, Christiana Securities, the 20th-century company) are primarily relevant to the United States 1866–1919 wiki.

sources/goodrich-history-united-states.title: [source] A History of the United States of America (Goodrich, 1823)
sources/goodrich-history-united-states.content:
A History of the United States of America (Goodrich)
Author: Rev. Charles A. Goodrich
Edition: Third Edition — Hartford: Barber & Robinson, MDCCCXXIII (1823)
Working text: Internet Archive plain OCR historyofuniteds00ingood (digitized 2010 with funding from the Institute of Museum and Library Services through an Indiana State Library LSTA Grant)
Raw extract: wiki/raw/goodrich-history-united-states.txt
Extract stats: 20,577 lines · ~146,899 words · 1,019,844 bytes
Overview
Rev. Charles A. Goodrich’s A History of the United States of America is a Hartford school and popular history of the early national republic, issued in its third edition in 1823 with engravings. The District of Connecticut copyright notice records deposit on the eighth day of March in the forty-seventh year of Independence under the title “A history of the United States of America, by Rev. Charles A. Goodrich, with engravings.” The work is built not as a continuous unnumbered narrative but as Eleven Periods, each “distinguished by some striking characteristic, or remarkable circumstance,” set out in a GENERAL DIVISION that opens the body and is then carried through running page heads of the form PERIOD … dates … topic.
Period I runs from the discovery of America by Columbus (1492) to the first permanent English settlement at Jamestown (1607) and is distinguished for Discoveries. Period II runs from Jamestown (1607) to the accession of William and Mary (1689) and is distinguished for Settlements of the original states. Period III covers the three colonial wars of King William, Queen Anne, and George II (1689–1756). Period IV is the French and Indian War (1756–1775). Period V is the War of the Revolution (Lexington 1775 to the disbanding of the army at West Point, 1783). Period VI is the formation and establishment of the Federal Constitution (1783–1789). Periods VII–XI are presidential administrations: Washington (1789–1797), Adams (1797–1801), Jefferson (1801–1809), Madison and the late war with Great Britain (1809–1817), and Monroe to “the present time” as of the early 1820s (text page heads PERIOD XI….1817….1822). A printer’s note at the close states that there are 400 pages in the work, plus 24 for plates not included, making 424 pages.
The raw file is continuous Internet Archive OCR (not Hathi leaf markers). Soft-hyphen line breaks and period-head OCR noise (PERIOD iII, PERIOD V1I, &c.) are common; the imprint period structure itself is stable.
Full Period-by-Period Breakdown
Period I — Discoveries (1492–1607)
From Columbus’s discovery through the principal Spanish, French, and English voyages along the eastern coast of North America down to the eve of Jamestown. Goodrich characterizes the period as little more than accounts of expeditions that discovered and more or less explored the principal countries along the Atlantic seaboard. Running heads mark PERIOD I….1492….1607….DISCOVERIES through the early leaves.
Period II — Settlements (1607–1689)
From the settlement of Jamestown to the accession of William and Mary. The text details settlements effected or attempted within the future United States, including wars with the natives, disputes between proprietors and colonies, and the formation of governments, as circumstances that “pertain to, and form a part of, the settlement of new countries.” It embraces the settlement of most of the original states—Massachusetts (including Maine), Connecticut, Rhode Island, New-Hampshire, New-York, New-Jersey, Pennsylvania, Maryland, Delaware, North and South Carolina, and Virginia. Colonial crises such as the Salem witchcraft prosecutions appear in late Period II / early Period III leaves (Cotton Mather’s Magnalia on the afflicted; nineteen executed; special court and release).
Period III — Three colonial wars (1689–1756)
From William and Mary’s accession to England’s declaration of war against France opening the French and Indian War (1756). Because the colonies remained attached to the English crown, they were thrice involved in wars between England and France while the French held Canada and were leagued with powerful Indian tribes; the colonies became the theatre of those operations. Goodrich therefore marks the period as most remarkable for the wars of King William, Queen Anne, and George II.
Period IV — French and Indian War (1756–1775)
From the 1756 declaration of war to the commencement of hostilities by Great Britain against the American colonies in the battle of Lexington (1775). Distinguished for the French and Indian War proper and the run-up to colonial resistance.
Period V — Revolution (1775–1783)
From Lexington (1775) to the disbanding of the American army at West Point, New York (1783). Distinguished for the War of the Revolution. This is the longest stretch of the book by bulk: continuous running heads PERIOD V….1775….1783….REVOLUTION carry campaign and political narrative through the war years to peace and demobilization.
Period VI — Establishment of the Federal Constitution (1783–1789)
From the disbanding of the army (1783) to Washington’s inauguration as President under the Federal Constitution (1789). Distinguished for the formation and establishment of the Federal Constitution. Running heads: PERIOD VI….1783….1789….ESTABLISHMENT OF [the Federal Constitution].
Period VII — Washington’s administration (1789–1797)
From Washington’s inauguration (1789) to John Adams’s inauguration (1797). Distinguished for Washington’s Administration. Early sections stress the inaugural religious language (“my fervent supplications to that Almighty Being…”) and the first business of the new government: revenue by impost and tonnage; executive departments (Jefferson State, Hamilton Treasury, Knox War, Randolph Attorney General); federal judiciary under John Jay with Rutledge, Wilson, Cushing, Harrison, and Blair; support of public credit.
Period VIII — Adams’s administration (1797–1801)
From Adams’s inauguration (1797) to Jefferson’s (1801). Distinguished for Adams’s Administration. The transition from Washington closes free navigation of the Mississippi and New-Orleans deposit, evacuation of British posts, and Mediterranean treaties with Algiers and Tripoli, shaded by French discontent. Section II opens on Washington’s recall of Monroe and despatch of C. C. Pinckney as minister plenipotentiary to adjust differences as France meditated depredations on West India commerce.
Period IX — Jefferson’s administration (1801–1809)
From Jefferson’s inauguration (1801) to Madison’s (1809). Distinguished for Jefferson’s Administration. Opens with Jeffersonian principles—freedom of religion, press, and person under habeas corpus and impartial juries—as the “creed of our political faith.” Section II marks the commencement of the administration by removals from responsible and lucrative offices. The period covers the Louisiana years, commercial restriction, and the approach of non-intercourse and war pressure through the end of Jefferson’s second term (embargo repeal and non-intercourse with France and Britain appear at the Period X hinge).
Period X — Madison’s administration and the late war (1809–1817)
From Madison’s inauguration (1809) to Monroe’s (1817). Distinguished for Madison’s Administration and the late War with Great Britain. Early leaves recount Erskine’s arrangement (orders in council of January and November 1807), the non-intercourse frame of March 1809, and the abrupt close of correspondence with Jackson (Erskine’s successor) for alleged insult. The bulk treats the war years—campaigns, the capture of Washington, and peace—under continuous PERIOD X….1809….1817 heads.
Period XI — Monroe’s administration (1817–1822)
From Monroe’s inauguration (1817) to “the present time” of the third edition (page heads through 1822). Distinguished for Monroe’s Administration. Includes Monroe’s tour examining fortifications and public institutions; the December message on national credit, lake naval reduction with Great Britain, and repeal of internal duties; Mississippi admitted as a sovereign state (11 December in the narrative); suppression of privateer and slave-trade establishments at Galvezton and related islands under Captains Henly and others; and later leaves on Illinois, Arkansas, Alabama, Missouri, and Florida in the index apparatus. Closes with index matter and the printer’s count of 400 text pages + 24 plate pages = 424.
Key Data Points

















































AttributeDetailAuthorRev. Charles A. GoodrichTitleA History of the United States of America. With Engravings.Edition / imprintThird Edition. Hartford: Barber & Robinson, MDCCCXXIII (1823)CopyrightDistrict of Connecticut deposit, 8 March, 47th year of IndependenceWorking textInternet Archive historyofuniteds00ingood (IA OCR stream)Raw filewiki/raw/goodrich-history-united-states.txtLines / words / bytes20,577 · ~146,899 · 1,019,844StructureGENERAL DIVISION + Eleven Periods (I Discoveries … XI Monroe 1817–1822); not numbered “chapters”Printer’s page count400 text + 24 plates = 424 (end note)SignificanceEarly national school history with a complete eleven-period frame from discovery through Monroe; dense on Revolution, first four administrations, and the War of 1812 for the wiki’s 1800–65 scope
Relationship to the Wiki
Goodrich supplies a single-volume, periodized national narrative written inside the early Monroe years—contemporary to the close of the War of 1812 settlement and the first Missouri-statehood generation—rather than a later multi-volume partisan history. It complements Hildreth’s denser constitutional-era narrative (vols. IV–VI in this batch) as a shorter school text with explicit period boundaries (Washington–Adams–Jefferson–Madison–Monroe) useful for entity and event scaffolding. It pairs with Irving’s western narratives and the Adams Memoirs / LOA Diaries as a popular New England imprint’s framing of the same federal decades.

sources/grant-personal-memoirs.title: [source] Personal Memoirs of U. S. Grant (Grant, 1885)
sources/grant-personal-memoirs.content:
Personal Memoirs of U. S. Grant
Author: Ulysses S. Grant (1822–1885)
First published: 1885–1886 (Charles L. Webster & Company; two volumes)
Working text: Global Grey 2020 Complete EPUB via Anna’s Archive (hash dabbfe7a91e87dbbfd6261696b11d945)
Raw extract: wiki/raw/grant-personal-memoirs.txt (pandoc plain from EPUB)
Extract stats: 28,241 lines · ~280,710 words
Overview
Ulysses S. Grant (1822–1885) wrote Personal Memoirs of U. S. Grant in 1885 while dying of cancer and under financial pressure after a business failure. The work was first published in two volumes by Charles L. Webster & Company; this working text is the Global Grey 2020 digital “Complete” edition (both volumes in one file) via Anna’s Archive (hash dabbfe7a91e87dbbfd6261696b11d945). Grant’s dedication is dated New York City, 23 May 1885. The memoirs cover ancestry and boyhood, West Point, the Mexican War, Pacific Coast service and resignation, private life at Galena, and the Civil War from Belmont and Fort Donelson through Shiloh, Vicksburg, Chattanooga, the Overland Campaign, Appomattox, and the closing operations against Johnston, ending with reflections on the armies, foreign policy episodes after the war, and the peace.
Grant states that he had long refused to write for publication until illness, the Century Magazine articles, and money need led him to continue the work as a continuous narrative of campaigns he directed or observed. He aims to describe events as he understood them, to do justice to subordinates, and to avoid mere controversy. Contemporary names and spellings in the extract (Spottsylvania, Haines’ Bluff, McLean’s house, &c.) are preserved as printed.
The pandoc plain extract is clean digital prose (not scan OCR), with modern Global Grey front matter and a machine table of contents before the dedication. Body structure: Dedication + Preface + Chapters 1–70 + Conclusion + Appendix (74 sections). Chapters 1–16 run from ancestry through the Mexican War, California, and Galena; Chapters 17–70 and the Conclusion carry the rebellion from 1861 to the grand review and postwar reflections. The Appendix opens with Grant’s official report of 22 July 1865 on operations of the armies 1864–65 and related documentary material referenced from the narrative.
Full Chapter-by-Chapter Breakdown
Dedication
These volumes are dedicated to the American soldier and sailor. Ulysses S. Grant, New York City May 23rd, 1885
Preface
“Man proposes and God disposes.” There are but few important events in the affairs of men brought about by their own choice. Although frequently urged by friends to write my memoirs I had determined never to do so, nor to write anything for publication. At the age of nearly sixty-two I received an injury from a fall, which confined me closely to the house while it did not apparently affect my general health. This made study a pleasant pastime. Shortly after, the rascality of a business partner developed itself by the announcement of a failure. This was followed soon after by universal depression of all securities, which seemed to threaten the extinction of a good part of the income still retained, and for which I am indebted to the kindly act of friends. At this juncture the editor of the Century Magazine asked me to write a few articles for him. I consented for the money it gave me; for at that moment I was living upon borrowed money. The work I found congenial, and I determined to continue it. The event is an important one for me, for good or evil; I hope for the former. In preparing these volumes for the public, I have entered upon the task with the sincere desire to avoid doing injustice to anyone, whether on the National or Confederate side, other than the unavoidable injustice of not making mention often where special mention is due. There must be many errors of omission in this work, because the subject is too large to be treated of in two volumes in such way as to do justice to all the officers and men engaged.
The first volume, as well as a portion of the second, was written before I had reason to suppose I was in a critical condition of health. Later I was reduced almost to the point of death, and it became impossible for me to attend to anything for weeks. I have, however, somewhat regained my strength, and am able, often, to devote as many hours a day as a person should devote to such work. I would have more hope of satisfying the expectation of the public if I could have allowed myself more time. I have used my best efforts, with the aid of my eldest son, F. D. Grant, assisted by his brothers, to verify from the records every statement of fact given. The comments are my own, and show how I saw the matters treated of whether others saw them in the same light or not. With these remarks I present these volumes to the public, asking no favor but hoping they will meet the approval of the reader. U. S. Grant. Mount Macgregor, New York, July 1, 1885.
Chapter 1 — Ancestry—Birth—Boyhood
My family is American, and has been for generations, in all its branches, direct and collateral. Mathew Grant, the founder of the branch in America, of which I am a descendant, reached Dorchester, Massachusetts, in May, 1630. In 1635 he moved to what is now Windsor, Connecticut, and was the surveyor for that colony for more than forty years. He was also, for many years of the time, town clerk. He was a married man when he arrived at Dorchester, but his children were all born in this country. His eldest son, Samuel, took lands on the east side of the Connecticut River, opposite Windsor, which have been held and occupied by descendants of his to this day. I am of the eighth generation from Mathew Grant, and seventh from Samuel. Mathew Grant’s first wife died a few years after their settlement in Windsor, and he soon after married the widow Rockwell, who, with her first husband, had been fellow-passengers with him and his first wife, on the ship Mary and John, from Dorchester, England, in 1630. Mrs. Rockwell had several children by her first marriage, and others by her second. By intermarriage, two or three generations later, I am descended from both the wives of Mathew Grant. In the fifth descending generation my great grandfather, Noah Grant, and his younger brother, Solomon, held commissions in the English army, in 1756, in the war against the French and Indians. Both were killed that year. My grandfather, also named Noah, was then but nine years old.
I then bought a work on algebra in Cincinnati; but having no teacher it was Greek to me. My life in Georgetown was uneventful. From the age of five or six until seventeen, I attended the subscription schools of the village, except during the winters of 1836–7 and 1838–9. The former period was spent in Maysville, Kentucky, attending the school of Richardson and Rand; the latter in Ripley, Ohio, at a private school. I was not studious in habit, and probably did not make progress enough to compensate for the outlay for board and tuition. At all events both winters were spent in going over the same old arithmetic which I knew every word of before, and repeating: “A noun is the name of a thing,” which I had also heard my Georgetown teachers repeat, until I had come to believe it—but I cast no reflections upon my old teacher, Richardson. He turned out bright scholars from his school, many of whom have filled conspicuous places in the service of their States.
I had as many privileges as any boy in the village, and probably more than most of them. I have no recollection of ever having been punished at home, either by scolding or by the rod. But at school the case was different. The rod was freely used there, and I was not exempt from its influence. I can see John D. White—the school teacher—now, with his long beech switch always in his hand. It was not always the same one, either. Switches were brought in bundles, from a beech wood near the school house, by the boys for whose benefit they were intended. Often a whole bundle would be used up in a single day. I never had any hard feelings against my teacher, either while attending the school, or in later years when reflecting upon my experience. Mr. White was a kindhearted man, and was much respected by the community in which he lived. He only followed the universal custom of the period, and that under which he had received his own education.
Chapter 2 — West Point—Graduation
In the winter of 1838–9 I was attending school at Ripley, only ten miles distant from Georgetown, but spent the Christmas holidays at home. During this vacation my father received a letter from the Honorable Thomas Morris, then United States Senator from Ohio. When he read it he said to me, “Ulysses, I believe you are going to receive the appointment.” “What appointment?” I inquired. “To West Point; I have applied for it.” “But I won’t go,” I said. He said he thought I would, and I thought so too, if he did. I really had no objection to going to West Point, except that I had a very exalted idea of the acquirements necessary to get through. I did not believe I possessed them, and could not bear the idea of failing. There had been four boys from our village, or its immediate neighborhood, who had been graduated from West Point, and never a failure of anyone appointed from Georgetown, except in the case of the one whose place I was to take. He was the son of Dr. Bailey, our nearest and most intimate neighbor. Young Bailey had been appointed in 1837. Finding before the January examination following, that he could not pass, he resigned and went to a private school, and remained there until the following year, when he was reappointed. Before the next examination he was dismissed. Dr. Bailey was a proud and sensitive man, and felt the failure of his son so keenly that he forbade his return home.
My sojourn in New York was shorter, but long enough to enable me to see the city very well. I reported at West Point on the 30th or 31st of May, and about two weeks later passed my examination for admission, without difficulty, very much to my surprise. A military life had no charms for me, and I had not the faintest idea of staying in the army even if I should be graduated, which I did not expect. The encampment which preceded the commencement of academic studies was very wearisome and uninteresting. When the 28th of August came—the date for breaking up camp and going into barracks—I felt as though I had been at West Point always, and that if I stayed to graduation, I would have to remain always. I did not take hold of my studies with avidity, in fact I rarely ever read over a lesson the second time during my entire cadetship. I could not sit in my room doing nothing. There is a fine library connected with the Academy from which cadets can get books to read in their quarters. I devoted more time to these, than to books relating to the course of studies. Much of the time, I am sorry to say, was devoted to novels, but not those of a trashy sort.
No, sir—ee; I’ll sell my shirt first!!” The horse trade and its dire consequences were recalled to mind. The other circumstance occurred at home. Opposite our house in Bethel stood the old stage tavern where “man and beast” found accommodation, The stableman was rather dissipated, but possessed of some humor. On my return I found him parading the streets, and attending in the stable, barefooted, but in a pair of sky-blue nankeen pantaloons—just the color of my uniform trousers—with a strip of white cotton sheeting sewed down the outside seams in imitation of mine. The joke was a huge one in the mind of many of the people, and was much enjoyed by them; but I did not appreciate it so highly. During the remainder of my leave of absence, my time was spent in visiting friends in Georgetown and Cincinnati, and occasionally other towns in that part of the State.
Chapter 3 — Army Life—Causes Of The Mexican War—Camp Salubrity
On the 30th of September I reported for duty at Jefferson Barracks, St. Louis, with the 4th United States infantry. It was the largest military post in the country at that time, being garrisoned by sixteen companies of infantry, eight of the 3rd regiment, the remainder of the 4th. Colonel Steven Kearney, one of the ablest officers of the day, commanded the post, and under him discipline was kept at a high standard, but without vexatious rules or regulations. Every drill and roll-call had to be attended, but in the intervals officers were permitted to enjoy themselves, leaving the garrison, and going where they pleased, without making written application to state where they were going for how long, etc., so that they were back for their next duty. It did seem to me, in my early army days, that too many of the older officers, when they came to command posts, made it a study to think what orders they could publish to annoy their subordinates and render them uncomfortable. I noticed, however, a few years later, when the Mexican war broke out, that most of this class of officers discovered they were possessed of disabilities which entirely incapacitated them for active field service. They had the moral courage to proclaim it, too. They were right; but they did not always give their disease the right name. At West Point I had a classmate—in the last year of our studies he was roommate also—F. T. Dent, whose family resided some five miles west of Jefferson Barracks.
Often since a fear has crossed my mind lest that book might turn up yet, and fall into the hands of some malicious person who would publish it. I know its appearance would cause me as much heartburning as my youthful horse-trade, or the later rebuke for wearing uniform clothes. The 3rd infantry had selected camping grounds on the reservation at Fort Jessup, about midway between the Red River and the Sabine. Our orders required us to go into camp in the same neighborhood, and await further instructions. Those authorized to do so selected a place in the pine woods, between the old town of Natchitoches and Grand Ecore, about three miles from each, and on high ground back from the river. The place was given the name of Camp Salubrity, and proved entitled to it. The camp was on a high, sandy, pine ridge, with spring branches in the valley, in front and rear. The springs furnished an abundance of cool, pure water, and the ridge was above the flight of mosquitoes, which abound in that region in great multitudes and of great voracity. In the valley they swarmed in myriads, but never came to the summit of the ridge. The regiment occupied this camp six months before the first death occurred, and that was caused by an accident.
I place my opposition to duelling on higher grounds than here stated. No doubt a majority of the duels fought have been for want of moral courage on the part of those engaged to decline. At Camp Salubrity, and when we went to New Orleans Barracks, the 4th infantry was commanded by Colonel Vose, then an old gentleman who had not commanded on drill for a number of years. He was not a man to discover infirmity in the presence of danger. It now appeared that war was imminent, and he felt that it was his duty to brush up his tactics. Accordingly, when we got settled down at our new post, he took command of the regiment at a battalion drill. Only two or three evolutions had been gone through when he dismissed the battalion, and, turning to go to his own quarters, dropped dead. He had not been complaining of ill health, but no doubt died of heart disease. He was a most estimable man, of exemplary habits, and by no means the author of his own disease.
Chapter 4 — Corpus Christi—Mexican Smuggling—Spanish Rule In Mexico
Corpus Christi—Mexican Smuggling—Spanish Rule in Mexico—Supplying Transportation. Early in September the regiment left New Orleans for Corpus Christi, now in Texas. Ocean steamers were not then common, and the passage was made in sailing vessels. At that time there was not more than three feet of water in the channel at the outlet of Corpus Christi Bay; the debarkation, therefore, had to take place by small steamers, and at an island in the channel called Shell Island, the ships anchoring some miles out from shore. This made the work slow, and as the army was only supplied with one or two steamers, it took a number of days to effect the landing of a single regiment with its stores, camp and garrison equipage, etc. There happened to be pleasant weather while this was going on, but the land-swell was so great that when the ship and steamer were on opposite sides of the same wave they would be at considerable distance apart. The men and baggage were let down to a point higher than the lower deck of the steamer, and when ship and steamer got into the trough between the waves, and were close together, the load would be drawn over the steamer and rapidly run down until it rested on the deck. After I had gone ashore, and had been on guard several days at Shell Island, quite six miles from the ship, I had occasion for some reason or other to return on board. While on the Suviah—I think that was the name of our vessel—I heard a tremendous racket at the other end of the ship, and much and excited sailor language, such as “damn your eyes,” etc.
When they gained their independence, after many years of war, it was the most natural thing in the world that they should adopt as their own the laws then in existence. The only change was, that Mexico became her own executor of the laws and the recipient of the revenues. The tobacco tax, yielding so large a revenue under the law as it stood, was one of the last, if not the very last, of the obnoxious imposts to be repealed. Now, the citizens are allowed to cultivate any crops the soil will yield. Tobacco is cheap, and every quality can be produced. Its use is by no means so general as when I first visited the country. Gradually the “Army of Occupation” assembled at Corpus Christi. When it was all together it consisted of seven companies of the 2nd regiment of dragoons, four companies of light artillery, five regiments of infantry—the 3rd, 4th, 5th, 7th and 8th—and one regiment of artillery acting as infantry—not more than three thousand men in all. General Zachary Taylor commanded the whole. There were troops enough in one body to establish a drill and discipline sufficient to fit men and officers for all they were capable of in case of battle.
Some of the houses were still standing. Goliad had been quite a village for the period and region, but some years before there had been a Mexican massacre, in which every inhabitant had been killed or driven away. This, with the massacre of the prisoners in the Alamo, San Antonio, about the same time, more than three hundred men in all, furnished the strongest justification the Texans had for carrying on the war with so much cruelty. In fact, from that time until the Mexican war, the hostilities between Texans and Mexicans was so great that neither was safe in the neighborhood of the other who might be in superior numbers or possessed of superior arms. The man we found living there seemed like an old friend; he had come from near Fort Jessup, Louisiana, where the officers of the 3rd and 4th infantry and the 2nd dragoons had known him and his family. He had emigrated in advance of his family to build up a home for them.
Chapter 5 — Trip To Austin—Promotion To Full Second Lieutenant—Army Of Occupation
When our party left Corpus Christi it was quite large, including the cavalry escort, Paymaster, Major Dix, his clerk and the officers who, like myself, were simply on leave; but all the officers on leave, except Lieutenant Benjamin—afterwards killed in the valley of Mexico—Lieutenant, now General, Augur, and myself, concluded to spend their allotted time at San Antonio and return from there. We were all to be back at Corpus Christi by the end of the month. The paymaster was detained in Austin so long that, if we had waited for him, we would have exceeded our leave. We concluded, therefore, to start back at once with the animals we had, and having to rely principally on grass for their food, it was a good six days’ journey. We had to sleep on the prairie every night, except at Goliad, and possibly one night on the Colorado, without shelter and with only such food as we carried with us, and prepared ourselves. The journey was hazardous on account of Indians, and there were white men in Texas whom I would not have cared to meet in a secluded place. Lieutenant Augur was taken seriously sick before we reached Goliad and at a distance from any habitation. To add to the complication, his horse—a mustang that had probably been captured from the band of wild horses before alluded to, and of undoubted longevity at his capture—gave out. It was absolutely necessary to get forward to Goliad to find a shelter for our sick companion.
On my return, I found that our application had been approved at Washington. While in the 7th infantry I was in the company of Captain Holmes, afterwards a Lieutenant-general in the Confederate army. I never came in contact with him in the war of the Rebellion, nor did he render any very conspicuous service in his high rank. My transfer carried me to the company of Captain McCall, who resigned from the army after the Mexican war and settled in Philadelphia. He was prompt, however, to volunteer when the rebellion broke out, and soon rose to the rank of major-general in the Union army. I was not fortunate enough to meet him after he resigned. In the old army he was esteemed very highly as a soldier and gentleman. Our relations were always most pleasant. The preparations at Corpus Christi for an advance progressed as rapidly in the absence of some twenty or more lieutenants as if we had been there. The principal business consisted in securing mules, and getting them broken to harness. The process was slow but amusing. The animals sold to the government were all young and unbroken, even to the saddle, and were quite as wild as the wild horses of the prairie. Usually a number would be brought in by a company of Mexicans, partners in the delivery. The mules were first driven into a stockade, called a corral, inclosing an acre or more of ground.
The animals cost but little in the first instance, and when picketed they would get their living without any cost. I had three not long before the army moved, but a sad accident bereft me of them all at one time. A colored boy who gave them all the attention they got—besides looking after my tent and that of a classmate and fellow-lieutenant and cooking for us, all for about eight dollars per month, was riding one to water and leading the other two. The led horses pulled him from his seat and all three ran away. They never were heard of afterwards. Shortly after that someone told Captain Bliss, General Taylor’s Adjutant-General, of my misfortune. “Yes; I heard Grant lost five or six dollars’ worth of horses the other day,” he replied. That was a slander; they were broken to the saddle when I got them and cost nearly twenty dollars. I never suspected the colored boy of malicious intent in letting them get away, because, if they had not escaped, he could have had one of them to ride on the long march then in prospect.
Chapter 6 — Advance Of The Army—Crossing The Colorado—The Rio Grande
At last the preparations were complete and orders were issued for the advance to begin on the 8th of March. General Taylor had an army of not more than three thousand men. One battery, the siege guns and all the convalescent troops were sent on by water to Brazos Santiago, at the mouth of the Rio Grande. A guard was left back at Corpus Christi to look after public property and to take care of those who were too sick to be removed. The remainder of the army, probably not more than twenty five hundred men, was divided into three brigades, with the cavalry independent. Colonel Twiggs, with seven companies of dragoons and a battery of light artillery, moved on the 8th. He was followed by the three infantry brigades, with a day’s interval between the commands. Thus the rear brigade did not move from Corpus Christi until the 11th of March. In view of the immense bodies of men moved on the same day over narrow roads, through dense forests and across large streams, in our late war, it seems strange now that a body of less than three thousand men should have been broken into four columns, separated by a day’s march. General Taylor was opposed to anything like plundering by the troops, and in this instance, I doubt not, he looked upon the enemy as the aggrieved party and was not willing to injure them further than his instructions from Washington demanded. His orders to the troops enjoined scrupulous regard for the rights of all peaceable persons and the payment of the highest price for all supplies taken for the use of the army.
As far as the eye could reach to our right, the herd extended. To the left, it extended equally. There was no estimating the number of animals in it; I have no idea that they could all have been corralled in the State of Rhode Island, or Delaware, at one time. If they had been, they would have been so thick that the pasturage would have given out the first day. People who saw the Southern herd of buffalo, fifteen or twenty years ago, can appreciate the size of the Texas band of wild horses in 1846. At the point where the army struck the Little Colorado River, the stream was quite wide and of sufficient depth for navigation. The water was brackish and the banks were fringed with timber. Here the whole army concentrated before attempting to cross. The army was not accompanied by a pontoon train, and at that time the troops were not instructed in bridge building. To add to the embarrassment of the situation, the army was here, for the first time, threatened with opposition. Buglers, concealed from our view by the brush on the opposite side, sounded the “assembly,” and other military calls. Like the wolves before spoken of, they gave the impression that there was a large number of them and that, if the troops were in proportion to the noise, they were sufficient to devour General Taylor and his army. There were probably but few troops, and those engaged principally in watching the movements of the “invader.
The supplies brought from Corpus Christi in wagons were running short. Work was therefore pushed with great vigor on the defences, to enable the minimum number of troops to hold the fort. All the men who could be employed, were kept at work from early dawn until darkness closed the labors of the day. With all this the fort was not completed until the supplies grew so short that further delay in obtaining more could not be thought of. By the latter part of April the work was in a partially defensible condition, and the 7th infantry, Major Jacob Brown commanding, was marched in to garrison it, with some few pieces of artillery. All the supplies on hand, with the exception of enough to carry the rest of the army to Point Isabel, were left with the garrison, and the march was commenced with the remainder of the command, every wagon being taken with the army. Early on the second day after starting the force reached its destination, without opposition from the Mexicans. There was some delay in getting supplies ashore from vessels at anchor in the open roadstead.

There were no possible means of obtaining news from the garrison, and information from outside could not be otherwise than unfavorable. Sometimes one would start to run, bowing his back and kicking up until he scattered his load; others would lie down and try to disarrange their loads by attempting to get on the top of them by rolling on them; others with tent-poles for part of their loads would manage to run a tent-pole on one side of a sapling while they would take the other. I am not aware of ever having used a profane expletive in my life; but I would have the charity to excuse those who may have done so, if they were in charge of a train of Mexican pack mules at the time.

The town is on a small stream coming out of the mountain-pass, and is backed by a range of hills of moderate elevation. To the north, between the city and Walnut Springs, stretches an extensive plain. On this plain, and entirely outside of the last houses of the city, stood a strong fort, enclosed on all sides, to which our army gave the name of “Black Fort.” Its guns commanded the approaches to the city to the full extent of their range. By a movement by the left flank Garland could have led his men beyond the range of the fire from Black Fort and advanced towards the northeast angle of the city, as well covered from fire as could be expected.
